one_line_idea: Confidence-based label cleaning entrenches the teacher's biases in the student: samples where the teacher is confidently wrong survive cleaning, creating a measurable self-confirmation loop.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Auto-label pipelines filter or fix labels using the labeling model's own confidence or a related model's agreement, so retained labels are exactly those consistent with the model family's beliefs, right or wrong.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cleaning by model confidence transforms unbiased-looking noise reduction into bias amplification: the cleaned dataset over-represents the teacher's systematic errors, and students trained on it show amplified versions of those same biases relative to students trained on raw noisy labels.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For teacher models with characterized systematic errors, students trained on confidence-cleaned labels will reproduce those errors at equal or higher rates than the teacher, while students trained on raw labels plus generic regularization will reproduce them at lower rates.
why_important: Bias amplification through data pipelines is invisible to standard metrics; if cleaning is an amplifier, widely deployed pipelines are quietly homogenizing model errors across the industry.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Confirmation bias is discussed in pseudo-labeling for semi-supervised learning, but quantified bias amplification through cleaning steps in auto-label pipelines may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Characterize a teacher's systematic error on a probe set, run confidence-based cleaning versus no cleaning on its auto-labels, train matched students, and measure error inheritance rates on the probe.
main_risk: Distinguishing inherited bias from independently learned bias requires probes where the correct answer is unambiguous and the teacher error is well characterized.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cleaning is assumed to move labels toward truth, since removed labels are demonstrably noisier on average.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Average noise reduction and tail bias amplification are compatible: cleaning removes random errors (where confidence is low) while preserving systematic ones (where confidence is high), shifting the error budget from benign to malignant.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one teacher with a known failure mode, clean its labels by confidence, and simply measure the failure-mode prevalence in retained versus removed labels; no student training needed for the first check.

judge_C_adversary.reason: Confidently-wrong survival and difficulty-correlated deletion are the two failure modes of one confidence-based-cleaning audit; a single kept/removed/downstream accounting tests both.

one_line_idea: The soft-versus-hard pseudo-label debate reduces to teacher calibration: soft labels win with calibrated teachers and lose with miscalibrated ones, and a calibration measurement predicts the winner per setup.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Distillation and self-training practice is split between soft teacher distributions and hard argmax labels, with contradictory published findings about which is better in which setting.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The value of soft labels is exactly the value of the teacher's uncertainty information, which is positive when calibrated and negative (misleading) when miscalibrated, so teacher calibration error is the moderating variable that reconciles the contradictory literature.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across teachers spanning a range of calibration quality (with temperature manipulations as controlled interventions), the soft-versus-hard student gap will correlate with teacher calibration, crossing zero near a measurable calibration threshold.
why_important: A predictive rule replaces trial-and-error in every distillation and self-training pipeline, and adds a concrete reason to calibrate teachers before auto-labeling.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temperature effects on distillation are known, but an explicit moderator analysis tying the soft-hard gap to measured teacher calibration may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix task and student, vary teacher calibration via recalibration and deliberate miscalibration, train soft and hard students per teacher, and regress the student gap on teacher calibration error.
main_risk: Calibration manipulations also change label entropy, a confounder needing entropy-matched controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Soft labels are generally assumed richer and better, with hard-label wins treated as anomalies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Soft labels transmit the teacher's confidence structure verbatim; transmitting a wrong confidence structure should be worse than transmitting none, making calibration the gate on their value.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One teacher, three temperature settings, six short student runs; the gap-versus-calibration trend is visible within two days.

one_line_idea: Most of what is booked as label noise in dense annotation is actually irreducible instruction ambiguity, and synthetic data with a single rendering convention trains models to be confidently wrong about genuinely ambiguous pixels.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Inter-annotator disagreement in dense labeling arises partly from mistakes and partly from pixels whose correct label is genuinely underdetermined by the annotation instructions, while synthetic renderers resolve every pixel deterministically by construction.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large fraction of dense-label disagreement is ambiguity rather than error, and models trained on convention-deterministic synthetic labels learn artificially low uncertainty on ambiguous regions, harming calibration and downstream decision quality on real data.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing disagreement on multiply annotated real data into consistency-resolvable error and persistent ambiguity will attribute a major share to ambiguity, and synthetic-trained models will show systematically overconfident predictions precisely on high-ambiguity regions compared to real-trained models.
why_important: Downstream consumers of dense predictions (planning, measurement, medical review) rely on uncertainty being honest exactly where scenes are ambiguous; convention-trained overconfidence is a safety-relevant defect invisible to accuracy metrics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotator disagreement is studied, but connecting synthetic-data determinism to region-level overconfidence on real ambiguity may be a new causal claim.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use multiply annotated real data to map ambiguity regions, compare confidence profiles of synthetic-trained and real-trained models on those regions, and test an ambiguity-injection remedy (stochastic label sampling in synthetic rendering).
main_risk: Separating ambiguity from correlated annotator error requires enough independent annotations per image, which limits usable datasets.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Disagreement is treated as noise to be adjudicated away, and deterministic synthetic labels are treated as the ideal endpoint of that adjudication.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the world genuinely underdetermines some labels, the correct target is a distribution, and deterministic supervision teaches a lie precisely where honesty matters most.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare confidence of one synthetic-trained and one real-trained public segmentation model on boundary bands versus interiors; overconfidence localization is checkable purely by evaluation.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: WAVE1 FLAG: wave1 family B-075/B-084 (ambiguity vs error decomposition); synthetic-convention overconfidence claim is the new element.

one_line_idea: Missing-annotation noise (unlabeled true objects treated as background) dominates wrong-label noise in detection training, and exhaustively labeled synthetic data makes the resulting precision-recall distortion worse, not better.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real detection datasets systematically miss some true objects, which training treats as hard negatives, while synthetic data labels every instance exhaustively; models are commonly trained on both without modeling the missingness difference.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant label-noise channel in detection is false negatives in real annotation, and mixing exhaustively labeled synthetic data teaches recall behavior that real-benchmark evaluation (scored against incomplete labels) then punishes as false positives, creating a structural precision-recall convention gap.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models trained with more exhaustive synthetic data will show apparent precision drops on incompletely labeled real benchmarks, a fraction of which will be revealed as correct detections by targeted re-annotation of their false positives, and missingness-aware losses will recover the penalized performance.
why_important: This means part of the measured sim-to-real detection gap is an evaluation artifact of benchmark missingness, and that a known-fixable loss modification is being left unused.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Missing-annotation effects are studied in isolation, but their interaction with exhaustive synthetic labels as a specific mixing pathology may be unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train detectors with varying synthetic fractions, sample their real-benchmark false positives for human re-verification, quantify the wrongly-penalized fraction as a function of synthetic share, and test unlabeled-aware losses.
main_risk: Re-verification is label-intensive and must be blinded to avoid annotator bias toward validating model outputs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Exhaustive synthetic labels are assumed strictly beneficial, and benchmark labels are treated as complete for scoring purposes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training and evaluation encode contradictory conventions about unannotated objects, and the model caught between them pays the price in measured precision.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually review a hundred false positives of one synthetic-heavy detector on a real benchmark and count genuine objects among them; an afternoon of inspection bounds the artifact size.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis after cross-shard dedup vs D+E+F and collision check vs the 248 wave-1 accepted ideas; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Synthetic-data quality filters are task-anticorrelated: filters tuned for classification-style aesthetics remove exactly the cluttered, occluded, hard scenes that dense tasks need most.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large-scale pipelines apply generic quality and aesthetics filters to synthetic and web data before training, and these filters were largely validated on classification or retrieval outcomes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Image properties that generic filters penalize (clutter, occlusion, motion blur, unusual viewpoints) are positively valuable for dense tasks, so a single quality scalar is a category error and per-task filter inversion improves dense-task outcomes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training dense-task models on filter-accepted versus filter-rejected halves of a synthetic pool will show the rejected half is competitive or better for detection and segmentation transfer, while the accepted half wins for classification-style probes.
why_important: One-size-fits-all curation is being institutionalized in data infrastructure; demonstrating task-anticorrelation would force task-conditional curation into pipeline design.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Filter ablations exist for classification outcomes, but a systematic task-conditional evaluation showing sign flips for dense tasks may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply a standard quality filter to a synthetic pool, train matched models for classification, detection, and segmentation on accepted, rejected, and random halves, and compare transfer per task.
main_risk: Rejected halves also contain genuine garbage (rendering failures), so the experiment needs a coarse validity screen to separate hard content from broken content.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher filter scores are assumed to indicate universally better training data regardless of downstream task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense tasks earn their keep on precisely the visual conditions that make images score poorly on aesthetics, so optimizing curation for cleanliness optimizes away the training signal for hardness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Score an existing synthetic detection dataset with a public quality filter and check whether per-image filter score anticorrelates with that image's contribution to hard-case performance via a quick influence approximation.

judge_C_adversary.reason: WAVE1 COLLISION: quality filters helping classification while removing what dense tasks need restates accepted C-102 (quality filtering helps some tasks, hurts others, hidden by averages) with a named mechanism and filter-inversion arm.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: ANOMALY: Quality filters anti-select dense-task value; the rejected half may train better — a category error in scalar quality. WAVE1 FLAG: wave1 collision risk C-102 (quality filtering helps some tasks, hurts others); dense-task filter-inversion prediction is the new element.

one_line_idea: The training value of a synthetic sample is predictable at generation time from generator-internal signals, enabling curation before rendering and saving most of the generation compute that post-hoc filtering wastes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Curation of synthetic data happens after generation: full images are produced, embedded, scored, and mostly discarded, so the compute spent generating rejected samples is wasted by design.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Generator-internal quantities available early in the sampling process (prompt statistics, early-step denoising trajectories, guidance disagreement, latent-space novelty relative to already-generated samples) predict post-hoc curation decisions well enough to skip generating most rejected samples.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A lightweight predictor trained on generator internals will anticipate the post-hoc filter's keep-or-drop decision with high agreement, and generation-time curation will match post-hoc-curated data quality at a substantially lower total compute budget.
why_important: Generation compute is the dominant cost of synthetic data at scale; predicting value before paying for full sampling changes the economics of every generative data pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Early-exit ideas exist for generation quality, but coupling generation-time internal signals to downstream training value for curation may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log generator internals for a large sample run, apply a standard post-hoc curation pipeline, train the internal-signal predictor, then compare students trained on generation-time-curated versus post-hoc-curated data at matched final dataset size and total compute accounting.
main_risk: Internal signals may predict image quality but not training utility, which depends on the existing dataset composition and the task.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Curation is conceptualized as a dataset postprocessing stage, separate from and downstream of generation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The generator computes rich information about each sample as a byproduct of producing it, and discarding that information only to re-estimate quality from pixels is an obvious inefficiency.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Check whether early-denoising-step statistics correlate with a post-hoc filter score over a few thousand samples; a correlation study requiring one generation run and no training.

one_line_idea: Embedding-coverage diversity metrics saturate long before task utility does, and compositional attribute diversity keeps paying after coverage metrics flatline, exposing a blind spot in curation dashboards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic dataset diversity is monitored with embedding-space coverage measures (cluster counts, dispersion, nearest-neighbor distances), which are known to compress compositional differences that embeddings represent weakly.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Beyond a modest scale, additional utility from synthetic data comes from compositional novelty (new attribute-object-relation combinations) that embedding coverage barely registers, so datasets tuned to maximize coverage metrics underperform datasets tuned for compositional spread at equal size.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Two synthetic datasets matched on embedding-coverage metrics but differing in controlled compositional diversity will produce measurably different downstream performance, with the compositional dataset winning on generalization probes involving novel combinations.
why_important: Curation dashboards drive large generation decisions; if their diversity axis is blind to what matters, teams are optimizing a saturated proxy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compositional generalization is studied for models, but the mismatch between coverage metrics and compositional utility of training data may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Procedurally generate datasets where embedding coverage and compositional spread are independently controlled, train matched models, and evaluate on standard plus compositional-generalization test suites.
main_risk: Fully decoupling the two axes is hard because compositional changes move embeddings somewhat; the design needs verification that coverage metrics are truly matched.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Embedding-space coverage is treated as a sufficient statistic for dataset diversity in curation practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Embeddings are trained to collapse task-irrelevant variation, and combinatorial structure is exactly the kind of variation that gets collapsed while still mattering for downstream generalization.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one generator, produce a prompt set with permuted attribute combinations versus repeated common combinations at matched embedding dispersion, and compare quick-probe performance after short training.

one_line_idea: For low-resource target domains, curating real web data to match a synthetic reference distribution beats curating synthetic data to match limited real samples, reversing the standard curation direction.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The standard pipeline treats real target data as the reference and adjusts synthetic data toward it, but in low-resource domains the real sample is tiny and unrepresentative, making it a noisy curation target.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A well-designed synthetic distribution can encode domain knowledge (coverage of conditions, balanced compositions) more faithfully than a small real sample encodes the true distribution, so using synthetic data as the reference to retrieve and filter abundant unlabeled web data yields better training sets than the reverse direction.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In domains with limited real data, a training set built by retrieving web images similar to a synthetic reference will outperform a synthetic set filtered toward the small real sample, at matched sizes, on held-out real evaluation.
why_important: Low-resource domains (industrial defects, rare medical conditions, minority geographies) are exactly where synthetic data is pitched; getting the curation direction right could matter more than generation quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Retrieval-augmented dataset building exists, but using synthetic data explicitly as the retrieval reference for real-data curation may be an unexplored inversion.
minimal_falsification_experiment: In a low-resource setting, build both directional pipelines from the same components (one synthetic reference, one small real reference, one web pool), train matched models on each output, and evaluate on genuinely held-out real data.
main_risk: The synthetic reference inherits its designer's blind spots, and a badly designed reference could systematically retrieve the wrong content with high confidence.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Real data, however scarce, is assumed to be the ground-truth reference that all curation should aim toward.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A tiny real sample is a high-variance estimate of the domain, while a synthetic distribution is a low-variance, possibly-biased one; in the small-sample regime the bias-variance tradeoff can favor the synthetic reference.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one domain, retrieve two web subsets using each reference and simply measure which subset's distribution better matches a large held-out real corpus that neither pipeline saw.

judge_C_meta.anomaly_note: Curating real web data to match a synthetic reference reverses the standard curation direction; nobody else inverts the arrow.

one_line_idea: Difficulty-based hard-example mining on synthetic pools preferentially selects generator failure artifacts rather than genuinely hard content, actively injecting shortcut features into training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Hard-example mining selects samples with high student loss, and on synthetic pools high loss arises both from genuinely difficult content and from generator artifacts (malformed objects, impossible geometry, corrupted text).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Loss-based mining cannot distinguish these two sources, and because artifacts are systematically weird, mining concentrates them, teaching students artifact-specific features and degrading real-data transfer relative to random selection at high mining rates.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Auditing mined subsets will show artifact rates far above pool average, and students trained on aggressively mined synthetic data will underperform random-selection students on real evaluations while outperforming them on synthetic held-out data, the signature of artifact overfitting.
why_important: Hard-example mining is a default tool being transplanted from real data (where high loss means hard) to synthetic data (where high loss often means broken), and the transplant may be silently harmful.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Artifact contamination of mined subsets seems unstudied as a distinct failure mode of curation on generated data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine a synthetic pool at several aggressiveness levels, audit artifact rates in the mined subsets, train students per level, and compare real-transfer against random-selection controls.
main_risk: Artifact identification requires human auditing or a detector whose own biases could distort the measured artifact rates.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] High-loss examples are assumed informative, and mining is treated as a free improvement over uniform sampling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On generated data, the loss ranks distributional weirdness, and the weirdest samples in a generator's output are its failures, not the task's frontier.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Mine the top-loss slice of one synthetic pool and visually audit a few hundred samples for artifacts; the artifact enrichment ratio is measurable in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Data-pruning conclusions invert with scale on synthetic pools: pruning helps at small training budgets and hurts at large ones, with a predictable crossover that current papers ignore by evaluating at single scales.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pruning studies typically report results at one or two dataset scales, while theory and scattered evidence suggest the value of keeping easy or redundant examples changes with the ratio of model capacity to data volume.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On synthetic pools, aggressive pruning improves results in data-rich-relative-to-capacity regimes but harms in capacity-rich regimes where models can exploit long-tail redundancy, producing a systematic scale-dependent sign flip with an estimable crossover point.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping training budget and pruning aggressiveness jointly will reveal an interaction where the optimal keep-ratio grows with budget, and pilot-scale fits will predict the crossover location at larger scales within useful tolerance.
why_important: Pruning recommendations derived at academic scales are applied at industrial scales; a sign flip means those recommendations could be exactly backwards where they matter most.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale-dependence of pruning is discussed theoretically, but a validated crossover-prediction protocol on synthetic pools may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one synthetic pool, grid over keep-ratios and training budgets, map the performance surface, fit the crossover, and validate the fit with one larger-budget run.
main_risk: The crossover may depend on task and architecture strongly enough that a single fitted law has little predictive reach.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A pruning method shown to help at benchmark scale is assumed to help at deployment scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The marginal value of a redundant example depends on whether the model has finished learning what it teaches, which is a function of scale, not a constant of the data.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two keep-ratios at two budgets on one pool (four runs) suffices to detect the interaction's sign.

one_line_idea: The optimal real-to-synthetic mixing ratio is predictable from gradient alignment between real and synthetic mini-batches measured early in training, eliminating expensive mixing-ratio sweeps.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners choose real-synthetic mixing ratios by sweeping full training runs, which is expensive and repeated for every new dataset, task, and architecture combination.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The utility of synthetic data at a given mixing ratio is governed by the geometry between real-data and synthetic-data gradients on the current model, so a short probe measuring gradient alignment across ratios early in training predicts the full-training optimum.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across dataset pairs and tasks, an alignment-based predictor computed from brief probe runs will rank mixing ratios with high agreement to full-sweep outcomes, selecting a near-optimal ratio at a small fraction of the sweep cost.
why_important: Mixing-ratio selection is a universal, repeated cost in synthetic-data adoption; a cheap predictor converts it into a fixed-cost measurement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-alignment ideas appear in multi-task and transfer learning, but a validated ratio-selection protocol for real-synthetic mixing may be absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several pairs, run full mixing sweeps as ground truth, compute early-training alignment statistics per ratio, and evaluate the predictor's ranking agreement and regret against the true optimum.
main_risk: Gradient alignment drifts over training, and early measurements may mispredict late-training dynamics, especially with learning-rate schedules.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mixing ratios are considered an empirical hyperparameter with no reliable shortcut other than sweeping.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If synthetic gradients conflict with real gradients, more synthetic data hurts regardless of volume arguments, and that conflict is directly measurable without finishing any training run.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one pair, compare the alignment-predicted ratio against a three-point sweep; agreement or disagreement is visible within a couple of days of compute.

judge_C_adversary.reason: Gradient-alignment prediction of the optimal mixing ratio targets the same quantity as F-097's fitted joint scaling law; competing instruments for one question belong in one study.

one_line_idea: Source-level scheduling (synthetic-then-real annealing) dominates example-level curriculum within synthetic data, so curation effort spent ordering synthetic examples is largely wasted.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Two scheduling ideas coexist: curricula over example difficulty within a dataset, and stage-wise schedules over data sources (pretrain on synthetic, anneal onto real), and their relative importance for synthetic-data training is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The performance-relevant scheduling decision is when to transition between synthetic and real sources, while within-synthetic example ordering contributes negligibly once the source schedule is right, because the domain shift dwarfs within-domain difficulty structure.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A factorial experiment crossing source schedules with within-source curricula will show large main effects for source scheduling, negligible effects for within-synthetic ordering, and no meaningful interaction, across tasks.
why_important: Curriculum design is engineering-heavy; knowing that only the source-level schedule matters would delete a whole work stream from synthetic-data pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both scheduling families are studied separately, but a direct factorial comparison in the synthetic-plus-real setting may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross three source schedules (mixed, synthetic-then-real, real-then-synthetic) with three within-synthetic orderings (random, easy-to-hard, hard-to-easy) and compare final real-data performance across the nine cells.
main_risk: The optimal source schedule may itself depend on the mixing ratio and total budget, complicating a clean factorial reading.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Curriculum benefits are assumed to be additive across levels, making example-level ordering worth engineering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The synthetic-real transition is the largest distribution change in the whole training trajectory, and optimization dynamics around large shifts plausibly dominate the small perturbations of example ordering.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare mixed versus synthetic-then-real schedules with random ordering only; if the source effect is small, the premise dies cheaply before running the full factorial.

one_line_idea: Influence-style valuation against a real validation set reveals that most of a typical synthetic pool has near-zero or negative training value, with the positive value concentrated in a small identifiable slice.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic pools are consumed wholesale or filtered by heuristics, and per-example contribution to real-data performance is rarely estimated because exact influence computation is expensive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The distribution of per-example value in synthetic pools is heavy-tailed and partly negative: a minority of examples drive the real-data gains, a majority are inert, and an identifiable subset actively hurts, so value-targeted selection can match full-pool training with a fraction of the data.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scalable influence approximations will identify a slice of the pool whose removal leaves performance unchanged or improved, and training on the top-valued slice alone will match full-pool training at a small fraction of the size, transferring across seeds and modest architecture changes.
why_important: If most synthetic data is inert, generation and training budgets are dominated by dead weight, and value-concentrated generation becomes the obvious next step.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Influence methods exist for real data; a systematic value-distribution characterization of synthetic pools with real-validation anchoring may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply a scalable influence approximation with a real validation anchor to one synthetic pool, characterize the value distribution, and run remove-and-retrain plus top-slice-only training to verify the causal reading.
main_risk: Influence approximations are noisy and model-state-dependent, and their errors could manufacture apparent heavy tails.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic data value is discussed at the dataset level, implicitly assuming examples contribute roughly uniformly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generators oversample their modes, so most samples repeat what the model already knows, while the informative tail and the harmful artifact tail both hide in the same low-density regions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Rank one pool with a cheap influence proxy, retrain without the bottom slice, and check for the predicted no-loss-or-gain outcome in two runs.

one_line_idea: Generative synthetic-data utility scales with distinct-prompt count, not image count: images-per-prompt beyond a small number is nearly wasted compute, making prompt engineering the real dataset-size lever.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic dataset sizes are reported in image counts, while generation pipelines produce many samples per prompt, and the redundancy structure between and within prompts is rarely analyzed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Within-prompt samples are so correlated that their marginal utility decays after a handful, so at fixed generation compute, spending on prompt diversity strictly dominates spending on samples-per-prompt, and the effective dataset size is closer to the prompt count than the image count.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched total image counts, datasets built with many prompts and few samples each will consistently outtrain datasets with few prompts and many samples each, and the utility curve versus samples-per-prompt will flatten after a small number.
why_important: This redefines the unit of synthetic-data accounting and redirects effort from generation throughput to prompt-space design, affecting cost models across the industry.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt diversity is intuitively valued, but a quantitative within-versus-between-prompt utility decomposition with compute-matched comparisons may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a generator and total budget, vary the prompt-count versus samples-per-prompt split across a grid, train matched students, and map performance over the split.
main_risk: Prompt sets differ in quality as well as count, so prompt sampling must be randomized from a fixed pool to isolate the count effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic dataset value is assumed to grow with image count, the number reported in every paper and product sheet.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conditional generators concentrate probability mass given a prompt, so within-prompt samples explore a tiny neighborhood, and information content grows with the number of neighborhoods, not the samples inside them.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two conditions (many-prompts-few-samples versus few-prompts-many-samples) at one budget with one student; the ordering is visible in two short runs.

one_line_idea: Procedural and abstract-image pretraining works by installing generic early-layer filters, so its benefit saturates at small scale and vanishes for foundation-scale models with long real-data training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pretraining on procedurally generated abstract imagery (fractal-like or formula-driven patterns) has been reported to help downstream vision tasks without any natural images, but the mechanism and its scaling behavior remain unsettled.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The benefit is confined to installing low-level filter structure that small models learn slowly from limited real data, so it shrinks as model scale, real-data volume, or training length grows, approaching zero in the foundation regime.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping model size and real-data budget will show the procedural-pretraining advantage decaying monotonically, and layer-wise transfer analysis will localize the surviving benefit to early layers whose filters converge to similar solutions regardless of initialization at scale.
why_important: Procedural pretraining is pitched as a data-rights-clean alternative to web pretraining; knowing its scaling ceiling determines whether that pitch survives contact with foundation-scale practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Procedural pretraining papers report positive results at modest scales; a systematic scaling study of where the benefit dies may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain on procedural data versus random initialization across a model-size and real-data grid, fine-tune identically, and map the advantage surface with layer-wise probing to localize the mechanism.
main_risk: Procedural-data recipes vary widely, and a weak recipe choice would understate the achievable ceiling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Procedural pretraining is discussed as a possible substitute for natural-image pretraining whose benefits could extend with better generation recipes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the value is generic filter installation, it is a fixed quantity that real data also provides given enough scale, so the two routes converge and the substitute framing collapses.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare procedural-pretrained versus scratch models at two model sizes with long real fine-tuning; the shrinking-gap trend is visible from four runs.

one_line_idea: Training students on generator-produced data is distillation, not discovery: it accelerates learning toward the generator's knowledge but cannot exceed it, and the ceiling is measurable.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic data from generative models is used to train students for capabilities the generator implicitly possesses, and papers sometimes imply the student can surpass what the generator's training distribution contained.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For distribution-level knowledge, generator-produced data acts as a compressed re-serialization of the generator's training distribution: students converge faster but asymptote at or below the generator-implied ceiling, with genuine exceedance possible only where an external signal (filtering by verifiable criteria, real labels) injects information the generator lacked.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Students trained on unfiltered synthetic data will asymptote below or at generator-matched capability across scales, while adding verifier-filtered selection will produce measurable exceedance, cleanly attributing any student-over-teacher gains to the external signal rather than to generation itself.
why_important: The field needs a clear account of when synthetic data creates capability versus merely transfers it; conflating the two inflates expectations for synthetic-only training loops.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distillation ceilings are understood for logits-based distillation; a controlled decomposition for image-generation-based training with verifier attribution may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a generator with known training distribution, train students on raw synthetic, verifier-filtered synthetic, and real data at matched budgets, and compare asymptotic performance against generator-derived ceilings.
main_risk: Defining and measuring the generator-implied ceiling is nontrivial and requires careful proxy tasks where the generator's knowledge can be independently quantified.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic data is often discussed as if scale alone could push students past their data-generating teacher.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Information cannot be created by resampling; only selection against an external criterion adds bits, so any exceedance must be traceable to the selector.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a small student on raw versus self-filtered synthetic data from one generator on a task with a checkable criterion, and test whether only the filtered arm exceeds the generator's own accuracy.

one_line_idea: Synthetic data helps foundation models where real data is thin: a density-targeted synthesis policy that generates in low-density regions of the real distribution beats uniform synthesis at equal budget.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic additions to pretraining corpora are typically generated broadly (generic prompts, uniform category coverage) without conditioning on where the real corpus is already dense versus sparse.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The marginal value of a synthetic sample is inversely related to real-data density at its location, so estimating the real corpus density and generating preferentially in sparse regions yields larger pretraining improvements than uniform or popularity-weighted generation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched generation and training budgets, density-targeted synthesis will outperform uniform synthesis on tail-heavy evaluations and match it on head evaluations, with the advantage growing as the synthetic fraction increases.
why_important: This gives synthetic data a principled role (tail densification) rather than a vague one (more data), and makes generation budgets much more efficient.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Targeted generation exists for specific known failure classes; a density-estimation-driven general policy for pretraining corpora may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate density over a real corpus in a fixed embedding space, generate synthetic data under uniform and inverse-density policies, pretrain matched models on each mixture, and evaluate with head-tail stratified suites.
main_risk: Generators are themselves weakest in low-density regions, so targeted generation may produce its worst samples exactly where they are requested.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic pretraining additions are treated as generic volume, with quality and diversity controls but no density conditioning on the real corpus.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In dense regions synthetic samples duplicate what exists; only in sparse regions can they change what the model sees, so uniform generation wastes most of its budget by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Generate two small synthetic sets (uniform versus inverse-density prompts) and fine-tune a pretrained model briefly on each mixture, comparing tail-slice metrics.

one_line_idea: Synthetic captions improve benchmark retrieval scores while quietly degrading robustness under distribution shift because they homogenize the text distribution that contrastive training consumes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Replacing noisy alt-text with model-generated captions improves standard contrastive-pretraining benchmarks, and the practice is spreading, while robustness evaluation of the resulting models is less systematic.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Generated captions occupy a narrower stylistic and semantic register than organic alt-text, and this text-side homogenization reduces the diversity pressure that gives contrastive models their distribution-shift robustness, creating a benchmark-robustness tradeoff invisible in standard reporting.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models pretrained on recaptioned corpora will beat alt-text models on in-distribution retrieval and classification while losing on shift-robustness suites, and the robustness loss will correlate with measured text-distribution entropy reduction.
why_important: If confirmed, corpus recaptioning trades away exactly the property (robustness) that made contrastive pretraining valuable, and the field is optimizing the visible half of the tradeoff.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Recaptioning gains are documented; the robustness cost and its mechanistic link to text-diversity collapse may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched models on the same images with organic versus generated captions versus mixtures, evaluate on in-distribution and shift suites, and correlate outcomes with text-side diversity statistics.
main_risk: Caption quality and diversity are confounded; mixtures and diversity-controlled caption generation are needed to separate them.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cleaner, more descriptive captions are assumed to be strictly better supervision for image-text pretraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Robustness in contrastive learning plausibly comes from the wild variability of natural supervision, and sanitizing that supervision removes the vaccine along with the noise.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare two public checkpoints differing mainly in caption source on a shift-robustness suite; if the tradeoff is absent there, the hypothesis weakens before any pretraining is run.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis after cross-shard dedup vs D+E+F and collision check vs the 248 wave-1 accepted ideas; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Rendering-based synthetic pretraining transfers to geometry-loaded tasks and not to semantics-loaded ones, and a task's geometry-semantics loading predicts its synthetic-pretraining benefit.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Graphics-rendered data has exact geometry but impoverished semantics (limited object identities, materials, and contexts), yet synthetic-pretraining evaluations aggregate over downstream tasks without characterizing what kind of information each task needs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Synthetic rendering pretraining installs geometric competence (depth, correspondence, contours) that transfers broadly, while its semantic content is too narrow to transfer, so the benefit across downstream tasks is predictable from a geometry-versus-semantics task decomposition.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a task battery, synthetic-pretraining gains will correlate strongly with a task's geometric loading (measured by how much frozen geometric features explain task performance) and weakly or negatively with semantic loading.
why_important: A predictive account of where synthetic pretraining pays lets teams decide per task without running the experiment, and clarifies what synthetic pretraining actually contributes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Task-transfer taxonomies exist, but an explicit geometry-semantics loading model validated as a predictor of synthetic-pretraining benefit may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched models on rendered versus real data, fine-tune on a battery of tasks with independently estimated geometry-semantics loadings, and test the predicted correlation pattern.
main_risk: Estimating task loadings independently of the pretraining conditions requires care to avoid circularity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic pretraining is evaluated as generically good or bad, with mixed results attributed to data quality rather than to task information structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Renderers produce exact geometry by construction and fake semantics by necessity, so the information they can install is structurally lopsided, and transfer should follow that structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one synthetic-pretrained and one real-pretrained checkpoint on one geometric task (depth) and one semantic task (fine-grained recognition) and check for the predicted crossover.
