one_line_idea: Test-time adaptation hyperparameters are implicitly tuned on the test distribution, making reported gains circular; shift-blind hyperparameter selection erases most of them.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation has no labeled validation data by definition, yet published methods report specific learning rates, momentum values, and update schedules that vary per benchmark.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The published hyperparameters encode oracle knowledge of the test shift, and under a rigorous protocol where hyperparameters must be fixed before seeing the shift, most methods lose most of their advantage over the unadapted baseline.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Selecting each method's hyperparameters on one shift family and deploying them unchanged on a different shift family will reduce average gains substantially and cause negative gains for some method-shift pairs. Falsified if: under shift-blind hyperparameter transfer (hyperparameters selected on one shift family, deployed unchanged on a different family), zero (0) method-shift pairs show negative adaptation gain (gain < 0 relative to the unadapted baseline), i.e. every tested method-shift pair keeps a non-negative gain.
why_important: If gains require knowing the shift in advance, the methods do not solve the stated problem, since knowing the shift in advance would allow far stronger interventions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Oracle model selection has been criticized in domain generalization, but an equivalent formal audit for the test-time adaptation literature, with cross-shift hyperparameter transfer as the headline protocol, may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a shift-blind protocol where hyperparameters are chosen on held-out synthetic shifts only, then evaluate several published methods on disjoint shift families and compare to their published-configuration results.
main_risk: Some gains may be genuinely hyperparameter-insensitive, so the audit must report per-method sensitivity rather than a single aggregate to avoid overclaiming.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers generally assume reported test-time adaptation gains would survive honest hyperparameter selection because the methods are described as unsupervised.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unsupervised objectives like entropy are known to be unstable to learning-rate choice, and instability plus per-benchmark tuning is the classic signature of oracle selection.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take two published methods, swap their per-benchmark hyperparameters across benchmarks, and check whether gains survive the swap on one backbone in a day.

one_line_idea: A frozen foundation model with a test-time nearest-neighbor or retrieval-augmented classifier matches gradient-based test-time adaptation at far lower risk.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Gradient-based test-time adaptation mutates model parameters on unlabeled data, which introduces collapse and drift risk, while nonparametric classifiers over frozen features can also absorb test-distribution information without touching weights.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Accumulating test embeddings in a memory and classifying by neighborhood vote or prototype update captures most of the benefit that parameter-updating adaptation achieves, because the useful adaptation signal is a shift in feature-space class geometry rather than in the features themselves.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On standard adaptation benchmarks with a strong frozen backbone, a memory-based nonparametric adapter will reach a large fraction of the gain of gradient-based methods while never degrading below the zero-shot baseline on any tested shift. Falsified if: the memory-based nonparametric adapter degrades below the zero-shot baseline (per-shift accuracy gain < 0 percentage points) on one or more tested shifts.
why_important: If true, deployments get most of the robustness benefit with a mechanism that is trivially reversible, auditable, and immune to weight collapse.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prototype and memory ideas exist in the literature, but a head-to-head risk-versus-gain comparison framing nonparametric adaptation as a safety-dominant substitute for gradient adaptation on foundation models may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement a streaming prototype or nearest-neighbor head over a frozen public backbone, compare against two gradient-based methods on the same shifts, and report both average gain and worst-case degradation.
main_risk: Memory-based methods depend on class balance in the stream, and heavily skewed streams could poison prototypes in a way that mirrors gradient collapse.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The field treats parameter updating as the substantive form of adaptation and nonparametric heads as weak baselines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With strong pretrained features, most shift-induced error is arguably in the classifier geometry, which is exactly the part a nonparametric head can fix without gradients.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one shift suite, streaming prototype head versus one entropy-minimization method, compare gain and worst-case drop in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Most of what test-time adaptation improves is calibration and decision thresholds, not representation quality, and a post-hoc output correction recovers the bulk of its accuracy gain.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation methods update internal parameters and report accuracy improvements under shift, but the mechanism of improvement is rarely decomposed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant effect of popular adaptation methods is equivalent to a shift-conditional rescaling and re-prioring of the output distribution, so a purely post-hoc correction that estimates test-class marginals and temperature achieves most of the same accuracy gain without touching features.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several methods and shifts, an output-layer-only correction pipeline will recover a majority of the accuracy gain of full adaptation, and the residual gain attributable to feature change will be small and shift-dependent. Falsified if: the output-layer-only correction pipeline (label-marginal + temperature fit on the same unlabeled test data) recovers <= 50% of the full-adaptation accuracy gain across the tested methods and shifts.
why_important: If gains live in the output layer, the field can replace risky weight surgery with cheap, transparent probability corrections and redirect research toward the genuinely hard residual.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mechanistic decompositions of where adaptation gains come from, separating output recalibration from representation change with matched-budget baselines, appear rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each method and shift, fit a label-marginal and temperature correction on the same unlabeled test data the method uses, compare accuracy gains, and measure feature-space movement to correlate residual gains with representation change.
main_risk: Estimating test-class marginals without labels is itself error-prone, and a weak estimator could understate how much of the gain is output-level.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation is assumed to repair internal representations damaged by shift, which is why parameter updates are considered necessary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Entropy-style objectives act most directly on logit sharpness and class priors, so the output-level interpretation matches the objective's actual gradient structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, three shifts, compare entropy-minimization gain to an unlabeled temperature-plus-prior correction on the same test batches in a day.

one_line_idea: Periodic hard reset to source weights beats sophisticated anti-forgetting machinery in continual test-time adaptation over long horizons.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Continual test-time adaptation methods add mechanisms like stochastic weight restoration and regularization toward source to prevent drift, adding complexity and hyperparameters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The entire benefit of these mechanisms is approximated by periodically resetting all adapted parameters to the source checkpoint, because the useful adaptation state is cheap to reacquire while accumulated drift is expensive to undo.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On long non-stationary streams, plain adaptation plus periodic reset will match or exceed dedicated continual-adaptation methods across most shift sequences, for some reset period spanning a wide tolerant range. Falsified if: plain adaptation plus periodic reset (at its best tested reset period) matches or exceeds the dedicated continual-adaptation methods' time-averaged accuracy on <= 50% of the tested shift sequences.
why_important: If a one-line baseline matches complex methods, the field's complexity is unjustified and evaluation practice failed to include the obvious control.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Reset appears as an ablation in some papers, but reset-period sweeps positioned as the primary baseline for the continual adaptation literature seem absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run two dedicated continual-adaptation methods and reset-augmented plain adaptation on standard corruption sequences and one natural drift stream, sweeping reset period logarithmically, and compare final and time-averaged accuracy.
main_risk: Reset timing may interact badly with abrupt shift boundaries, and an unlucky fixed period could strawman the baseline unless the sweep is wide.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Forgetting-prevention machinery is considered necessary because naive continual adaptation degrades, and reset is dismissed as wasteful.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation state for normalization-level updates is reacquired within tens of batches, so the amortized cost of resets is tiny compared to the compounding cost of drift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One corruption sequence, one continual method versus entropy minimization with three reset periods, compare time-averaged accuracy in a few GPU-hours.

one_line_idea: Episodic reset-per-shift evaluation protocols overstate test-time adaptation practicality, and realistic recurring mixed-shift streams reverse published method rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard protocols evaluate adaptation on one shift at a time, often resetting the model between shifts, while real streams interleave and revisit conditions such as day, night, and weather without announced boundaries.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method rankings are protocol-dependent, and under unannounced recurring mixed shifts, methods that look strong episodically will underperform simpler or memory-based approaches because their state management assumptions break.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing streams that interleave and revisit shift conditions will produce method rankings with low rank correlation to episodic-protocol rankings, and at least some published methods will fall below the never-adapt baseline. Falsified if: zero (0) published methods fall below the never-adapt baseline on the interleaved, revisiting mixed-shift streams.
why_important: Benchmark protocols function as the field's objective function; if the protocol rewards the wrong behaviors, the literature optimizes for scenarios that do not occur.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Continual adaptation benchmarks exist, but recurring-condition streams with unannounced revisits, explicitly designed to test state reuse, may be an unoccupied evaluation niche.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build recurring mixed streams from existing shift datasets with a hidden condition schedule, evaluate a representative method set, and compare rankings to the episodic protocol on identical underlying data.
main_risk: Stream construction choices such as revisit frequency could themselves determine rankings, so conclusions must be shown stable across schedule randomizations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Episodic per-shift results are read as predictive of deployment behavior on mixed streams.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Episodic protocols never test whether a method can exploit recurrence or recover from interleaving, which are the dominant structures of real drift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Interleave two alternating shift conditions into one stream, run three methods, check whether episodic winners still win, one day.

one_line_idea: Classical unsupervised domain adaptation methods built for weak backbones add approximately nothing on top of modern foundation-model features.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The unsupervised domain adaptation literature largely predates strong pretrained vision foundation models, and its methods were validated on backbones whose features were far weaker than current ones.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The gap those methods closed was a feature-quality gap, not a fundamental adaptation gap, so with a frozen strong foundation backbone plus simple target-side self-training, adversarial alignment and discrepancy-minimization methods provide no additional benefit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A re-evaluation of representative alignment-based methods on foundation-model backbones will show their marginal gain over source-only-plus-self-training shrinking to within noise on the majority of standard adaptation tasks. Falsified if: alignment-based methods retain a marginal gain over source-only-plus-self-training that exceeds run-to-run noise on more than 50% of the standard adaptation tasks (i.e. the predicted within-noise majority fails).
why_important: If backbone progress dissolved the problem the methods solved, ongoing method development on legacy benchmarks is misallocated effort, and the open problems lie elsewhere.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual observations of shrinking gains exist, but a systematic obsolescence audit of the adaptation method stack under modern backbones, with method families as the unit of analysis, may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix several standard adaptation dataset pairs, run source-only, self-training, and two classical alignment methods on both a legacy backbone and a modern foundation backbone, and compare marginal gains across backbone eras.
main_risk: Fair reimplementation of legacy methods on new architectures is nontrivial, and a weak port could unfairly deflate their measured contribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Alignment objectives are still presented as the core technology of domain adaptation, with the backbone treated as an interchangeable feature extractor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation features were trained on data spanning enormous visual diversity, so many benchmark domain gaps are plausibly already inside the pretraining envelope where no alignment is needed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One adaptation dataset pair, foundation backbone, source-only versus one adversarial-alignment method versus self-training, compare in a day.

one_line_idea: Marginal feature-alignment objectives actively hurt adaptation when source and target label distributions differ, and popular benchmarks hide this by having nearly matched label marginals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Aligning marginal feature distributions across domains is provably harmful when label proportions differ, since forcing marginals together must distort class-conditional structure, yet marginal alignment remains a default component.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard benchmark pairs have incidentally similar label marginals, which is why the harm is invisible; introducing controlled label-proportion mismatch will make alignment methods underperform source-only baselines with a severity that grows with the mismatch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Resampling target label proportions on existing benchmarks to create controlled mismatch will show alignment-based methods degrading below no-adaptation baselines beyond a modest mismatch level, while self-training degrades more gracefully. Falsified if: no tested marginal-alignment method falls below the no-adaptation baseline at any tested label-proportion mismatch level up to the maximum tested severity (zero method-x-mismatch cells with negative adaptation gain).
why_important: Real deployments almost never have matched label proportions across domains, so a failure mode invisible on benchmarks is a failure mode guaranteed in practice.

problem: [KNOWN FACT] Several classic adaptation benchmarks consist of everyday object categories across modest style gaps, a regime where zero-shot vision-language classification is now strong without any target data.

one_line_idea: Unsupervised model selection, not adaptation method choice, is the dominant source of variance in domain adaptation outcomes, and reported method gains are smaller than selection-induced spread.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Domain adaptation lacks labeled target validation data, so checkpoint and hyperparameter selection must use proxies, yet papers typically report a single selected result per method without quantifying selection uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The spread of target accuracy across defensible unsupervised selection criteria applied to one method's training run exceeds the typical published gap between competing methods, meaning the literature's method rankings are inside the selection noise band.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying several established unsupervised selection criteria to identical training runs of several methods will produce accuracy spreads per method that are larger than the median between-method gap reported on the same benchmarks. Falsified if: the accuracy spread across established unsupervised selection criteria applied to identical training runs does not exceed the median between-method gap reported on the same benchmarks (median per-method spread <= median between-method gap).
why_important: If selection dominates method choice, the field's real open problem is unsupervised validation, and method-ranking papers are measuring the wrong variable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Selection criteria have been compared in isolation, but a variance decomposition pitting selection spread against method gaps as the headline quantity may be new framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train several adaptation methods on several benchmark pairs, save dense checkpoints, apply a panel of unsupervised selection criteria, and decompose target-accuracy variance into method, pair, and selection components.
main_risk: The panel of selection criteria must be defensible and pre-registered, since including deliberately bad criteria would inflate the selection variance artificially.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers assume the selected checkpoints in papers reflect a solved or minor selection step rather than a major hidden degree of freedom.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unsupervised proxies correlate weakly with target accuracy in the shifted regime by definition of the problem, so large selection spread is the expected default, not the exception.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, one pair, dense checkpoints, three selection criteria, measure accuracy spread versus a published method gap, one day.

one_line_idea: Source data hurts more than it helps once a strong foundation initialization exists: source-free adaptation matches or beats joint source-plus-target training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard adaptation assumes simultaneous access to labeled source and unlabeled target data, while source-free variants adapt a source-trained model without source data and are usually framed as a constrained, weaker setting.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With a foundation-model initialization, continued training on source data anchors the model to source-specific decision structure, so removing source data during adaptation is neutral or beneficial rather than a handicap.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched-budget comparisons will show source-free pipelines equaling or exceeding joint training on a majority of benchmark pairs when both start from the same foundation initialization, reversing the presumed ordering of the two settings. Falsified if: source-free pipelines equal or exceed matched-budget joint source-plus-target training on <= 50% of the benchmark pairs when both start from the same foundation initialization.
why_important: Source-free adaptation is also the privacy-compatible and logistics-friendly setting, so evidence that it costs nothing would change default practice and data-retention requirements.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Source-free methods exist in volume, but a clean causal comparison isolating the marginal value of source-data access at fixed initialization and budget may not have been made central anywhere.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several benchmark pairs, fine-tune the same foundation initialization with and without source data in the adaptation phase at matched compute, using the same target-side machinery, and compare target accuracy.
main_risk: The result may hinge on how much source knowledge is already in the fine-tuned starting checkpoint, so the starting-point definition must be varied to check robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Source access is assumed to be strictly valuable, with source-free treated as damage control for when data cannot be shared.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information source data provides, task definition and class structure, is already captured by the initialization, leaving mostly its domain-specific biases as the marginal contribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two pairs, same initialization, adapt with and without source batches in the loss, matched steps, compare target accuracy in a day.

one_line_idea: A cheap a-priori adaptability score computed from foundation-model feature geometry predicts whether unsupervised adaptation will help, do nothing, or hurt on a given domain pair.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners cannot currently tell in advance whether running an adaptation method on a new domain pair will improve their model, and adaptation methods sometimes degrade performance.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Simple statistics of source and target embeddings under a frozen foundation model, such as class-cluster overlap and marginal distance decomposed into class-relevant and class-irrelevant directions, carry enough signal to predict the sign and rough magnitude of adaptation gain before any adaptation runs.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a broad grid of domain pairs and methods, a score fit on a subset of pairs will predict the sign of adaptation gain on held-out pairs well above chance, and its errors will concentrate on pairs with unusual label-shift structure. Falsified if: the adaptability score's held-out sign-of-gain prediction accuracy is at or below the chance rate (the majority-sign base rate of the held-out pairs).
why_important: A reliable go or no-go signal converts adaptation from a gamble into a decision procedure, which matters more for practice than another point of average accuracy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Transferability estimation exists for choosing source models, but pre-run prediction of unsupervised adaptation gain, as opposed to transfer accuracy, may be an unformalized problem.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble many domain pairs from existing benchmarks, run two adaptation methods on each to obtain ground-truth gains, compute candidate embedding statistics per pair, and evaluate held-out-pair prediction of gain sign and magnitude.
main_risk: The grid of available benchmark pairs is small and correlated, so the score could overfit benchmark idiosyncrasies and fail on genuinely new domain types.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Whether adaptation helps is treated as an empirical question answered by running the method, not something predictable from data statistics alone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation gain is bounded by how much recoverable structure the target embedding already contains, and that quantity is directly measurable from the embeddings themselves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten domain pairs, one method, three candidate statistics, check rank correlation between statistics and realized gains, two days.

one_line_idea: Adaptation methods developed on synthetic-to-real style gaps systematically fail on real-to-real shifts such as geography and time, because the two gap types have different structure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A large fraction of adaptation research validates on synthetic-to-real transfers, whose gaps are dominated by rendering statistics, while deployment shifts are usually real-to-real changes in geography, time, sensor, or population.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Methods tuned for rendering-gap transfer exploit low-level regularities absent in real-to-real shifts, so their ranking and even their sign of benefit fail to transfer from the synthetic-to-real regime to real-to-real regimes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A cross-regime evaluation will show low rank correlation between method performance on synthetic-to-real tasks and on real-to-real tasks, with some celebrated methods providing no benefit in the latter regime. Falsified if: every evaluated method provides positive benefit (adaptation gain > 0) on the real-to-real tasks (zero methods with no benefit).
why_important: If the field's main validation regime is unrepresentative, its accumulated method ranking is misleading for nearly all practical adopters.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both regimes have benchmarks, but a deliberate regime-transfer study of the method stack, framed around the structural difference between rendering gaps and real-world gaps, may be unclaimed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select methods spanning alignment, self-training, and image-translation families, evaluate each on matched synthetic-to-real and real-to-real tasks, and compare per-regime rankings.
main_risk: Real-to-real tasks vary widely among themselves, so several distinct real-to-real shifts are needed before concluding regime-level generality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Strong synthetic-to-real results are read as evidence of general adaptation capability rather than regime-specific fit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rendering gaps concentrate in textures and low-level statistics that translation-style methods directly model, while geographic shifts change object frequencies and layouts, which those methods do not touch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One translation-based method and one self-training method on one synthetic-to-real and one geographic-shift task, compare gain patterns, two days.

one_line_idea: Invariance-penalty methods fail on vision benchmarks because the annotated environments are not causally meaningful, and with environments constructed from capture metadata the same methods start working.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Invariance-penalty objectives assume environments that vary spuriously correlated factors while preserving causal structure, but vision benchmarks define environments by dataset provenance or style, which mixes many factors arbitrarily.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The reported failure of invariance penalties is an environment-quality failure rather than a theory failure, so re-partitioning existing data into environments aligned with plausible nuisance factors, such as capture hardware or acquisition context, will recover measurable invariance-penalty gains over plain training.

Falsified if: with metadata-based environment definitions on identical data, the invariance-penalty method fails to exceed plain training on one or more shifts aligned with the chosen nuisance factor (not consistently above).
why_important: The community may have discarded a correct principle because its benchmarks tested it with malformed inputs, which would be a costly false negative for the field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Environment-quality has been discussed theoretically, but a controlled same-data environment-swap experiment on vision benchmarks may not have been executed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick datasets with rich capture metadata, define provenance-based and metadata-based environment partitions of identical data, train invariance methods under both, and evaluate on shifts targeting the metadata factor.
main_risk: Metadata-based environments may correlate with labels, which would confound the comparison and require careful stratification.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Invariance penalties are widely considered empirically refuted for realistic vision tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The refutation experiments never satisfied the methods' stated assumptions, so the empirical record tests the benchmarks as much as the methods.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One metadata-rich dataset, two environment partitions, one invariance method versus plain training, evaluate on a metadata-aligned shift, two days.

one_line_idea: A leakage audit of the domain-generalization literature: quantifying how much of reported progress evaporates under strictly source-only model selection.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Model selection using held-out target-domain data leaks test information, the issue is documented, yet selection protocols in published papers remain heterogeneous and are often under-specified.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of claimed post-baseline progress on multi-domain benchmarks is attributable to lenient selection protocols, and re-selecting under a strict source-only rule will compress the published progress curve toward flatness.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Reproducing a sample of published configurations and re-running model selection under a strict protocol will reduce the median claimed improvement over plain training by a large fraction and flip the sign for some methods. Falsified if: strict source-only re-selection flips the sign of the claimed improvement over plain training for zero (0) of the reproduced methods.
why_important: The audit converts a known qualitative concern into a quantitative correction factor for the literature, informing how much trust downstream users should place in leaderboard progress.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The protocol critique is established; an executed quantitative audit across many published methods with a single strict re-selection may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select a representative sample of published methods with public code, re-run each under the strict source-only selection protocol on the same benchmarks, and report published-versus-audited gaps.
main_risk: Reproduction failures unrelated to selection could be misattributed to leakage, so each reproduction must first match the published number under the original protocol.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers assume reported gains would survive honest selection because the leakage issue is considered common knowledge that authors avoid.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Selection under shift is close to the core difficulty of the problem, so leniency there can manufacture nearly arbitrary apparent gains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two published methods with code, re-select strictly on one benchmark, compare against published numbers, two days.

judge_A_meta.master_note: adaptive-overfitting adjacency: C-032 measures test-reuse gains; G-029's object is selection-protocol leakage in the DG literature specifically.

one_line_idea: Frozen foundation-model embeddings with classical two-sample tests detect deployment distribution shift better than dedicated learned shift detectors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Production monitoring needs to detect when input distributions change, and the dedicated literature offers learned detectors, density models, and per-task calibration, all of which add training and maintenance burden.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The detection problem becomes easy in a good representation, so a frozen general-purpose embedding combined with classical multivariate two-sample statistics matches or beats specialized detectors across realistic shift types at a fraction of the operational cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a battery of natural and synthetic shifts at varying severities and sample sizes, the embedding-plus-classical-test approach will dominate specialized methods in detection power at matched false-positive rates for most shift types. Falsified if: the embedding-plus-classical-test approach achieves higher detection power at matched false-positive rate than the specialized detectors on <= 50% of the tested shift types.
why_important: Monitoring is deployed far more widely than adaptation, and a simple dominant recipe would set the correct default for industry practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pieces of this recipe are used ad hoc; a rigorous power-versus-sample-size comparison across shift families against the dedicated-method literature may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix shift scenarios with controlled severity, run the simple recipe and several dedicated detectors, and report power curves versus sample size at fixed false-positive rate.
main_risk: Power depends on which embedding is used, and a single embedding choice may not represent the recipe fairly across shift types.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shift detection is presented as requiring task-specific learned components, which is why dedicated methods keep being developed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two-sample testing in a representation that linearizes semantic variation is close to the statistically optimal reduction of the problem, leaving little room for specialized machinery.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One embedding, one kernel-based two-sample test versus one learned detector on three shift types, power at fixed sample size, one day.

judge_A_meta.tension_note: vs G-041: classical two-sample tests on frozen embeddings suffice for shift detection vs embedding statistics are dominated by low-level factors that mask semantic shift.

one_line_idea: Most distribution shifts flagged by monitoring systems do not harm accuracy, and harm-calibrated detection, not shift detection, is the correct monitoring objective.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Statistical tests detect any distributional difference given enough samples, including benign changes such as compression settings or camera upgrades that leave model accuracy unchanged, and every alarm consumes engineering attention.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In realistic deployment streams the majority of statistically detectable shifts are accuracy-neutral, so detectors optimized for distributional sensitivity have precision far below what harm-targeted detectors achieve at equal recall of genuinely harmful shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Instrumenting shift scenarios with ground-truth accuracy change will show weak correlation between statistical shift magnitude and realized harm, and a detector trained or calibrated on harm proxies will strictly dominate the precision-recall tradeoff of pure distributional detectors. Falsified if: a pure distributional detector matches or exceeds the harm-calibrated detector at one or more operating points of the harmful-shift recall versus false-alarm curve (strict dominance fails).
why_important: Alarm fatigue is the reported failure mode of monitoring in practice, and reframing the objective from shift to harm addresses the actual operational problem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The shift-versus-harm distinction is acknowledged in scattered places, but benchmark construction and detector evaluation centered on harm labels rather than shift labels may be largely unoccupied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build scenarios pairing each shift with measured accuracy change on labeled probes, evaluate distributional detectors and harm-proxy detectors on harmful-shift recall versus false-alarm rate, and compare curves.
main_risk: Harm ground truth requires labels under shift, which is expensive, so scenario coverage may be narrow and favor certain shift families.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detecting distribution change is treated as inherently valuable, with harm assessment deferred to human follow-up.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Statistical detectability scales with sample size without bound while harm does not, so the two objectives provably diverge as monitoring windows grow.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five shifts with known accuracy impact, one two-sample detector, check ordering of alarm strength versus realized harm, hours.

one_line_idea: Embedding-space shift detection is dominated by low-level image statistics, masking semantic shifts; band-separated tests are needed to see what actually changed.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Shift detectors operating on deep embeddings report a single shift score, while real changes decompose into low-level factors like compression and color and high-level factors like content and population, with very different operational implications.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard embedding statistics respond much more strongly to low-level factors than to semantic factors of equal harm, so a semantic shift co-occurring with a mild low-level change is detected as the low-level change and its semantic component goes unnoticed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In factorial scenarios crossing low-level and semantic changes, single-score detectors will show scores dominated by the low-level factor, while a decomposition that separates frequency-band and semantic-subspace components will recover both factors independently. Falsified if: in the factorial grid of low-level x semantic changes calibrated to equal accuracy harm, the low-level factor accounts for <= 50% of the single-score detector response (its main effect does not exceed the semantic factor's).
why_important: Monitoring that reports a shift but misattributes its nature triggers wrong responses, such as recalibrating a camera when the population changed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shift attribution into interpretable low-level versus semantic components, validated on factorial scenarios, may be missing from the monitoring literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a factorial grid of low-level transformations crossed with semantic composition changes, run standard detectors and the band-separated variant, and measure factor-recovery accuracy.
main_risk: The semantic subspace must be defined without circularity, for example from an independent model, or the decomposition validates itself.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A large embedding-shift score is read as indicating meaningful change, with the nature of the change left to manual investigation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-level statistics permeate every dimension of learned embeddings, while semantic differences concentrate in lower-dimensional structure, so magnitude-based scores are biased toward the former.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One dataset, apply compression change versus class-mixture change calibrated to equal accuracy harm, compare a standard detector's scores, hours.

one_line_idea: Anytime-valid sequential tests on foundation-model embeddings give deployment shift alarms with controlled false-alarm rates, which matters more in practice than the detection-power race.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployment monitoring is sequential, with decisions made continuously as data arrives, yet most shift-detection research evaluates fixed-sample tests that do not control error under continuous monitoring.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Martingale-based and conformal sequential tests over frozen embeddings provide practically sufficient detection latency while guaranteeing false-alarm control under continuous monitoring, and the lack of such control, not lack of power, is why practitioners distrust current detectors.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On simulated month-long streams with rare injected shifts, fixed-sample detectors re-applied repeatedly will produce false-alarm rates far above nominal, while sequential-valid methods will hold their guarantees with detection latency within a small factor of the fixed-sample optimum. Falsified if: repeatedly re-applied fixed-sample detectors realize false-alarm rates at or below their nominal level on shift-free month-long streams, or the sequential-valid methods violate their nominal false-alarm guarantee.
why_important: A monitoring alarm that fires spuriously every week gets ignored, so error control under continuous operation is the binding constraint for adoption.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Sequential testing theory is mature, but its combination with foundation-model embeddings and an evaluation centered on operational false-alarm budgets for vision deployment may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate long streams from existing datasets with controlled shift injections, run repeated fixed-sample tests versus sequential-valid tests, and report realized false-alarm rates and detection latencies.
main_risk: Sequential methods can be conservative, and excessive latency on subtle harmful shifts would undercut the practical argument.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The field's implicit objective is maximal detection power on fixed samples, with repeated-testing error treated as an implementation footnote.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Repeated testing without correction inflates false alarms mechanically, so any deployment using fixed-sample tests continuously is operating far from its nominal error rate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One simulated stream without any shift, repeated fixed-sample testing versus one conformal martingale, count false alarms over the stream, hours.

one_line_idea: Drift root-cause attribution, assigning a detected shift to interpretable factors via counterfactual reweighting in foundation-feature space, is more valuable and more tractable than drift detection itself.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] When monitoring flags a shift, engineers must manually determine what changed, whether capture conditions, content mixture, or population, and this diagnosis step has no standard tooling despite being where the operational cost lies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reweighting reference data to match the shifted stream within interpretable factor subspaces of a foundation embedding, and measuring how much each factor's reweighting explains the detected divergence, produces attribution that agrees with ground-truth causes in controlled scenarios.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On scenarios with known injected causes, the attribution procedure will rank the true factor first in a large majority of cases, including mixed-cause scenarios where it will approximately recover the mixing proportions. Falsified if: the attribution procedure ranks the true injected factor first in <= 50% of the known-cause scenarios (failing even a bare majority, the weakest reading of 'a large majority').
why_important: Attribution turns an alarm into an action, and automated diagnosis would remove the main human bottleneck in monitoring pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shift explanation appears in tabular settings; a factor-attribution framework over vision foundation features with counterfactual reweighting validation may be open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define factor subspaces for capture, content, and population using metadata or probe directions, inject single- and mixed-cause shifts into streams, and score the attribution against ground truth.
main_risk: Factor subspaces overlap in learned embeddings, and entangled factors may make clean attribution impossible beyond coarse categories.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection is treated as the scientific problem and diagnosis as an engineering afterthought left to manual inspection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information needed for attribution is already present in which embedding directions moved, so the problem is representation and bookkeeping rather than new statistics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inject a pure capture-condition shift, check whether reweighting only the capture subspace explains most of the divergence, hours.

one_line_idea: Dataset curation filters make benchmark test sets systematically easier than deployment data, and the curation-induced optimism is quantifiable by reconstructing the rejected data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark datasets are assembled with quality filters, deduplication, canonical viewpoints, and annotator-agreement requirements, all of which remove exactly the ambiguous and atypical inputs that deployments must handle.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The accuracy gap between curated test sets and uncurated streams from the same nominal distribution is large, model-dependent, and dominated by the curation filters themselves, so re-collecting data with filters removed provides a direct measurement of curation optimism.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating models on filter-relaxed re-collections matched for content category will show accuracy drops substantially larger than test-set resampling noise, with model rankings partially reordered relative to the curated sets. Falsified if: accuracy drops on filter-relaxed re-collections matched for content category do not exceed the test-set resampling noise band.
why_important: Curation optimism inflates every deployment forecast made from benchmark numbers, and quantifying it per filter tells us which curation choice does the damage.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Harder re-collections of specific benchmarks exist, but factor-attributed measurement of which curation filters cause how much optimism may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-collect data for a subset of classes with each curation filter selectively disabled, evaluate a model panel per condition, and attribute the accuracy gap across filters.
main_risk: Re-collection changes more than the intended filter, and time drift between original and new collection could confound the attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Curated test accuracy is treated as an unbiased estimate of performance on the underlying visual task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Selection on quality and agreement is selection on easiness, and conditioning a test distribution on easiness biases accuracy upward by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For ten classes, scrape fresh unfiltered images, evaluate one model against its curated-set accuracy on the same classes, one day.

judge_A_meta.master_note: curation family: C-058 (curation adds little), F-040 (quality filters anti-select dense value); G-049's reconstruct-the-rejected-data optimism measurement is the delta.

one_line_idea: Shuffling time-stamped datasets hides temporal drift; time-respecting splits materially change both absolute accuracy and model rankings on the same data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many vision datasets are collected over months or years and carry timestamps, but standard practice shuffles all data before splitting, destroying temporal structure and hiding any drift between collection and deployment eras.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training on early data and testing on late data from the same dataset will reveal consistent accuracy drops and ranking changes relative to shuffled splits, demonstrating that conventional splits overstate deployment performance even with zero nominal domain change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several timestamped datasets, time-respecting splits will show accuracy below shuffled splits by margins exceeding resampling noise, with the gap growing as the temporal distance between train and test windows increases. Falsified if: time-respecting splits show accuracy deficits versus shuffled splits that stay within resampling noise on the tested timestamped datasets.
why_important: Every deployment is a time-respecting split of reality, so shuffled-split benchmarks systematically overpromise, and the gap is measurable with data that already exists.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal splits are standard in some applied domains; a systematic audit across general vision benchmarks quantifying the shuffled-versus-temporal gap and its effect on model rankings may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify public vision datasets with usable timestamps, construct matched shuffled and temporal splits at equal sizes, train and evaluate a model panel on both, and report gap and ranking stability.
main_risk: Timestamps sometimes correlate with content or class balance changes, so drift attribution needs class-marginal controls to separate input drift from prior drift.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Within-dataset shuffling is treated as harmless because the data comes from one collection effort assumed homogeneous.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cameras, platforms, content trends, and photographic conventions all change within multi-year collection windows, so homogeneity across time is an assumption contradicted by how the data was produced.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One timestamped dataset, earliest-third training and latest-third testing versus shuffled equivalent, one model, compare accuracies, one day.

judge_A_meta.master_note: HIGH: time-respecting splits vs shuffled splits is family-adjacent to C-029 (benchmark aging) and is standard practice in time-series/recsys evaluation (known-practice risk, UNVERIFIED). Kept for the vision-benchmark ranking-change claim; novelty gate first-in-line.

one_line_idea: Realistic dependence structure in deployment streams breaks conformal prediction coverage for vision models, and the realized coverage gap is large enough to matter operationally.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage under exchangeability, and vision deployments violate exchangeability through temporal autocorrelation, bursts of related inputs, and feedback effects, yet conformal wrappers are promoted for deployment uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under realistic vision-stream dependence, realized coverage of standard conformal methods deviates from nominal by operationally meaningful margins in stretches that matter, such as during bursts, even when long-run average coverage looks acceptable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Replaying dependent streams built from real video, sessions, or temporally sorted data will show local coverage collapsing well below nominal during dependence bursts, with the deficit predicted by burst autocorrelation strength. Falsified if: realized local (sliding-window) coverage during dependence bursts stays at or above the nominal coverage level.
why_important: Users of conformal sets act on per-period reliability, and a method that holds on average while failing during exactly the correlated episodes when systems are stressed provides false assurance.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Non-exchangeable conformal theory exists; empirical quantification of local coverage failure on realistic vision streams, with burst-level analysis, may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct streams with graded dependence from video frames and session data, run standard and dependence-adjusted conformal methods, and report local coverage distributions rather than averages.
main_risk: Local coverage is itself a noisy quantity, and window-size choices for measuring it could exaggerate or hide the failures.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Conformal guarantees are perceived as distribution-free robustness that transfers to deployment with minor caveats.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The guarantee is conditional on exchangeability, which deployment streams violate structurally rather than marginally, and violated premises void the theorem exactly when correlations spike.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Calibrate conformal on shuffled frames, deploy on ordered video, measure coverage in sliding windows, hours.

judge_A_meta.master_note: HIGH: C-015 (conformal marginal coverage hides conditional failures under shift) is the accepted neighbor; G-053's delta is dependence/exchangeability violation in streams rather than conditional coverage.

one_line_idea: Shared-source structure within single datasets violates i.i.d. assumptions enough that cluster-aware resampling changes benchmark conclusions, not just error bars.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web-collected datasets draw many images from the same websites, photographers, and events, and both train and test splits inherit this cluster structure, potentially placing near-siblings across the split boundary.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-split sibling leakage inflates measured accuracy and compresses measured differences between models of different capacity, so cluster-aware re-splitting will lower absolute numbers and re-order some model comparisons, particularly favoring models that generalize rather than memorize source-specific signatures.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-splitting popular benchmarks by estimated source cluster will reduce accuracy for all models with the reduction correlated to model capacity, and will change the sign of some published pairwise comparisons. Falsified if: cluster-aware re-splitting leaves the accuracy of one or more models un-reduced, or flips the sign of zero (0) published pairwise model comparisons.
why_important: If split construction determines conclusions, benchmark results encode data-plumbing artifacts, and the fix, cluster-aware splitting, is cheap once the structure is estimated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Leakage studies exist for duplicates; systematic source-cluster re-splitting of standard vision benchmarks with conclusion-level impact analysis may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate source clusters via metadata and embedding linkage, re-split benchmarks with clusters kept intact, retrain or re-evaluate a model panel, and diff conclusions against original splits.
main_risk: Cluster estimation errors could either manufacture or hide the effect, so sensitivity to linkage thresholds must be reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Random splits are assumed adequate because obvious duplicates were removed during dataset construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deduplication removes near-identical images but not stylistic and contextual siblings from shared sources, which still carry predictive signatures models can exploit.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, group test images by domain-of-origin metadata, compare model accuracy on images with versus without training-split siblings from the same source, one day.

one_line_idea: Foundation-model robustness gains on shift benchmarks are largely pretraining-coverage effects, and an explicit coverage audit deflates claimed robustness to genuine novelty.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prior analyses have reported that pretraining data distribution, more than architecture or objective, drives out-of-distribution performance of image-text models, yet robustness results are still routinely presented as intrinsic model properties.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For most celebrated foundation-model robustness results, the shifted test distribution is well covered by pretraining data, and robustness measured against coverage-controlled shift strata will show ordinary, unremarkable degradation, reducing claimed robustness to a data-coverage bookkeeping fact.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Quantifying per-benchmark coverage of shifted test data under open pretraining corpora will explain the bulk of variance in effective robustness across benchmarks, and low-coverage strata will show degradation comparable to non-foundation baselines. Falsified if: pretraining-coverage scores explain <= 50% of the variance in effective robustness across benchmarks.
why_important: The distinction between being robust and having seen it before determines whether robustness transfers to genuinely new deployment conditions, which is the question buyers of these models actually have.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The data-centric explanation is established qualitatively; a quantitative coverage-stratified re-analysis of the standard robustness benchmark suite may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For open-corpus models, define coverage scores of shifted test sets under the pretraining distribution, stratify effective-robustness measurements by coverage, and test whether coverage explains cross-benchmark robustness variance.
main_risk: Coverage metrics based on embedding proximity are circular if the same model defines the embedding, requiring an independent reference model.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Foundation-model robustness is widely narrated as an emergent capability of scale rather than a reflection of what the pretraining crawl happened to contain.
why_it_might_be_wrong: No mechanism has been demonstrated by which a statistical learner outperforms on distributions it lacks exposure to, making coverage the default explanation until excluded.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One open-corpus model, coverage scores for two shift benchmarks, correlate per-class coverage with per-class robustness, one day.

one_line_idea: No robustness method Pareto-dominates across shift types, and shift-type profiles should replace single-number robustness leaderboards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness papers report averaged scores across heterogeneous shift collections, producing single-number comparisons and state-of-the-art claims that imply uniform superiority.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method gains are strongly shift-type-specific with pervasive trade-offs, so across a broad method panel virtually no method will dominate another on all shift families, and averaged leaderboards mask anticorrelated specializations.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A per-family re-analysis of published methods will show most method pairs exhibiting reversed orderings across at least one pair of shift families, and average-score leaders failing to lead in most individual families. Falsified if: <= 50% of method pairs exhibit an ordering reversal across at least one pair of shift families, or the average-score leader leads in >= 50% of the individual shift families.
why_important: Deployment involves specific expected shifts, and a profile tells a practitioner what to use, while an average tells them almost nothing and rewards benchmark-portfolio tuning.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Per-dataset numbers exist inside papers; a cross-literature dominance analysis formalizing the no-dominance claim may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble per-shift-family results for a broad method panel via reproduction, compute pairwise dominance relations across families, and quantify the prevalence of trade-offs.
main_risk: Reproduction noise could manufacture apparent trade-offs, so per-family differences must be tested against seed variance before counting reversals.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Averaged robustness scores are treated as a meaningful total ordering of methods, sustaining state-of-the-art claims.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Different shift families have close to orthogonal causes, and a single intervention improving all of them simultaneously would be mechanistically surprising.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five methods with published per-dataset numbers, build the dominance matrix across shift families, count reversals, hours with published data plus verification.

one_line_idea: Subpopulation-shift benchmarks overstate the availability of group labels, and under realistic group-label-free conditions the reported superiority of group-robust methods over plain training shrinks or vanishes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Group-robustness benchmarks supply annotated group labels for training or validation, and leading methods consume them, while real deployments rarely have reliable group annotation at any stage.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The advantage of group-robust methods is concentrated in their privileged access to group labels for model selection, so under a strict no-group-information protocol, including selection, their worst-group performance advantage over well-tuned plain training will largely disappear.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running benchmark suites under a no-group-labels-anywhere protocol will compress the gap between group-robust methods and plain training with strong regularization, with remaining differences within selection noise for most datasets. Falsified if: under the no-group-labels-anywhere protocol, group-robust methods retain a worst-group-accuracy advantage over strongly regularized plain training that exceeds selection noise on more than 50% of the datasets.
why_important: Practitioners without group labels need to know whether these methods offer them anything, and the benchmarks as configured cannot answer that question.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The role of group-labeled validation is acknowledged in parts of the literature; a strict full-pipeline no-group-information audit across the benchmark suite may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a protocol forbidding group labels in training and selection, re-run representative methods and strong plain baselines across standard subpopulation benchmarks, and compare worst-group accuracy distributions.
main_risk: Worst-group evaluation itself requires group labels, which is legitimate for measurement, but leakage through repeated evaluation-informed development must be guarded against.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Group-robust methods are believed to substantially beat plain training on subpopulation shift, as leaderboards configured with group labels indicate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Selection on worst-group validation accuracy is a powerful optimizer, and granting it exclusively to some methods is an uncontrolled advantage unrelated to their stated mechanisms.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, one group-robust method versus tuned plain training, both selected without group labels, compare worst-group accuracy, one day.

judge_A_meta.master_note: selection-privilege arm of the statistics family: group labels used for selection are the hidden oracle.

one_line_idea: The optimal adaptation learning rate under gradual drift is a function of measurable drift speed, and an adaptive-rate law derived from it beats every fixed-rate configuration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Online adaptation methods use fixed learning rates chosen by benchmark tuning, while drift in deployments varies in speed over time, and rate misconfiguration causes either lag behind the drift or noise amplification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] There is a stable functional relationship between drift speed, estimable from windowed embedding statistics, and the regret-minimizing adaptation rate, so a controller that sets the rate from estimated speed will approach oracle-rate performance across drift regimes without per-deployment tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across streams spanning slow, fast, and varying drift, the speed-tracking controller will match the best fixed rate in each regime and beat every single fixed rate on the mixed regime, approaching the oracle schedule within a small margin. Falsified if: one or more fixed adaptation rates match or exceed the speed-tracking controller on the mixed-drift regime.
why_important: Rate selection is the main deployment-blocking hyperparameter of online adaptation, and replacing it with a measurement-driven law removes the need for per-site tuning that no operator can perform.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Drift-adaptive step sizes exist in online learning theory; an empirically validated speed-to-rate law for deep vision adaptation with drift-speed estimation from embeddings may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate drift streams with controlled speeds, sweep fixed rates to map the oracle rate per speed, fit the speed-to-rate relationship, then validate the controller on held-out mixed-speed streams.
main_risk: Drift-speed estimation from embeddings may confuse drift with noise bursts, and a controller reacting to noise would amplify exactly what it should damp.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation rates are treated as method constants to be benchmarked once, rather than as quantities that must track a property of the environment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tracking theory in simpler settings makes the optimal rate scale with the drift-to-noise ratio, and there is no reason deep adaptation escapes that structural dependence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three drift speeds, five fixed rates, verify the optimal rate shifts with speed and a two-point controller interpolation beats fixed rates on a mixed stream, one day.

one_line_idea: Online adaptation methods are broken by realistic non-uniform arrival processes such as class bursts, and arrival-robustness should be a first-class evaluation axis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real input streams arrive with strong temporal structure, bursts of similar content, session effects, and diurnal cycles, while adaptation benchmarks feed methods class-balanced shuffled batches.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Popular adaptation methods implicitly rely on within-window class diversity, so realistic bursty arrival will cause prior-collapse updates and accuracy loss even with zero distribution shift, and method rankings under bursty arrival will differ sharply from shuffled-arrival rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Replaying identical data in shuffled versus bursty orders will produce large accuracy differences for adaptation methods but not for frozen models, with some methods degraded below the frozen baseline purely by arrival order. Falsified if: zero (0) adaptation methods fall below the frozen-model baseline under bursty replay of identical data.
why_important: Arrival structure is universal in deployment and free to simulate in evaluation, so ignoring it inflates reported reliability at no benefit.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporally correlated test streams appear in a few papers; arrival-order robustness as a systematic evaluation axis with burst-parameterized stress tests may be unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix datasets and shifts, replay streams under parameterized arrival processes varying burst length and class concentration, and measure each method's accuracy as a function of arrival parameters.
main_risk: Bursty replay changes the effective local distribution, so the analysis must separate arrival-order effects from genuine local-distribution effects with frozen-model controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shuffled arrival is treated as a neutral simplification rather than an assumption doing load-bearing work in reported results.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectives that sharpen predictions toward the recent window's statistics will chase bursts by design, and burst-chasing is indistinguishable from prior collapse at the update level.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, same corrupted data replayed shuffled versus sorted-by-class, compare accuracy trajectories, hours.

one_line_idea: Generic distribution-divergence measures do not predict transfer performance drop across domains, while cheap hypothesis-disagreement measures do, and the field keeps reporting the wrong quantity.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers routinely report input-space or feature-space divergences between domains as evidence of domain gap, implicitly suggesting these numbers relate to how much performance will drop, without validating that relationship.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Task-agnostic divergences correlate weakly with realized accuracy drop because they weight task-irrelevant variation, whereas disagreement between hypotheses trained or probed on the two domains tracks the drop closely, making disagreement the correct reportable statistic.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A meta-evaluation across many domain pairs will show task-agnostic divergence explaining little variance in accuracy drop while classifier-disagreement measures explain most of it, with the gap widest for visually dramatic but task-irrelevant shifts. Falsified if: classifier-disagreement measures explain <= 50% of the variance in realized accuracy drop across the domain-pair grid.
why_important: Practitioners triage adaptation effort using gap numbers, and if the standard numbers are uninformative, effort is being allocated by noise.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Theory relating disagreement to transfer exists; a broad empirical meta-evaluation ranking gap measures by predictive validity for modern vision models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a large set of domain pairs with measured transfer drops for fixed models, compute a panel of divergence and disagreement measures per pair, and rank measures by explained variance in drop.
main_risk: Disagreement measures need unlabeled target data and a probe-training protocol, and protocol choices could flatter disagreement unless standardized.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Feature-space divergence between domains is treated as a meaningful proxy for expected performance degradation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Divergence sums over all directions of variation while performance depends only on decision-relevant directions, so the correlation between them is structurally unprotected.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty domain pairs, one divergence and one disagreement measure against known drops, compare correlations, one day.

one_line_idea: The synthetic-to-real gap in super-resolution is dominated by unmodeled noise and compression, not by blur-kernel mismatch, so blind-kernel estimation attacks a second-order problem.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Super-resolution models trained on bicubically downsampled pairs degrade sharply on real photographs, and much of the blind-SR literature attributes this gap primarily to unknown blur kernels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Matching realistic sensor noise and compression statistics alone, while keeping a deliberately wrong bicubic kernel, recovers the majority of the synthetic-to-real transfer gap; kernel realism alone recovers only a minority share.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a factorial ablation toggling kernel realism, noise realism, and compression realism independently, the noise and compression factors will show larger main effects on real-photo restoration quality than the kernel factor. Falsified if: training with realistic noise plus compression while keeping the bicubic kernel closes <= 50% of the real-photo restoration quality gap to the fully realistic pipeline (equivalently, kernel realism retains the majority share of the gap in the 2x2x2 factorial).
why_important: Blind-kernel estimation is a large subfield; if kernel mismatch is second-order, research effort and model capacity should be redirected toward noise and compression modeling.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual pipelines ablate their own components, but a clean factorial attribution of the synthetic-to-real gap across kernel, noise, and compression with interaction terms may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched SR models on a 2x2x2 factorial of degradation realism (kernel, noise, compression), evaluate all eight on the same held-out real-photo set, and estimate main effects and interactions of each factor on restoration quality.
main_risk: Real degradations entangle the three factors, so a factorial synthetic design may fail to represent real interaction structure and understate the kernel effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Unknown blur kernels are treated as the central obstacle of blind super-resolution, with noise and compression handled as secondary nuisances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Consumer photos are dominated by in-camera denoising and compression whose artifact statistics deviate from training assumptions far more than mild optical blur deviates from bicubic.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one bicubic-only pretrained SR model against one trained with realistic noise plus compression but a bicubic kernel on a handful of real photos; if the second closes most of the visible gap, kernel mismatch is not dominant.

one_line_idea: Per-image single-kernel estimation in blind SR is a mis-specified problem because real point-spread functions are spatially varying and chromatically aberrated.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Most blind SR methods estimate one spatially uniform blur kernel per image, while real lens blur varies across the field of view and differs per color channel.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The residual error from forcing a single uniform kernel is larger than the error from moderate kernel misestimation, so improving per-image kernel estimators has hit a floor imposed by the uniformity assumption itself.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Restoration with an oracle spatially varying kernel field will outperform restoration with the best possible single uniform kernel by a margin larger than the spread among competing single-kernel estimators. Falsified if: the oracle spatially-varying-kernel restoration's quality margin over the best single uniform kernel is <= the quality spread among competing single-kernel estimators.
why_important: It would explain diminishing returns in kernel-estimation research and redirect effort to spatially varying degradation representations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spatially varying blur is studied in deblurring, but quantifying the uniformity-assumption floor specifically for blind SR pipelines may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate realistic field-varying, channel-dependent blur, then compare restoration quality using the oracle varying kernel field versus the optimal single uniform kernel fit, versus current estimators.
main_risk: For narrow-field crops the spatial variation may be negligible, making the conclusion crop-size dependent.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better single-kernel estimation is assumed to be the path to closing the blind-SR gap.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optical design guarantees corner-versus-center blur differences and lateral chromatic aberration in consumer lenses, so the single-kernel model is physically wrong for full frames.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fit a single kernel to synthetic field-varying blur and measure the reconstruction penalty of the fit alone; if the penalty exceeds typical estimator differences, the assumption is the bottleneck.

one_line_idea: Restoration models fail systematically on non-photographic content because both degradation models and image priors are photo-centric, and a content-type failure taxonomy would expose this blind spot.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration models are trained almost exclusively on photographs, while real usage includes scanned documents, screenshots, illustrations, maps, and rendered graphics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On non-photographic content, restoration models exhibit reproducible failure families (halo artifacts on flat-color edges, texture invention on smooth fills, font distortion) whose severity is predictable from the content type, and light content-type conditioning removes most of these failures.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A content-type-stratified evaluation will show failure rates on non-photographic classes that are multiples of photographic failure rates for the same models, and per-type adapters will close most of the gap. Falsified if: per-content-type adapters close <= 50% of the non-photographic-versus-photographic failure-rate gap, or stratified failure rates on non-photographic classes are below 2x the photographic rates (the minimal literal reading of 'multiples').
why_important: Non-photographic images are ubiquitous in practice (documents, UI captures), and their silent corruption by photo-centric restorers is a real product hazard.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Document-specific enhancement exists, but a unified failure taxonomy of general restoration models across content types may not have been built.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct degraded versions of documents, screenshots, and illustrations with known ground truth, evaluate general restoration models, and catalog failure families per content type.
main_risk: The taxonomy could fragment into endless subtypes, making the result descriptive rather than actionable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] General restoration models are assumed to degrade gracefully on non-photographic inputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both halves of the inverse problem (degradation model and prior) encode photographic statistics; on synthetic-flat content the prior injects photographic texture where none belongs, which is corruption rather than graceful degradation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Downsample and compress a text screenshot and an illustration, restore with a popular blind model, and inspect for invented texture and font damage; failures are typically visible on the first examples.
