one_line_idea: Classification-over-bins beats direct regression for dense continuous targets mainly because it bounds per-pixel gradient magnitude, so regression with matched per-pixel gradient clipping should erase most of the gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Discretize-then-classify target encodings (depth bins, quantized offsets) frequently outperform direct regression for dense prediction, and the standard explanation is that classification captures multimodality or richer supervision.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant active ingredient is gradient boundedness: cross-entropy over bins caps the per-pixel gradient regardless of error size, while L1/L2 regression lets outlier pixels dominate updates; on heavy-tailed targets this difference alone explains most of the gap, independent of any multimodality story.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Direct depth regression with per-pixel gradient clipping tuned to match the cross-entropy gradient-magnitude envelope will recover at least 60% of the (bin-classification minus plain-regression) delta1 gap on NYU Depth v2. Kill the idea if recovery is under 25%, or if bin classification retains its full advantage on a synthetic unimodal-target control where multimodality cannot be the explanation yet clipping-matched regression still loses.
why_important: Debunking the multimodality folklore in favor of a gradient-envelope mechanism tells practitioners they can keep simple regression heads (cheaper, no bin-design decisions) by fixing the optimizer side, and predicts exactly which target distributions need the fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Bins-vs-regression comparisons are common; the differentiation from this window's occupied idea W13-P1-B-024 (physical mixture fractions at boundaries) is explicit: this idea concerns gradient-envelope mechanics on arbitrary continuous targets, not physical mixing. The clipping-matched recovery design appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three arms on NYU Depth v2 (bins, plain L1, envelope-matched clipped L1) with matched backbones and schedules; log per-pixel gradient distributions to verify envelope matching; report delta1/AbsRel over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Adaptive bin methods entangle bin placement with encoding, so the comparison must use fixed uniform-in-log bins to isolate the envelope mechanism.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community narrative credits distributional expressiveness (soft targets, multimodality) for bin-classification gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ordinal structure loss in naive bin classification should hurt, yet bins still win; if the win survives envelope matching, the real mechanism may be the softmax's implicit temperature adaptation, not boundedness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ResNet-50 U-Net (torchvision, public) on NYU Depth v2 (public), 3 arms x 3 seeds, 8 epochs: about 1.5 days on one RTX 4090.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: target encoding (bins vs regression) with gradient-envelope matching
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: delta1 recovery fraction + gradient envelope statistics

one_line_idea: Bounded offset parameterizations in dense detection heads win over absolute-coordinate regression not for representational reasons but because they compress the target range into the optimizer's stable step-size band, so an LR sweep should rescue absolute coordinates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection heads regress normalized offsets relative to anchors, centers, or grid cells; folklore holds that absolute-coordinate regression is unlearnable, but the claim is almost never tested under matched tuning effort.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Offset parameterizations rescale the target distribution into a narrow numeric range, which co-adapts with default learning rates and initialization; absolute-coordinate failure is therefore primarily a step-size mismatch, and a proper LR/normalization sweep will close most of the gap on standard benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] FCOS-style training with absolute pixel-coordinate targets plus a 6-point LR sweep and target standardization will come within 2.0 box AP of the offset baseline on COCO. Kill the idea if the best absolute arm remains more than 5 AP behind, which would indicate a genuine representational advantage of relative encoding (e.g., translation-equivariant targets matching convolutional structure).
why_important: If the gap is mostly tuning, target-encoding design space for dense localization opens up (e.g., global coordinates useful for tracking or association heads); if the gap survives, this is clean evidence that equivariance-aligned targets matter beyond optimization, sharpening a widely repeated but untested folklore.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anchor-free papers ablate encodings under fixed LR; a tuning-matched adjudication between step-size and equivariance explanations appears missing. Distinct from occupied W13-P1-D-050 (mask-derived box targets), which changes supervision source, not coordinate parameterization.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train FCOS-ResNet-50 on COCO with (a) standard offsets, (b) absolute coordinates naive, (c) absolute standardized + LR sweep; report AP and per-scale AP over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Absolute targets break the fully convolutional weight-sharing assumption, so failure could reflect architecture-target mismatch rather than optimization, requiring a positional-encoding-augmented head as a control arm.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Relative offsets are considered obviously necessary, and absolute regression is dismissed without matched tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Translation equivariance is a strong structural prior; no LR schedule can substitute for targets the shared filters cannot express, so the 5 AP kill bar may trigger.
fastest_falsification_experiment: FCOS-R50 (public, mmdetection) on COCO (public) at 1x schedule, 8 arms total: about 4 days on one A100, or 1.5 days using a COCO-minitrain subset (public split) for the sweep and full COCO only for the final two arms.

one_line_idea: Softmax versus per-class sigmoid output parameterization in semantic segmentation determines whether co-occurring classes exchange gradients competitively, predicting opposite confusion dynamics for class pairs that frequently share boundaries.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation heads use mutually exclusive softmax or independent per-class sigmoids somewhat interchangeably (sigmoids especially in multi-label and open-vocabulary settings), with the choice rarely analyzed as a training-dynamics variable.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Softmax couples class logits so that every positive update for class A at a pixel is a negative update for class B, creating zero-sum dynamics concentrated at co-occurring class pairs; sigmoid decouples them. Therefore softmax training should show anti-correlated within-run fluctuations of confusable-pair accuracies and faster separation of frequently adjacent classes, while sigmoid should show independent drift and more inter-class leakage at shared boundaries.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For the top-5 co-occurring Cityscapes class pairs, the epoch-to-epoch correlation of per-class IoU fluctuations will be negative under softmax (mean r <= -0.3) and near zero under sigmoid (|r| <= 0.15), and sigmoid training will show at least 20% higher off-diagonal confusion mass restricted to adjacent-pair boundary bands. Kill the idea if fluctuation correlations do not differ by parameterization (gap < 0.15) or if confusion structure is identical within 5%.
why_important: It turns an arbitrary head-design choice into a predictable dynamics knob, with direct consequences for open-vocabulary and partially labeled settings where sigmoids are mandatory and the coupling loss must be replaced by something else.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Softmax-vs-sigmoid comparisons exist for final accuracy; the within-run anti-correlation signature and boundary-band confusion decomposition appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train SegFormer-B0 on Cityscapes with softmax and sigmoid heads, checkpoint every half epoch, compute per-class IoU trajectories and boundary-band confusion matrices, compare fluctuation correlation structure.
main_risk: Per-class IoU fluctuations are noisy at half-epoch resolution; distinguishing anti-correlation from evaluation noise needs many checkpoints and possibly multiple seeds, inflating cost moderately.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The head parameterization is considered an implementation detail that the loss and data dominate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Batch statistics and shared decoder features may couple classes far more strongly than the output nonlinearity does, drowning the softmax-specific zero-sum signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 (public, mmsegmentation) on Cityscapes (public), 2 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations with dense checkpointing: about 2 days on one A100.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: within-run per-class IoU fluctuation correlations + boundary-band confusion

one_line_idea: Supervising dense outputs in a frequency-decomposed basis lets one schedule which spatial frequencies are learned when, and this only changes outcomes under truncated training budgets, pinpointing spectral acquisition order as a budget-dependent bottleneck.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Networks fit low spatial frequencies before high ones (spectral bias), and dense-prediction outputs inherit this; practitioners compensate indirectly with long schedules or architectural tweaks rather than by controlling the supervision basis.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reweighting the loss in a wavelet or Fourier basis directly reallocates gradient across frequency bands, so a high-frequency-boosted schedule can pull forward detail acquisition; because the default ordering resolves itself given enough steps, the intervention's benefit should shrink to zero as budget grows, with a measurable crossover budget.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On monocular depth with a 25%-budget schedule, high-frequency-boosted supervision will improve high-frequency band error by at least 15% relative with under 3% interior/low-frequency degradation; at full budget the difference will fall below 3% on all bands. Kill the idea if short-budget high-frequency gains are under 5%, or if gains persist undiminished at full budget (which would falsify the budget-dependence claim, implying a permanent optimization barrier instead).
why_important: It converts spectral bias from a descriptive curiosity into a controllable schedule with a quantified regime of usefulness, directly relevant to anyone training dense models under compute truncation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency-domain losses exist in reconstruction niches; the budget-dependent crossover framing for dense prediction training dynamics appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train depth on NYU Depth v2 with standard vs wavelet-band-reweighted losses at 25%, 50%, 100% budgets; report band-resolved error (wavelet-decomposed residuals) and standard AbsRel at each budget.
main_risk: Band reweighting changes total loss scale and interacts with Adam's normalization; loss-scale renormalization per arm is required to avoid confounding with effective LR.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detail quality is assumed to be data- and architecture-limited, not schedule-limited, so frequency-scheduled supervision is not part of standard practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-frequency residuals are dominated by irreducible sensor noise in real datasets, so boosting them may amplify noise-fitting rather than pull forward genuine detail acquisition.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ResNet-50 U-Net (torchvision, public) on NYU Depth v2 (public), 2 loss arms x 3 budgets x 2 seeds: about 2 days on one RTX 4090; band-resolved evaluation is post-hoc on saved predictions.

one_line_idea: Dice loss is an implicit instance-size reweighting schedule whose strength grows as predictions sharpen, predicting that dice beats cross-entropy only when the target size distribution is heavy-tailed beyond a measurable threshold.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dice and cross-entropy dominate segmentation training and their relative merits are folklore (dice for imbalance, CE for stability), but no quantitative rule tells a practitioner which to use on a given dataset.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dice normalizes each structure's contribution by its predicted+true size, so per-pixel gradients scale inversely with structure size, and this reweighting intensifies during training as soft predictions contract toward the structure; dice-vs-CE outcomes are therefore governed by the tail exponent of the size distribution, not by class imbalance per se.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across datasets and resampled variants engineered to vary the structure-size tail (subsampling large instances), the dice-minus-CE gap will flip sign at a consistent tail statistic (within a factor of 2 across datasets), and time-resolved per-size gradient shares will show dice's small-structure share growing by at least 2x over training. Kill the idea if the sign flip point varies by more than 10x across datasets or if dice's gradient share is time-constant (within 20%).
why_important: It replaces the imbalance folklore with a testable size-tail law and a one-pass dataset statistic that predicts loss choice, and reveals that the loss embeds a hidden curriculum whose strength practitioners never scheduled deliberately.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dice gradient analyses exist for medical imbalance; the time-intensifying reweighting dynamics and cross-dataset sign-flip law appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train U-Net/DeepLabv3+ on Cityscapes instances and a resampled-size-tail variant with dice vs CE; log per-size-decile gradient shares over training; locate the gap sign flip as a function of tail statistic.
main_risk: Dice's batch-level formulation differs across codebases (per-image vs per-batch normalization), which changes the reweighting math and must be fixed and reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dice is preferred whenever foreground is rare, a class-imbalance story that ignores size-distribution shape and training-time dynamics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gap may be dominated by dice's different treatment of empty predictions (denominator instability), a numerical artifact independent of size tails.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ ResNet-50 (mmsegmentation, public) on Cityscapes (public) plus two size-resampled variants, 2 losses x 3 datasets x 2 seeds at 20k iterations: about 2.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Structured surrogate losses like Lovász hinge help exactly when a model's errors are spatially clustered, because their pixel-gradient coupling coordinates updates within an error blob, predicting the gain from a pre-training error-autocorrelation measurement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Lovász-softmax and similar IoU surrogates beat cross-entropy in some segmentation setups and not others, and the community has no account of which setups benefit.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] These losses couple gradients across pixels of the same class within an image (through the sorted-error construction), effectively making coordinated blob-level corrections; when errors are spatially independent the coupling adds variance without benefit, so the spatial autocorrelation length of the error field determines the sign of the effect.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 8 model-dataset configurations, the Lovász-minus-CE mIoU gap will correlate with pre-measured error autocorrelation length at Spearman rho >= 0.6, and configurations with autocorrelation below 4 pixels will show gaps within +-0.3 mIoU. Kill the idea if rho < 0.25 or if spatially-shuffled-error controls (patch-permuted training images) preserve the Lovász advantage, which would locate the mechanism elsewhere.
why_important: It converts an unreliable loss-choice folklore into a cheap pre-measurement rule and identifies gradient coupling, not metric alignment, as the operative property of structured surrogates.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Lovász losses are motivated as IoU surrogates (metric alignment); the error-autocorrelation moderator and the coupling mechanism appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 8 public segmentation configs spanning CNN/transformer and two datasets; measure baseline error autocorrelation; retrain each with Lovász; correlate gap with autocorrelation; add one patch-permuted control.
main_risk: Error autocorrelation and dataset identity are confounded; the resampled and permuted controls are essential to break the confound, adding arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Structured surrogates are believed to help because they optimize the evaluation metric more directly, implying dataset-independent gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The sorted-error construction also changes the effective example weighting (hardest pixels dominate), which is an OHEM-like mechanism that could explain gains without any spatial-coupling story.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 and DeepLabv3+ (both public) on Cityscapes and ADE20K (public), 8 configs x 2 losses at short 20k schedules: about 4 days on one A100; autocorrelation measurement is post-hoc on saved logits.

one_line_idea: Focal loss is functionally an annealed hard-pixel selection schedule: replacing it with explicit top-k pixel selection whose k follows focal's shrinking effective-support trajectory should reproduce its gains, killing the reweighting-form story.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Focal loss is the default for dense detection and many segmentation setups, credited to its specific polynomial down-weighting form; countless variants tweak the form.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] What matters is not the weighting form but the induced trajectory of effective support: as the model improves, the fraction of pixels with non-negligible focal gradient shrinks, making focal an automatic anneal from all-pixel to hard-pixel training; any selection scheme matching that support trajectory will match focal.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Explicit top-k cross-entropy with k(t) matched to focal's measured effective-support trajectory will come within 0.3 AP of focal on COCO with RetinaNet, while fixed-k arms will lose at least 1.0 AP, establishing the trajectory (not the form) as the active ingredient. Kill the idea if trajectory-matched top-k lags focal by more than 1.0 AP, which would mean the soft weighting form carries independent value.
why_important: A positive result collapses the focal-variant cottage industry into a single scheduling principle and gives a knob (support trajectory) that can be designed directly instead of through loss-form tinkering.

one_line_idea: Class-frequency loss reweighting interacts destructively with momentum: rare-class gradient bursts get smeared into subsequent unrelated batches, so reweighting gains should shrink as momentum grows, an interaction nobody tunes for.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Loss reweighting and momentum are both ancient, but their interaction through burst timing appears unmeasured in dense prediction.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reweighting strength and momentum are treated as orthogonal hyperparameters with no interaction worth reporting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Momentum smearing may actually help rare classes by extending their effective presence across steps (a mild replay), making the interaction positive rather than destructive.

one_line_idea: Whether combining two dense losses helps is determined by the spatial structure of their per-pixel gradient disagreement: structured disagreement (different losses own different pixel populations) yields complementary gains, diffuse disagreement yields averaging.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Compound losses (e.g., CE+dice) are ubiquitous defaults in dense prediction, yet combination outcomes vary by task and no principle distinguishes complementary pairs from redundant or conflicting ones.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-conflict analyses exist for multi-task learning across tasks; applying population-structured conflict analysis to same-task loss combination appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 10 documented loss pairs, measure disagreement structure on a half-epoch probe run, then train all singles and combinations to convergence and test whether the index predicts synergy sign.
main_risk: Defining pixel populations (boundary bands, size classes, frequency bands) involves choices; pre-registering three population partitions and requiring consistency guards against index shopping.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Compound losses are assumed beneficial by default (belt and suspenders), with failures attributed to weighting rather than structural redundancy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synergy might be driven by optimization-trajectory effects (early-phase stabilization) that a static disagreement snapshot cannot capture, requiring trajectory-resolved measurement.

one_line_idea: Temperature in pixel-level contrastive objectives sets the effective number of negatives that receive gradient, and the right temperature is determined by the intra-class visual diversity of the dataset, predicting opposite tuning directions for homogeneous versus diverse datasets.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temperature analyses exist for image-level contrastive learning; the dense-specific same-class contamination account with a diversity-conditioned tuning law appears new.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The trick is established practice; its time-constant account and budget-independence prediction appear untested.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The mean criterion is dominated by frequent classes that peak (and start overfitting) early, so the selected checkpoint predates rare-class convergence by a margin that grows with acquisition stagger; selecting per-class-optimal checkpoints (or stopping on a stagger-aware criterion) recovers rare-class accuracy at negligible frequent-class cost because their overfitting slope is shallow.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Staggered class learning is folk-observed; quantifying the stopping-rule tax and the recovery from stagger-aware selection appears new.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Connectivity studies concentrate on classification and pretraining; time-resolved basin-exit comparison across task types on matched backbones appears new.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Fine-tuning is assumed to stay near init (motivating merging/averaging practices) regardless of task type.

one_line_idea: Within-class appearance variance, not class frequency, is the dominant determinant of when a class is acquired during segmentation training, inverting the standard imbalance-centric account of late learners.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Some classes are learned much later than others in dense training, and lateness is conventionally attributed to class rarity, motivating frequency-based reweighting and sampling remedies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Acquisition time is governed by how many distinct appearance modes a class spans (its within-class feature variance): a rare but visually homogeneous class is learned quickly, while a frequent but heterogeneous class lags; frequency matters only through exposure count per appearance mode, so variance-per-exposure is the real clock.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across Cityscapes and ADE20K, partial correlation of class acquisition epoch (first epoch reaching 80% of final class IoU) with measured within-class feature variance, controlling for frequency, will exceed 0.5, while the reverse partial (frequency controlling variance) will be under 0.25; engineered homogeneous-rare vs heterogeneous-frequent class subsets will confirm the ordering. Kill the idea if the frequency partial dominates (>= 0.45 and larger than the variance partial) on both datasets.
why_important: If variance drives acquisition, remedies for late classes should target mode coverage (sampling per appearance mode) rather than raw frequency amplification, redirecting a whole family of imbalance interventions toward the actually operative variable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Class-difficulty analyses report correlations with frequency and size; a controlled partial-correlation adjudication with engineered class subsets appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class acquisition epochs from dense checkpoints; measure within-class variance using a frozen pretrained embedder; run partial correlations both ways; build two engineered subset datasets that decouple the variables and re-train.
main_risk: Feature-variance measurement depends on the embedder; using two unrelated public embedders and requiring agreement protects the statistic.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Late acquisition is explained by rarity, as encoded in ubiquitous frequency-reweighting defaults.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Variance and frequency are correlated in real datasets, and the engineered decoupling may create unnatural co-occurrence statistics that change acquisition for other reasons.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes + ADE20K (public) with dense checkpointing, plus 2 engineered-subset retrainings x 2 seeds: about 3 days on one A100; variance measurement uses public DINOv2 and ResNet-50 embedders.

one_line_idea: Delayed generalization (grokking-like) exists in dense prediction: under strong weight decay and small data, validation boundary quality jumps long after training loss saturates, with the delay controlled by the decay strength.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Delayed generalization long after training-set fit (grokking) is documented for algorithmic and some classification tasks; whether dense prediction exhibits the phenomenon, and in which output structures, is unknown.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense tasks have instance-idiosyncratic fit components (exact boundary placements on small training sets) and generalizable components (region semantics); with small data and strong decay, networks first fit boundaries idiosyncratically, then slowly consolidate to transferable boundary rules under the decay pressure, producing a late jump in validation boundary metrics while interior metrics track training loss conventionally.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On 500-image Pascal VOC subsets with weight decay at 10x standard, validation boundary F-score will improve by at least 5 points after the epoch where training loss has been within 1% of its final value for 100+ epochs, and the delay length will scale monotonically with decay strength across 3 levels; interior accuracy will show no comparable late jump (< 1 point). Kill the idea if no late boundary improvement above 2 points occurs at any decay level, or the delay does not vary with decay.
why_important: Extending delayed-generalization phenomenology to dense outputs would show that structured outputs have separable idiosyncratic-fit and consolidation phases by output region, informing early-stopping policy (stopping at train saturation discards the late consolidation) and connecting dense training to a growing dynamical literature.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Grokking studies concentrate on algorithmic/classification data; a region-resolved dense version with decay-controlled delay appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Small-data segmentation runs at 3 decay levels x 3 seeds with very long budgets and dense evaluation; decompose validation improvements into boundary bands vs interiors; measure delay statistics.
main_risk: Very long small-data runs are cheap per step but numerous; the phenomenon may also require specific data sizes, needing a small size ladder to find the operative regime.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense training is assumed to generalize (or not) monotonically with training progress, with nothing left to gain long after training loss saturates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The boundary-consolidation story may be wishful: late validation movement could be evaluation noise, which the 5-point bar and seed replication are set to filter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: U-Net R18 (public encoder) on 500-image VOC subsets (public), 9 runs x 2000 epochs at low resolution: about 3 days on one RTX 4090.

one_line_idea: Early training at low resolution creates a persistent thin-structure deficit that equal-compute high-resolution fine-tuning cannot repair, establishing a within-run critical period for spatial detail.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Progressive-resolution training (start small, finish large) is a common efficiency recipe, assumed lossless because final epochs see full resolution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Filters and attention patterns that resolve thin structures must form while gradients from those structures exist; at low resolution thin structures vanish from supervision, and the network commits capacity to coarse solutions that later high-resolution gradients only locally patch rather than restructure, leaving a permanent deficit relative to full-resolution-throughout training at matched total compute.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Progressive training (50% resolution for the first half) will end at least 2 IoU below full-resolution training on Cityscapes thin classes (pole, traffic sign/light) at matched compute, with the deficit shrinking by less than half when the high-resolution phase is doubled, while blob-class IoU matches within 0.3. Kill the idea if the thin-class deficit is under 0.8 IoU, or if doubling the high-res phase eliminates it (no critical period, just insufficient budget).
why_important: Progressive resolution is widely used to cut cost; a real critical period would mean the savings silently tax exactly the classes many applications care most about, and would be among the cleanest demonstrations that acquisition order constrains what is ultimately learnable within standard budgets.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Critical-period phenomena are shown for early-training deficits in classification; a resolution-specific, class-resolved version for dense prediction appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare full-resolution, progressive, and extended-progressive schedules at matched compute on Cityscapes; report class-resolved IoU with thin-class stratification; probe first-layer/early-block frequency selectivity at the switch point and end.
main_risk: Matched-compute accounting between resolutions has freedom (per-image vs per-pixel compute); pre-registering FLOP-matched budgets removes the ambiguity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The final training resolution is assumed to determine final detail capability, making progressive schedules a free lunch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern architectures with strong multi-scale features may retain enough plasticity for the late phase to fully restructure, erasing the deficit and revealing the critical period as an artifact of older architectures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 and DeepLabv3+ (public) on Cityscapes (public), 3 schedules x 2 architectures x 2 seeds FLOP-matched: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Detection training acquires localization before classification in a fixed order (matched-box quality saturates while class accuracy still climbs), and the lag between the two phases predicts which errors dominate the final model.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detector errors decompose into localization and classification components, analyzed on finished models by error-analysis tools; the temporal order in which these abilities form during training is not part of the standard picture.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Localization is supervised by geometrically smooth, high-signal regression gradients and matures early; classification of matched boxes requires finer feature discrimination and matures later; the phase lag is architecture- and data-dependent, and a long lag at the end of training (classification still climbing at budget exhaustion) manifests directly as a classification-dominated final error profile.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 4 public detector families on COCO, IoU-of-matched-boxes will reach 95% of its final value at least 25% (of total steps) earlier than classification accuracy on those same boxes, and the residual classification slope at budget end will rank-correlate (rho >= 0.6) with the classification share of final errors under standard error decomposition. Kill the idea if 2+ detector families show the reverse order, or the lag statistic fails to track final error composition.
why_important: An acquisition-order law for detection links budget decisions to error profiles (short budgets produce classification-starved detectors), suggesting phase-aware budget extension or late classification-focused emphasis instead of uniform longer training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error decompositions of finished detectors are standard; the within-run phase-ordering measurement and its predictive link to final error composition appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument training of Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, FCOS, and a DETR-family model on COCO with per-checkpoint matched-box IoU and matched-box classification accuracy; extract phase timings; correlate with final error decomposition.
main_risk: Matched-box statistics depend on the matching threshold; reporting at two IoU thresholds guards against threshold artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection abilities are assumed to co-evolve, with final error composition attributed to architecture rather than truncated acquisition phases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: End-to-end set-matching detectors (DETR-family) couple classification and localization through the matcher, potentially inverting or destroying the phase order for that family.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Four public mmdetection configs on COCO (public) at 1x schedules with checkpointing every 2k iterations: about 5 days on one A100; per-checkpoint analysis is post-hoc; a 2-family core (2.5 days) gives the first read.

one_line_idea: Attention-map organization in ViT-based dense models undergoes an abrupt within-run transition (entropy drop plus locality emergence), and dense-task transferability of the features begins rising only after this transition, making it a measurable readiness marker.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Trained ViTs show structured attention (locality in early layers, object-aligned patterns later); when this structure forms during dense training and what it gates is not established.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Attention organization is a phase transition rather than gradual drift: token-attention entropy drops sharply within a narrow step window as heads differentiate, and until this reorganization happens the features are poorly transferable to dense readouts; the transition time therefore separates an unproductive warm phase from a productive representation phase, and interventions that accelerate the transition (locality-biased init) shift the whole accuracy curve forward.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training SegFormer-style/ViT dense models from scratch on ADE20K subsets, mean attention entropy will complete at least 60% of its total drop within a window of at most 10% of training steps, frozen-feature dense-probe accuracy will begin its main rise within 5% of steps after that window in at least 3 of 4 runs, and locality-biased initialization will shift both events earlier by at least 20%. Kill the idea if the entropy drop is spread over more than 40% of training (no transition) or probe-rise timing is uncoupled from it.
why_important: A measurable readiness marker for dense representations enables schedule decisions (when fine-tuning phases can start, when to enable auxiliary objectives) keyed to internal state rather than step counts, and characterizes a genuine nonlinearity in dense-training dynamics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attention-structure analyses exist on finished models and language-model phase transitions are reported; the coupling of an attention transition to dense transferability timing appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From-scratch ViT dense training with dense checkpointing; track attention entropy per layer and frozen-feature probe accuracy; test event coupling and the init intervention.
main_risk: From-scratch ViT training on segmentation-scale data is unstable; using ImageNet-100 pretraining as the observed run (with dense probes) is a fallback that preserves the coupling question.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Representation quality is assumed to grow smoothly with training, without gating events worth scheduling around.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The entropy drop may be an epiphenomenon of LR warmup ending rather than an intrinsic reorganization, which the init intervention (which does not change warmup) is designed to expose.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ViT-S trained on ImageNet-100 (public) with ADE20K (public) dense probes at checkpoints, plus a locality-init arm, 2 seeds: about 3.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Class acquisition order in dense training is optimization-forced, not data-forced: aggressive class-balanced resampling shifts acquisition times but preserves the order, exposing a fixed difficulty hierarchy that data curricula cannot reorder.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Classes are acquired in a characteristic order during segmentation training, and data-centric practice implicitly assumes exposure schedules control what is learned when.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Acquisition order reflects intrinsic optimization difficulty (feature depth required, gradient signal geometry) rather than exposure statistics; resampling changes each class's clock speed but not the sequence, so even extreme rebalancing will fail to move early learners behind late learners, bounding what any within-run data curriculum can achieve.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under 10x class-balanced resampling on Cityscapes and ADE20K, the rank order of class acquisition epochs will correlate with the natural-sampling order at Kendall tau >= 0.7, with no class moving more than 2 rank positions in 3 of 4 runs, while absolute acquisition times shift by up to 40%. Kill the idea if tau < 0.45 or 3+ classes swap across the median rank, which would establish genuine data-forced ordering and validate curriculum control.
why_important: Either outcome is decision-relevant: order rigidity redirects effort from exposure curricula to loss/architecture interventions for late classes, while order plasticity would justify serious curriculum engineering; currently the community assumes plasticity without measurement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resampling is evaluated by final accuracy, not by whether it reorders acquisition; the order-invariance test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train natural vs 10x-balanced sampling with dense checkpoints on both datasets; compute acquisition epochs per class; compare rank orders and time shifts across seeds.
main_risk: Acquisition-epoch estimates are noisy for classes with flat late curves; defining acquisition at multiple thresholds (60/80/90% of final IoU) makes the rank comparison robust.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] What the model learns first is assumed to follow what it sees most, motivating exposure-based curricula.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Extreme resampling may alter effective co-occurrence contexts enough to genuinely change difficulty (context is part of the signal), producing order changes for reasons beyond exposure counting.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes + ADE20K (public), 2 sampling arms x 2 datasets x 2 seeds with checkpointing: about 3 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Epoch-wise double descent in dense prediction is spatially localized: boundary-band validation error is non-monotone over training while interior error descends monotonically, so the phenomenon's visibility depends on which metric a paper reports.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Epoch-wise double descent (validation error rising then falling again with training time) is documented for classification under label corruption and capacity stress; its existence and structure in dense prediction is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The idiosyncratic-fit-then-consolidation dynamics that produce epoch-wise double descent operate on the hardest, most idiosyncratic pixels, which concentrate near boundaries; interiors are learned smoothly. Dense double descent therefore exists but hides inside spatially aggregated metrics, explaining why it is rarely reported for segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training compact models on reduced Cityscapes (capacity-stressed regime), 8px-boundary-band validation error will show a rise of at least 3% relative followed by recovery in at least 3 of 4 seeds, while interior error rises by under 1% at the same epochs; aggregate mIoU will show a rise of under 1% (masked phenomenon). Kill the idea if no band shows non-monotonicity above noise (2x seed standard deviation) in any capacity-stressed configuration tested.
why_important: It locates a canonical deep-learning phenomenon inside structured outputs, warns that aggregate dense metrics can mask non-monotone generalization (checkpoint selection implications), and identifies boundary pixels as the idiosyncrasy-sensitive population in dense training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Double-descent studies target classification and simple regression; a spatially-resolved dense version appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capacity-stressed segmentation runs (small models, reduced data, long budgets) with dense evaluation; decompose validation error into boundary bands vs interiors over time; replicate across 4 seeds and 2 capacity levels.
main_risk: The phenomenon may require label corruption to appear at practical scales; a corrupted-boundary arm is a fallback that changes the claim's scope but keeps the spatial-localization question intact.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense-task validation curves are assumed monotone under standard settings, so no one schedules or selects checkpoints around a mid-training degradation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary error may be dominated by irreducible placement noise that drowns a small non-monotone component below the pre-registered detection bar.
fastest_falsification_experiment: U-Net R18 (public) on quarter-size Cityscapes (public), 2 capacities x 4 seeds x long budgets at low resolution: about 3 days on one RTX 4090; band decomposition is post-hoc.

one_line_idea: Within-run neural collapse in segmentation heads is class-asymmetric: frequent-class features collapse toward their class means early while rare-class features never fully collapse, and the residual within-class variance identifies which classes still benefit from continued training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Neural collapse (within-class feature variance shrinking to class means at the end of classification training) is documented for balanced classification; its dynamics in imbalanced dense prediction heads are uncharted.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Collapse progress per class is set by effective gradient exposure, so dense heads exhibit a moving frontier: frequent classes reach near-collapse early (after which their accuracy is optimizer-noise-bound), rare classes remain far from collapse at budget end (data/exposure-bound); the per-class collapse gap therefore partitions classes into those that longer training can still help and those needing other interventions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes, the within-class-to-between-class variance ratio in the penultimate head features will differ by at least 4x between the most and least frequent class quintiles at budget end, per-class IoU gains from 2x budget extension will concentrate (>= 70%) in classes above the median residual-variance, and frequent-quintile gains will be under 0.3 IoU. Kill the idea if the collapse ratio spread is under 1.5x, or budget-extension gains are uncorrelated with residual variance (rho < 0.25).
why_important: It imports a precise theoretical object (collapse geometry) into dense training as a practical training-sufficiency diagnostic per class, replacing guesswork about whether longer training will help with a measurable geometric criterion.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Neural collapse under imbalance is studied theoretically for classification (minority collapse); a within-run, per-class diagnostic application to dense heads appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument segmentation training to record per-class feature statistics in the head; compute collapse trajectories; extend budget 2x and attribute per-class gains against residual variance at the original endpoint.
main_risk: Pixel features are spatially correlated, so variance statistics need subsampled, decorrelated pixel sets to avoid trivially inflated within-class variance for large-region classes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Longer training is assumed to lift all boats slowly, without a geometric criterion for which classes remain trainable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rare-class residual variance may reflect genuine multi-modality that no amount of training collapses, decoupling the diagnostic from budget-extension gains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), instrumented run + 2x-budget extension x 2 seeds: about 2.5 days on one A100; feature statistics are computed online at negligible cost.

one_line_idea: Interior and boundary pixels of the same instance send systematically conflicting gradients through shared decoder features, and the depth at which the conflict peaks tells you where decoupled decoding pays off.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation decoders process all pixels through shared features, and architectures with separate boundary streams sometimes help; when and where separation is warranted is decided by trial and error.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Boundary pixels need high-frequency, position-sensitive features while interiors need smoothed semantic evidence; through shared channels these demands produce negatively-aligned gradient components whose magnitude is layer-localized (largest in mid-decoder), so splitting only the layers above the measured conflict peak captures the benefit of dual-stream designs at a fraction of the parameters.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-layer cosine between interior-pixel and boundary-pixel gradient aggregates will be below -0.1 in a contiguous mid-decoder band and near zero elsewhere across two architectures, and splitting decoders only above the conflict peak will recover at least 70% of the full dual-stream mIoU gain with under 30% of its parameter overhead. Kill the idea if conflict cosines are everywhere above -0.03 (no structured conflict) or split-at-peak recovers under 30% of the dual-stream gain.
why_important: It grounds boundary-stream architecture folklore in a measurable optimization quantity, turns an architecture search into a one-run diagnostic, and adds evidence that spatial populations within one task behave like conflicting tasks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-conflict analysis is standard across tasks in multi-task learning; applying population-conflict profiling within a single dense task to place architectural splits appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument DeepLabv3+ and SegFormer training with per-layer population-gradient cosines (interior vs 8px boundary band); train full dual-stream and split-at-peak variants; compare gains and costs.
main_risk: Population gradients aggregated per layer may hide channel-level structure; a channel-resolved follow-up is the natural refinement if layer-level conflict is weak.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boundary streams are motivated representationally (edges need their own features), with no optimization-conflict measurement behind the design choice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conflict may be beneficial regularization rather than harm, in which case splitting at the conflict peak could reduce accuracy despite faithful conflict measurements.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), instrumented baselines + 2 split variants x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: In joint segmentation+depth training, destructive gradient conflict is confined to the top decoder layers, so splitting only those layers should recover nearly all of the fully-split architecture's benefit, replacing task-architecture folklore with a conflict-localization rule.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multi-task dense models choose between shared decoders (cheap, interference-prone) and fully split decoders (expensive, interference-free) largely by convention, with mixed reports on which wins.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Task conflict between dense tasks is not uniform across depth: early features (edges, geometry primitives) serve both tasks with aligned gradients, while late decoder layers specialize task-specifically; measured per-layer conflict will show a sharp rise near the top, and architecture splits placed at the measured conflict onset will capture the full-split benefit with minimal parameter cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On NYU Depth v2 seg+depth training, per-layer task-gradient cosines will be above +0.1 in the encoder and below -0.1 only in the top quarter of decoder layers, and split-at-onset will come within 20% of the full-split's combined-metric gain over fully-shared while adding under 35% of full-split parameters. Kill the idea if conflict is depth-uniform (no onset), or split-at-onset recovers under 40% of the full-split benefit.
why_important: Multi-task dense deployment is common (robotics, driving) and decoder duplication is the dominant memory cost; a conflict-measurement-driven split rule converts an architecture decision into a cheap diagnostic while testing whether gradient conflict is actually the operative harm in shared decoders.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-surgery and task-grouping literatures measure whole-network conflict; layer-resolved conflict used as an architecture-placement rule for dense task pairs appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument shared-decoder seg+depth training with per-layer task-gradient cosines; train fully-shared, fully-split, and split-at-onset variants at matched budgets; compare combined metrics and costs over 2 seeds.
main_risk: The combined-metric definition (how to weigh seg vs depth) affects the verdict; reporting both single-task metrics separately with a dominance criterion avoids aggregation games.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Task interference is treated as a global property to be fixed by loss weighting or gradient surgery, not as a localizable structure to be routed around architecturally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conflict measured on gradients may not translate to accuracy harm (the network may average conflicting demands harmlessly), decoupling the diagnostic from the architecture outcome.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Deep supervision is ubiquitous but its mechanism is asserted, not decomposed; the profile-matching and content-degradation controls appear untested.

one_line_idea: Optimal task weights in multi-task dense training are those that equalize per-task gradient noise-to-signal ratios measured mid-run, replacing grid search over weights with a two-measurement rule.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multi-task dense training requires task-weight tuning that consumes most of the practical effort; automatic weighting schemes exist but disagree with each other and with grid-search optima across setups.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Late training is noise-floor-limited: the task whose gradient noise dominates the shared parameters sets everyone's plateau, so the weight vector that equalizes per-task noise-to-signal ratios (gradient variance over squared mean, measured on shared parameters mid-run) coincides with the grid-search optimum; existing schemes work exactly when they approximate this equalization.

why_important: It offers a mechanistic account of what task-weight tuning actually finds, compresses an expensive search into two measurements, and adjudicates between competing automatic-weighting stories with a single falsifiable criterion.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Homoscedastic-weighting-style and gradient-norm-based schemes exist; the specific noise-to-signal equalization law tested against grid-search ground truth appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid-search task weights on two dense pairs to locate optima; measure per-task gradient statistics on shared parameters at several weights; test whether equalization predicts the optimum location.
main_risk: Gradient statistics drift over training, so the measurement time matters; testing at three measurement points establishes whether a single mid-run snapshot suffices.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Task weighting is treated as an empirical search problem or delegated to heuristic schemes with no agreed governing quantity.

one_line_idea: Confusable class pairs in segmentation exhibit zero-sum oscillation during training, with epoch-to-epoch accuracy fluctuations that are anti-correlated pairwise, revealing that late training redistributes a fixed decision boundary rather than improving both classes.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For a confusable pair, the shared feature evidence is nearly fixed late in training, so gradient updates that help one class necessarily push the shared decision boundary against the other; late-phase per-class fluctuations for such pairs will be strongly anti-correlated (unlike unrelated pairs), and the anti-correlation magnitude identifies which confusions are boundary-redistribution problems (needing feature enrichment) versus under-training problems (fixable by more steps).

Kill the idea if confusable-pair correlations are indistinguishable from random pairs (gap < 0.15) or anti-correlation fails to predict budget-extension futility.
why_important: It gives a within-run signature separating two causes of persistent confusion that currently get the same remedy (train longer), directing effort toward feature-level interventions where oscillation proves redistribution, and documents a concrete zero-sum dynamic inside dense training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Confusion matrices are endpoint artifacts in standard practice; the temporal anti-correlation signature and its budget-futility prediction appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dense-checkpoint training on both datasets; compute per-class IoU fluctuation correlation matrices over the late phase; compare confusable vs random pairs; extend budget and attribute gains against anti-correlation strength.
main_risk: Evaluation noise inflates apparent fluctuations; using large validation subsets and 3 seeds separates measurement noise from dynamical oscillation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Late-training fluctuations are treated as seed/eval noise, and persistent confusions as uniformly needing more data or capacity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fluctuations may be driven by BN statistic drift affecting both classes of a pair symmetrically, masking or mimicking the zero-sum signature.

one_line_idea: The classification and box-regression branches of dense detectors conflict on shared features with a characteristic time signature (regression gradients shrink as boxes converge while classification persists), explaining mechanistically why decoupled-head designs win and when they stop mattering.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Early in training both branches need coarse localization features and their gradients align; as boxes converge, regression gradients shrink and rotate toward high-frequency refinement directions while classification gradients keep demanding invariant semantic features, so branch conflict on shared features grows over training; the benefit of decoupling therefore accrues late, scales with the measured late-phase conflict, and disappears for short schedules.

Kill the idea if the cosine stays positive throughout, or if decoupling's gain is budget-independent (within 20%), or late-only decoupling captures under 40%.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Decoupled heads are established practice; the temporal conflict signature and phase-swap decomposition appear untested.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Decoupled heads are believed to work because the two subtasks simply need different features, a static account with no schedule prediction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benefit may come from doubled head capacity rather than conflict removal; a widened-coupled-head control at matched parameters directly tests this rival.

one_line_idea: In panoptic training, stuff-region gradients numerically dominate thing-region gradients through sheer pixel count, suppressing instance-discrimination learning; branch-specific batch composition (alternating thing-rich and stuff-rich crops) should fix this without any loss reweighting.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The lag is partly a gradient-budget artifact: stuff regions contribute most supervised pixels per batch, so shared features drift toward stuff-optimal statistics between sparse thing-gradient events; composing batches to alternate thing-dense and stuff-dense crops concentrates thing gradients into coherent updates (less inter-batch dilution), improving thing performance at equal data and loss settings.

Kill the idea if PQ-things improves by under 0.5, or if matching the same thing-gradient share via loss reweighting achieves the same gain (composition adds nothing beyond reweighting).
why_important: It locates part of a well-known performance asymmetry in batch-composition dynamics rather than loss design, and offers a data-scheduling fix orthogonal to the heavily explored weighting/architecture axes, with a built-in control that adjudicates composition against reweighting.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Thing/stuff asymmetry is discussed via losses and architectures; the batch-composition timing mechanism with a reweighting-equivalence control appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Panoptic FPN training with standard vs alternating-composition batching vs gradient-share-matched reweighting on COCO-panoptic; log per-batch thing/stuff gradient shares; compare PQ decompositions over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Crop composition changes object-scale statistics simultaneously; matching crop-scale distributions across arms isolates the composition timing variable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Thing-stuff imbalance is treated as a loss-weighting problem, with batch composition considered interchangeable as long as the epoch-level distribution matches.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If momentum and Adam smooth gradient timing sufficiently, epoch-level composition is all that matters and the alternating scheme will match plain shuffling.

one_line_idea: Teacher-student dense self-distillation has a two-phase structure with a measurable phase boundary: before teacher-student agreement crosses a threshold the teacher acts as a denoiser, after it the loop locks in student errors, so distillation weight should be scheduled against measured agreement, not time.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Mean-teacher-style self-distillation for dense tasks feeds a moving average of the student back as a target; confirmation of student errors is a known qualitative risk, managed by hand-tuned schedules.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] While teacher-student disagreement is high, teacher targets carry independent-enough information to denoise the student; once agreement exceeds a threshold, the residual teacher signal is dominated by the student's own systematic errors reflected back, and continued distillation pressure entrenches them; the transition is detectable online as the point where teacher-corrections stop correlating with ground-truth error reduction on a small labeled probe.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In semi-supervised Cityscapes distillation, the correlation between accepted teacher-corrections and probe-measured error reduction will decay from significantly positive to near zero as pixel-level agreement passes a threshold (within a 5-point agreement window consistent across seeds), and cutting distillation weight at the measured crossing will beat the best fixed schedule by at least 0.5 mIoU. Kill the idea if the correlation shows no agreement-linked decay, or measured-crossing cutoff fails to beat fixed schedules by more than 0.1 mIoU.
why_important: It replaces open-loop distillation schedules with a closed-loop rule based on an observable, and quantifies the onset of self-confirmation, the central failure mode of self-training, as a reproducible transition rather than an anecdote.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Confirmation bias in self-training is discussed qualitatively; an online agreement-threshold law with a closed-loop cutoff test appears untested. minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrumented mean-teacher training with a held-out labeled probe; track agreement, correction-utility correlation, and run cutoff-at-crossing vs fixed-schedule arms over 2 seeds.
main_risk: The labeled probe must be small to keep the semi-supervised setting honest; correlation estimates on small probes are noisy, requiring temporal smoothing that could blur the transition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Distillation strength schedules are set by time-based heuristics, with confirmation risk managed by confidence thresholds rather than loop-state measurements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Agreement may saturate so early that the useful-denoising phase is negligible in modern setups, making the schedule question moot (also an informative outcome).

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mixing augmentations are heavily studied at the metric level; the boundary-gradient-budget accounting and band-masked variant appear new.

one_line_idea: Frozen-BN folklore in detection fine-tuning works because small-batch BN statistic noise acts as an uncontrolled multiplicative perturbation on all downstream computation, so noise-corrected BN (larger virtual batches) should erase the freezing advantage and flip the recommendation at scale.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection fine-tuning recipes freeze backbone BN layers by default, a decade-old folklore justified by small per-GPU batch sizes, and carried unchanged into regimes where it may no longer apply.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The harm from live BN at small batches is statistic noise (batch mean/variance estimates jitter), which multiplies activations and destabilizes fine-tuning atop converged features; the harm is therefore a monotone function of statistic noise, so live BN with synchronized or accumulated statistics (large virtual batch) should match or beat frozen BN, and frozen BN should actively hurt when data statistics differ from pretraining.

Kill the idea if noise-corrected live BN still trails frozen BN by more than 0.7 AP (freezing does more than remove statistic noise), or frozen BN wins even under strong statistic mismatch.
why_important: The freeze ritual is applied universally, including where it is likely counterproductive; a noise-based account gives the boundary (statistic noise vs statistics mismatch) and modern hardware makes the corrected alternative practical.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The freeze default is well known; the decomposition into statistic-noise vs statistic-mismatch channels with a virtual-batch adjudication appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {frozen, live, live+virtual-batch} x {matched-statistics target, shifted-statistics target subset} on COCO fine-tuning; log BN statistic variance per arm; compare AP.
main_risk: Virtual-batch BN implementations differ (sync vs accumulation vs precise-BN recomputation); testing two implementations guards the conclusion against implementation artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Freezing BN is considered strictly safer for fine-tuning, an unconditional recipe rule.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Freezing may additionally act as beneficial regularization (fixing feature scales), a channel the noise correction cannot reproduce, which would keep frozen BN ahead and kill the idea informatively.

one_line_idea: BN running-statistics momentum is an implicit schedule that should be tied to the LR schedule: as LR decays, statistics lag the (now slowly moving) weights less, so the fixed default momentum over-smooths late training and under-smooths early training, and matching the two schedules removes a persistent train-eval gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] BN maintains running statistics with a fixed momentum (typically 0.1) for evaluation, while training uses batch statistics; late-training evaluation metrics for dense models often jitter or lag training behavior, usually attributed to generic noise.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The optimal statistics-averaging window depends on how fast the underlying activations drift, which is set by the LR schedule; a fixed momentum is therefore wrong twice (too long a memory early when activations move fast, too short late when they are nearly static and noise dominates), and scheduling BN momentum proportionally to LR aligns the estimator with the drift rate, shrinking the train-eval gap and its jitter.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] LR-proportional BN momentum will reduce late-training evaluation jitter (standard deviation of val mIoU across the last 20 checkpoints) by at least 40% and improve final selected-checkpoint mIoU by at least 0.3 on Cityscapes small-batch training, with the measured statistics-lag (distance between running and instantaneous-precise statistics) reduced at least 2x late. Kill the idea if jitter reduction is under 15%, or precise-BN recomputation at each checkpoint (the gold standard) shows no gap for fixed momentum in the first place.
why_important: It identifies a silent coupling between two schedules everyone sets independently, offers a zero-cost recipe improvement, and explains a source of checkpoint-selection noise that plagues small-batch dense training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Precise-BN (recomputing statistics) is a known evaluation fix; scheduling the running momentum against LR as a within-run law appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {fixed momentum, LR-proportional momentum, precise-BN recompute} on small-batch Cityscapes training; measure statistics lag, val jitter, and final accuracy over 3 seeds.
main_risk: If precise-BN already solves everything cheaply, the scheduled-momentum contribution is redundant in practice, though the law about lag structure would still stand.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] BN momentum is a fixed constant of the layer, unrelated to the LR schedule.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Late-phase evaluation jitter may be dominated by genuine decision-boundary oscillation (weight-space), not statistics estimation, leaving momentum scheduling without a target.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public) at batch 4, 3 arms x 3 seeds at 40k iterations: about 2.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: The BN-vs-GN choice for dense training is governed by a two-dimensional phase boundary in (images per batch, pixels per image): BN wins only above a critical image count that itself grows with resolution, giving a chartable decision diagram instead of contradictory folklore.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] GroupNorm is known to beat BN at small batch sizes, and BN to win at large ones, but dense training varies both image count and per-image pixel count, and recipes carry normalization choices between regimes where the folklore was never validated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] BN's statistic quality depends on effective sample diversity per batch, which for dense features is driven by image count (pixels within an image are correlated and add little), while GN's cost is discarding cross-image statistics; therefore the BN-GN crossover sits at an image-count threshold that is nearly independent of pixel count, predicting BN's regime shrinks at high resolution where memory forces low image counts, and the whole plane is chartable with a modest grid.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a (batch images {2,4,8,16}) x (resolution {512, 768, 1024}) grid on Cityscapes, the BN-GN accuracy crossover will occur at an image count consistent across resolutions within one grid step, while a pixels-per-batch account would predict crossover shifts of 2+ steps that will not materialize. Kill the idea if the crossover tracks total pixels rather than image count (shifting systematically with resolution), or if no stable crossover exists (interaction dominated by LR coupling).
why_important: It replaces a one-dimensional folklore with the actual decision surface practitioners face, and settles whether within-image pixels contribute meaningful normalization statistics, a question with consequences for all batch-statistic methods on dense features.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] BN-vs-GN batch-size curves exist for classification and detection at fixed resolution; the two-dimensional dense-task phase diagram with the image-count invariance claim appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the 12-cell grid with both normalizations at matched tuned LR per cell (small sweep), 1 seed per cell plus replicated boundary cells; locate crossovers per resolution row.
main_risk: Per-cell LR tuning is essential (BN and GN prefer different LRs) and dominates cost; skipping it would fabricate crossovers.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Normalization choice is guided by a single batch-size rule of thumb, assumed portable across resolutions and tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-resolution features may decorrelate enough spatially that within-image pixels do add statistic value, dragging the crossover along a pixels-per-batch contour instead.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 BN/GN variants (public) on Cityscapes (public), 12 cells x 2 norms x mini LR sweep at 20k iterations: about 5 days on one A100 40GB; the 2-resolution subgrid (2.5 days) already tests the invariance claim.

one_line_idea: fp16 training with loss scaling loses rare-class gradient contributions first, because their sparse, small-magnitude gradients sit closest to the underflow boundary, creating a class-selective precision tax that fp32 and bf16 do not share.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Mixed-precision (fp16 with dynamic loss scaling) is the default for dense training; its accuracy impact is audited at the aggregate-metric level, where it appears safely negligible.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Underflow in fp16 gradients is not class-neutral: rare classes contribute gradients that are both sparse and small (few pixels, often small structures), so a disproportionate fraction of their gradient mass falls below representable magnitude even with global loss scaling (which is set by the largest gradients); the resulting deficit is invisible in mIoU but measurable in rare-class IoU and in the fraction of underflowed gradient mass per class.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes with fp16+dynamic scaling vs bf16 vs fp32 at identical settings, rare-quintile class IoU will trail fp32 by at least 0.8 IoU under fp16 while frequent-quintile classes match within 0.2, per-class underflow accounting will show at least 5x higher underflowed-mass fraction for rare classes, and bf16 will match fp32 within 0.3 everywhere. Kill the idea if rare-class fp16 deficits are under 0.3 IoU or underflow mass shows no class asymmetry.
why_important: A class-selective precision tax would mean thousands of mixed-precision dense results carry a small systematic bias against exactly the classes applications care about, with a trivial fix (bf16 or per-class-aware scaling) once documented.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mixed-precision audits check aggregate parity; class-resolved underflow accounting for dense training appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the three precision arms with per-class gradient underflow instrumentation (count masked gradient mass below fp16 min-normal per class at the head); compare class-quintile IoU across arms over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Dynamic loss scaling adapts over training, so underflow must be integrated across the run, and instrumentation must not itself alter scaling decisions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mixed precision is regarded as accuracy-neutral for vision given loss scaling, full stop.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adam's normalization may rescue small gradients (the update direction survives even if magnitudes quantize), leaving no accuracy trace despite real underflow events.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 3 precision arms x 3 seeds at 40k iterations on an A100 (supports bf16): about 2.5 days; instrumentation is a backward-hook counter.

one_line_idea: Multi-resolution dense training works smoothly for LayerNorm architectures but silently degrades BN-based hybrids, because BN statistics are resolution-dependent while LN normalizes per token, predicting a normalization-conditioned verdict on variable-resolution schedules.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Variable-resolution and multi-scale training schedules are common for dense models, and are applied across architectures as if normalization were a neutral bystander.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Activation statistics at BN layers shift with input resolution (feature-map spatial statistics change with scale), so a batch mixing resolutions or a schedule alternating them forces BN running statistics to track a moving mixture, degrading both training stability and eval-time statistics fidelity; LN-family normalization is per-sample and scale-robust, so transformer-style models tolerate the same schedules, explaining anecdotal architecture-dependent reports about multi-scale training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under an alternating-resolution schedule on Cityscapes, a BN-based CNN will lose at least 1.0 mIoU relative to fixed-resolution training at matched compute while an LN-based transformer loses under 0.3, and per-resolution BN statistic distances will be at least 3x the within-resolution batch noise; per-resolution BN statistics (separate buffers per scale) will recover at least 70% of the BN loss. Kill the idea if BN and LN degrade equally (within 0.3), or per-resolution buffers recover under 30% (mechanism not statistics-based).
why_important: Multi-scale schedules are recommended generically; a normalization-conditioned rule prevents silent degradation in CNN pipelines and identifies the cheap fix (scale-specific statistics), while adding a concrete case to the growing map of normalization-schedule interactions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution-dependent BN statistics are folk-known in deployment (inference-resolution mismatch); the training-schedule version with the buffer-fix decomposition appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed vs alternating resolution schedules on {DeepLabv3+ (BN), SegFormer (LN)} with matched compute; log per-resolution statistic distances; add per-resolution-buffer BN arm; compare mIoU over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Compute matching between fixed and alternating schedules requires care (aspect ratios, crop content); FLOP-matched budgets with identical crop statistics per arm are pre-registered.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multi-scale training is architecture-neutral good practice for dense robustness across scales.
why_it_might_be_wrong: BN's statistic mixing may act as beneficial scale-robustness regularization, actually helping generalization across evaluation resolutions and offsetting the fidelity loss.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 2 schedules x 2 architectures + 1 buffer-fix arm, 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: resolution schedule x normalization type + per-scale statistics
