one_line_idea: BN's train-mode stochasticity is a load-bearing regularizer in dense training: reproducing its measured noise distribution via explicit activation-noise injection under fixed statistics should recover most of BN's generalization advantage over deterministic normalization.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] BN outperforms deterministic alternatives in some dense regimes even when statistic-quality arguments favor the alternatives, hinting at a second mechanism beyond statistics estimation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Batch-statistic jitter perturbs every activation multiplicatively each step, a structured noise correlated within channels and batches; this noise regularizes like a channel-coherent dropout variant, and its contribution can be isolated by freezing statistics (removing estimation) while injecting noise matched to the measured jitter distribution, decomposing BN into estimator + regularizer.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes at batch 8, frozen-statistics BN with matched injected noise will recover at least 60% of the (live BN minus frozen-statistics BN) mIoU gap, and mismatched noise (white, channel-incoherent, same marginal variance) will recover under 25%, establishing that the correlation structure, not just the magnitude, carries the effect. Kill the idea if matched injection recovers under 25% of the gap (regularization channel negligible) or incoherent noise works just as well (structure irrelevant).
why_important: Decomposing BN's two roles lets architecture designers keep the regularization without batch coupling (injectable into GN/LN pipelines), and clarifies decade-old confusion about why BN sometimes wins beyond its statistic quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] BN-as-regularizer is a known qualitative claim; the measured-distribution injection test with a structure-matched vs unmatched control on dense tasks appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure BN statistic-jitter distributions during live training; run arms {live BN, frozen BN, frozen+matched-noise, frozen+white-noise}; compare mIoU and training curves over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Matching the full joint noise distribution is impossible; matching per-channel marginal plus batch-coherence structure is the pre-registered approximation, and its adequacy is itself informative.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] BN's benefit is attributed primarily to optimization smoothing and statistic estimation, with its noise treated as a side effect.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The regularization channel may only matter at small data scales; at Cityscapes scale both frozen arms may match live BN, nullifying the decomposition target.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 4 arms x 3 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100; jitter measurement is one instrumented epoch.

one_line_idea: In normalization-free dense training, adaptive gradient clipping thresholds map onto an equivalent BN batch-size curve, unifying two stability mechanisms as one effective constraint on relative update size and predicting threshold transfer across tasks without tuning.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Normalization-free networks stabilized by adaptive gradient clipping (bounding update-to-weight ratios) train competitively in classification, but porting them to dense tasks requires re-tuning the clipping threshold with no guidance on what it corresponds to.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Both BN and adaptive clipping ultimately bound the relative change a step can impose on a unit's computed function; if so, there is a mapping between clipping threshold and effective BN batch size that equalizes a measurable stability statistic (per-unit relative function change per step), and thresholds chosen by matching that statistic on a new dense task will be near-optimal without task-specific sweeps.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The relative-update statistic measured on stable BN baselines will identify a clipping threshold for the normalization-free variant within a factor of 2 of the sweep-optimal threshold on both Cityscapes segmentation and NYU Depth v2, with the statistic-matched run reaching within 0.5 mIoU/0.01 delta1 of the swept optimum. Kill the idea if the statistic-matched threshold misses the swept optimum by more than 4x or costs more than 1.5 mIoU, showing the two mechanisms are not exchangeable through this invariant.
why_important: A validated invariant would demystify stability tuning for normalization-free dense models (attractive for deployment reasons) and support a general principle: stability folklore across mechanisms reduces to bounding per-step relative function change.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Adaptive clipping for norm-free networks exists in classification; the cross-mechanism invariant and transfer rule for dense tasks appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure the relative-update statistic on BN baselines; sweep clipping thresholds for norm-free variants on two dense tasks; test whether statistic matching locates the optimum.
main_risk: Norm-free dense architectures are less standardized; adapting a public norm-free backbone to segmentation adds engineering that must be held fixed across arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Clipping thresholds are task-specific constants to be swept, unrelated to any normalization equivalent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense-task instabilities may be dominated by loss-surface events (rare high-loss crops) that clipping and BN handle differently, breaking any single-statistic equivalence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: NFNet-style backbone (public weights) with segmentation/depth heads on Cityscapes + NYU Depth v2 (public), threshold sweeps x 2 tasks at short schedules: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: bf16 and fp16 dense training differ mainly through loss-scaling dynamics rather than representational precision: fp16 with an oracle (perfect, non-adaptive) loss scale should match bf16, isolating the real cost of fp16 as scale-controller misbehavior during gradient-magnitude transients.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] bf16 is displacing fp16 for training stability, explained by exponent range; for dense vision the practical difference is confounded with the dynamic loss-scaling controller that fp16 requires and bf16 omits.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] fp16's mantissa is adequate for dense-vision gradients; its failures arise when the dynamic scaling controller reacts to gradient-magnitude transients (schedule changes, hard batches) with scale reductions that then underflow small gradients for thousands of steps; with a fixed oracle scale chosen post-hoc, fp16 matches bf16, implying the fix is controller design, not format switching, where bf16 hardware is unavailable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes and COCO short-schedule training, fp16-with-oracle-scale will match bf16 within 0.2 mIoU/AP while standard dynamic-scaled fp16 shows at least one scale-reduction episode per run and trails by at least 0.4 in at least one setup; aligning scale-reduction episodes with underflow-mass spikes will show temporal coincidence (>= 80% of underflow mass within episode windows). Kill the idea if oracle-scaled fp16 still trails bf16 by more than 0.4 (mantissa/precision genuinely matters) or dynamic-scale runs show no episodes yet still trail.
why_important: It assigns blame precisely within mixed-precision folklore (controller vs format), guiding practitioners on fp16-only hardware toward better controllers instead of resignation, and documents how transient controller dynamics leave lasting accuracy marks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] bf16-vs-fp16 comparisons abound at the format level; the oracle-scale decomposition isolating controller dynamics on dense tasks appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {bf16, fp16-dynamic, fp16-oracle-fixed-scale} on two dense setups with underflow and scale-event logging; compare final metrics and episode-aligned underflow accounting over 2 seeds.
main_risk: The oracle scale must be discovered by pilot runs per setup; if no single fixed scale avoids both overflow and underflow across the run, the decomposition itself fails informatively (format range genuinely binds).
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] bf16's advantage is attributed to number format properties, with the scaling controller treated as a solved auxiliary detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention-heavy dense models may produce genuine fp16 overflow in activations (not gradients), a format limitation no gradient-scale oracle fixes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 on Cityscapes and RetinaNet-R50 on COCO (public), 3 precision arms x 2 setups x 2 seeds at short schedules on an A100: about 3.5 days; logging is hook-based.

one_line_idea: Online hard-example mining is a feedback dynamical system with two regimes: a stable regime where the mined set evolves slowly and mining helps, and a limit-cycle regime where the mined set flips between populations and mining underperforms plain training, with the regime identifiable online from mined-set overlap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] OHEM and hard-pixel mining sometimes improve dense training and sometimes destabilize it, with practitioners adjusting mining ratios by trial and error.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Mining couples model state to data selection: training on mined pixels lowers their loss, ejecting them from the mined set and re-admitting previously easy pixels whose loss rose from neglect; depending on mining ratio and LR this feedback settles (stable frontier) or oscillates (populations alternate); consecutive-epoch mined-set Jaccard overlap distinguishes the regimes, predicting mining's benefit sign without waiting for final metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across mining ratios {10%, 25%, 50%} and LRs on Cityscapes, runs with late-phase mined-set Jaccard >= 0.5 will beat their no-mining twins by at least 0.5 mIoU on average, runs with Jaccard <= 0.2 will trail by at least 0.3, and the overlap statistic measured at one-third of training will classify final benefit sign with at least 80% accuracy over 12 configurations. Kill the idea if benefit sign is uncorrelated with mined-set overlap (classification accuracy < 60%) or no configuration exhibits the low-overlap oscillation regime.
why_important: It reframes a widely used heuristic as a controllable dynamical system with an online health signal, letting practitioners auto-tune or abort mining instead of discovering failures at evaluation time, and connecting selection-feedback dynamics to measurable training outcomes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] OHEM variants are abundant; treating mined-set persistence as a regime diagnostic with a pre-registered classification test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid mining ratio x LR with mined-set logging on Cityscapes; compute overlap trajectories; test the early-overlap classifier of final benefit against no-mining twins.
main_risk: Mined-set composition can drift with LR schedule independent of feedback; comparing against a frozen-model mining control (mine with a fixed snapshot) separates feedback dynamics from schedule drift.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mining is viewed as a static emphasis choice whose failures are attributed to noisy labels or excessive ratios, not to an identifiable oscillation regime.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Momentum and Adam smoothing may damp the feedback everywhere in practical ranges, leaving only the stable regime and nothing to classify.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 12 mining configs + twins at 20k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100; overlap logging is nearly free.

one_line_idea: The crop-size folklore for segmentation decomposes into a normalization-statistics component and a context component, and controlled statistic-swapping shows which one carries the large-crop advantage, with opposite architectural implications.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training on larger crops improves segmentation accuracy in most reports, attributed by default to richer context; but crop size simultaneously changes BN statistic quality, pixel correlation per batch, and boundary-to-interior pixel ratios.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial share of the large-crop advantage flows through normalization statistics (larger crops give more stable per-batch activation statistics at fixed image count), not through longer-range context reaching the loss; swapping statistics across crop regimes (computing BN statistics from large crops while supervising small ones, and vice versa) will attribute the advantage between the two channels, and the context share will concentrate on large-object classes only.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes DeepLabv3+ (BN), statistic-swapped small-crop training will recover at least 40% of the large-crop advantage overall, the remaining context component will be at least 3x larger on the biggest-object classes than on small-object classes, and GroupNorm replication will shrink the statistics component below 15%. Kill the idea if statistic swapping moves accuracy by under 10% of the crop gap (statistics channel negligible) and the context component shows no class-size structure.
why_important: Crop size is among the most compute-expensive knobs in dense training; knowing that part of its benefit is a normalization artifact (cheaply replaceable) versus true context (worth paying for, but only for certain classes) changes how training pipelines spend memory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crop-size effects are folklore-tier; the statistic-swap attribution design appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {small crop, large crop, small crop + large-crop statistics, large crop + small-crop statistics} under BN, plus GN replication; class-size-stratified accuracy decomposition over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Statistic swapping requires a two-stream implementation (supervision crops and statistics crops per batch), whose engineering must not alter effective batch composition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Large crops help because context helps, an explanation applied uniformly across classes and normalization schemes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The advantage may be dominated by a third channel, boundary-to-interior pixel ratio shifts in the loss, which the design should extend to monitor via band-resolved loss shares.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 BN/GN (public) on Cityscapes (public), 6 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100 40GB.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: advantage attribution decomposition by channel and class size

one_line_idea: Per-pixel loss computation is massively redundant: the safe pixel-subsampling rate for loss evaluation is set by the spatial correlation length of the gradient field, giving a measurable dial that trades compute for nothing until a sharp knee.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense losses are computed at every labeled pixel by default; pixel-sampled losses appear in some methods for other reasons (noise robustness, class balance) but the pure-redundancy question, how few pixels suffice, lacks a governing quantity.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Neighboring pixels contribute nearly identical gradients through shared receptive fields, so the information content of the per-pixel loss field is governed by its spatial correlation length; random sampling at spacing below that length loses nothing (gradient estimator variance barely rises), while sampling beyond it degrades sharply, producing a knee whose location is predictable from a one-epoch correlation measurement and which shifts with architecture (larger receptive fields tolerate sparser sampling).
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes, training with losses computed on a random 25% of pixels will match full-loss training within 0.2 mIoU while 5% sampling loses at least 0.8 mIoU, the measured knee will match the gradient-field correlation length within a factor of 2, and a larger-receptive-field architecture will show its knee at proportionally sparser sampling. Kill the idea if accuracy degrades smoothly with no knee, or the knee location is uncorrelated with measured correlation length across architectures.
why_important: Loss computation and its backward pass on high-resolution outputs are a real compute cost; a validated redundancy law licenses principled subsampling and connects receptive-field geometry to supervision efficiency, a quantity relevant to any dense objective.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pixel-sampled losses exist ad hoc; the correlation-length law with architecture-dependent knee prediction appears new.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crop sampling is treated as a solved preprocessing detail; the overlap-correlation law and effective-batch accounting appear unexamined.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Positional shortcuts are known in other SSL contexts (padding artifacts); the within-image-negative pathway, its growth dynamics, and the debiased-sampling fix for dense contrastive learning appear new. why_it_might_be_wrong: Position information may be a useful feature (dense tasks need it), so the shortcut may be benign or even beneficial, showing up as no downstream gap despite decodability differences.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense tasks concentrate late-phase learning in small pixel populations (boundaries, rare classes), collapsing the effective sample count per batch as interiors saturate; the gradient noise scale therefore rises steeply within-run, meaning early training is over-batched (wasted parallelism) and late training under-batched (noise-limited), and a batch ramp tracking measured noise achieves better accuracy-per-FLOP than any fixed batch.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-noise-scale batch selection is established methodology; its within-run drift structure for dense tasks and the tracking-ramp consequence appear untested.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Loss spikes are treated as stochastic accidents of batching, worth suppressing but not explaining.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Edge-of-stability studies use monolithic networks on classification; module-resolved analysis on dense architectures with an exploitation test appears new.

problem: [KNOWN FACT] The community continues to argue ConvNets versus ViTs using point comparisons at single scales, while language-model lore holds that architecture mostly shifts scaling constants rather than exponents; the vision version of this claim is asserted more than tested.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Tail-class AP improves with pretraining data scale but is nearly flat in model scale at fixed data, while head-class AP shows the reverse sensitivity, because tail performance is coverage-limited and head performance is capacity-limited.

one_line_idea: The crossover scale where generic encoder plus light decoder matches specialized end-to-end models is predictable from task output complexity, giving each dense task a forecastable retirement date for bespoke architectures.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Task-specialized architectures have been progressively displaced by generic pretrained encoders in classification, then detection, at different times, but the displacement pattern is narrated historically rather than modeled.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For each dense task there is a crossover encoder scale beyond which frozen-generic-plus-light-decoder matches the best specialized pipeline at fixed downstream budget, and the crossover compute grows systematically with a measurable proxy of output structural complexity (output entropy per image given the input class).

why_important: It converts the recurring will-foundation-models-eat-this-task debate into a forecast with a stated variable, guiding both research investment and product architecture decisions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The displacement narrative is common; a quantitative crossover-scale law against an output-complexity variable appears unattempted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For depth, keypoints, detection, and edge estimation, evaluate generic-encoder pipelines across a public scale ladder against the best public specialized model at matched downstream budget, locate crossovers, and correlate with the complexity proxy.
main_risk: Defining a fair matched-budget comparison between generic and specialized pipelines involves contestable choices that could dominate the measured crossover locations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generic encoders are assumed to eventually subsume all dense tasks, with timing considered unpredictable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Crossovers may be driven by community attention and engineering effort rather than any intrinsic task property, making them historically contingent and unforecastable.

one_line_idea: Decoder scaling has an exponent near zero once past a small size: in encoder-decoder dense pipelines, virtually all scalable improvement lives in the encoder axis, and decoder growth is dead compute.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense-prediction systems allocate parameters across encoder and decoder by convention, and decoder families keep growing without scaling-law justification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With a frozen or lightly tuned foundation encoder, downstream error versus decoder parameters saturates within a small decoder budget because the decoder can only recombine information the encoder already exposes at its token resolution, so decoder scaling exponents are near zero while encoder scaling exponents remain substantial.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a 30x decoder-parameter range at fixed encoder, fitted decoder-scaling exponents on depth and keypoint error will be under 0.02 in magnitude beyond 5M decoder parameters, at least 5x smaller than the encoder exponent measured on the same tasks; the idea is falsified if decoder exponents exceed half the encoder exponent or meaningful gains continue past 20M decoder parameters.
why_important: Parameter allocation in deployed dense systems is a recurring engineering decision; a near-zero decoder exponent would simplify it to a rule and free compute for resolution or encoder quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Decoder ablations exist per paper; a decoder-versus-encoder exponent comparison framed as an allocation law appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix 2 public encoders, sweep decoder capacity over 30x for 2 dense tasks with matched training budgets, fit decoder exponents, and compare against encoder-ladder exponents on the same tasks.
main_risk: Some decoder families add resolution-recovering structure (not just parameters), so parameter count alone may be the wrong decoder-scale variable and the sweep must control for architecture type.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Bigger decoders are assumed to help dense tasks, and decoder growth is treated as a legitimate way to spend a parameter budget.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For tasks requiring long-range reasoning over outputs, decoder capacity may genuinely scale, making the null result task-family-specific.
fastest_falsification_experiment: About 24 short trainings over public datasets with 2 frozen public encoders, one A100: about 3 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: A domain-mixture scaling law for real web data: target-domain transfer follows a fittable function of mixture weight and total data, so optimal real-data mixtures at large scale are predictable from small pilot grids.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision pretraining corpora are assembled from heterogeneous real sources (photos, products, documents, aerial, illustrations) with mixture weights chosen by availability or intuition, and mixture effects are only measured at endpoint scale, if at all.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Downstream error on a target domain follows a joint law in (mixture weight of the relevant source, total data budget) with smooth, monotone structure analogous to language data-mixing laws, so mixture optimization can be done by fitting the law on small runs rather than by large-scale trial and error.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A mixture law fitted on runs at 1/16 of reference scale will predict target-domain probe error of unseen mixtures at reference scale within 20% relative error for at least 8 of 10 test mixtures; the idea is falsified if prediction errors exceed 40% relative for half the test mixtures.
why_important: Mixture design is among the highest-leverage, least-principled decisions in vision pretraining; a validated real-data mixing law would replace guesswork with a fitted planning tool.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-mixing laws have been studied for language pretraining; a validated vision analogue over real image sources appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 4 real source pools from public corpora, pretrain small models over a mixture-weight grid at 2 scales, fit the joint law at small scale, and verify predictions on held-out mixtures at the larger scale.
main_risk: Cross-source redundancy (the same content appearing in multiple sources) can bend the law and require an effective-weight correction, complicating the clean parametric story.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mixture weights are believed to matter but to be discoverable only through expensive endpoint experiments at full scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mixture effects in vision may be dominated by discrete threshold phenomena (a source either covers a needed concept or not), resisting smooth-law description.
fastest_falsification_experiment: About 30 small pretrains over public source pools (subsets of DataComp-style corpora partitioned by source type) on one A100: about 6-7 GPU-days.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] OCR-adjacent capability is a threshold function of the absolute number of legible-text images seen in pretraining, largely independent of total corpus size, so resampling a fixed corpus to move text-image share moves reading ability and typographic-attack susceptibility together in a dose-dependent way.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Typographic attacks and OCR behaviors of CLIP are documented; a controlled composition intervention establishing the dose-response and the capability-vulnerability coupling appears missing.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Reading-like behavior may require caption-side supervision naming the text content, making image-side share alone insufficient to move capability.

one_line_idea: Regional data share obeys a saturating law with a cheap equalization frontier: raising under-represented regions' share improves region-specific performance steeply at first, at near-zero cost to head-region performance until a measurable knee.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web-scale image corpora over-represent North American and European content, and models perform measurably worse on concepts, scenes, and objects photographed elsewhere; mitigation proposals lack quantitative composition guidance.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Region-specific performance follows a saturating power law in that region's data share, and because head-region performance sits deep in its own saturation regime, reallocating share to under-represented regions traces a strongly asymmetric trade-off frontier with a wide near-free zone.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On matched-size corpora with under-represented-region share swept from 2% to 30%, region-specific retrieval/classification probes will gain at least 8 absolute points while head-region probes lose at most 1 point up to a knee at or beyond 20% share; the idea is falsified if head-region losses exceed 3 points before under-represented gains reach 5 points (no free zone).
why_important: It replaces moral exhortation about geographic coverage with a fitted frontier that tells corpus builders exactly how much equalization is free and where real trade-offs begin.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Geographic performance disparities are documented (e.g., household-object studies across income and region); the fitted share-reallocation frontier appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Partition a public geo-tagged corpus by region, build share-controlled matched-size resamples, pretrain small models, and evaluate region-stratified probe suites to trace the frontier.
main_risk: Region correlates with content type and camera statistics, so probes must separate region-of-content effects from image-quality effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Improving under-represented-region performance is assumed to require either much more data or an accuracy sacrifice on majority domains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regional gaps may be driven by caption language and annotation conventions rather than image share, in which case reallocating images moves little.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 4 small pretrains on share-controlled resamples of public geo-tagged data plus probe evaluation, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Object-centric bias of ImageNet-style data is a known critique; a controlled share-sweep measuring the dense-versus-classification trade-off at matched size appears missing.

main_risk: Scene-centric photos differ in resolution and quality statistics, so matched-quality resampling is needed to isolate composition from image quality.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong crop augmentation may already convert object-centric photos into pseudo-scene training signal, muting the composition effect.

one_line_idea: The native-resolution distribution of the pretraining corpus imprints a scale prior on encoders: models systematically underperform at object scales rare in their corpus, and resolution-mix reshaping moves the failure profile predictably.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Corpora mix images of very different native resolutions and object scales, then training pipelines resize everything to fixed input sizes; the surviving effect of the original scale distribution on model behavior is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Despite resize normalization, the distribution of object-scale-in-pixels in the corpus imprints a prior: recognition and localization accuracy as a function of test-time object scale mirrors the training-time scale histogram, and reshaping the corpus scale mix shifts the accuracy-versus-scale profile in the corresponding direction.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Encoders pretrained on scale-mix-reshaped corpora (small-object-enriched versus large-object-enriched, matched size and content) will show opposite-signed accuracy differences of at least 4 points at the extreme test-scale bins, with profile shifts tracking the training histograms; the idea is falsified if the accuracy-versus-scale profiles differ by under 1.5 points everywhere despite the histogram intervention.
why_important: It reveals a composition variable that survives preprocessing and explains persistent scale-dependent failures, and it offers a data-level fix (scale-mix reshaping) that no augmentation currently targets deliberately.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale augmentation is standard, but the claim that corpus-level object-scale composition leaves a measurable prior after standard augmentation, with a controlled reshaping test, appears new territory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate object-scale histograms on a public corpus with a detector, build reshaped resamples, pretrain matched small encoders with identical augmentation, and evaluate accuracy versus test-time object scale on held-out data.
main_risk: Standard multi-scale crop augmentation may genuinely erase the corpus prior, yielding a null that is informative but less publishable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Resize-and-crop augmentation is assumed to fully decouple model behavior from the corpus scale distribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The imprint may exist but be too small to matter next to augmentation effects, making it a curiosity rather than a design lever.

one_line_idea: Concept drift of the visual world is fittable as a per-year decay law: models pretrained on older real crawls lose accuracy on newer-world probes at a measurable rate, giving corpora a quantifiable shelf life.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pretraining corpora are snapshots of the visual world at crawl time (products, vehicles, fashion, interfaces change), yet corpus age is absent from scaling and composition analysis, and models are deployed for years.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Accuracy on time-stamped probes decays approximately linearly-in-log-time with the gap between crawl vintage and probe vintage, with a decay constant that varies by category dynamism (fast for products/interfaces, near zero for natural kinds), so corpus vintage composition can be planned like depreciation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Pretraining matched models on real crawl slices from different years and probing with year-stamped test sets will show a monotone vintage-gap effect of at least 3 accuracy points per 5 years on dynamic categories and under 1 point on static categories; the idea is falsified if vintage effects are under 1 point per 5 years on dynamic categories or non-monotone in gap.
why_important: It prices data freshness against data volume for corpus maintenance, telling builders when refreshing beats growing and which categories drive the need.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal robustness studies exist for classifiers on shifting test sets; a vintage-controlled pretraining intervention with fitted per-category decay constants appears missing.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Corpus age is treated as irrelevant next to corpus size; refreshes happen for legal and availability reasons, not modeled performance decay.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Transfer to person-centric tasks (pose, attribute recognition) saturates in people-image share well below typical web levels, while per-individual memorization signal (re-identification of repeated individuals from embeddings) continues growing with share, creating a regime where share reduction is privacy-positive and utility-neutral.

one_line_idea: Contextual bias is a dose-dependent function of co-occurrence statistics in pretraining data: resampling rare-context images measurably improves out-of-context recognition at a fittable exchange rate.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Models rely on context (cows on grass, keyboards near monitors) and fail on out-of-context instances; the reliance is usually attributed to architecture or objective rather than quantified against the co-occurrence statistics of the training corpus.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Out-of-context failure rate is a smooth decreasing function of the count of decorrelated exemplars (object appearing outside its typical context) in pretraining, so corpus-level resampling that raises rare-context counts buys out-of-context accuracy at a measurable per-example exchange rate without hurting in-context accuracy.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contextual-bias phenomena are established; the controlled co-occurrence-resampling dose-response at matched corpus size appears missing.

one_line_idea: Vision pretraining tolerates far more data repetition than language lore implies: the per-epoch effective-data decay constant is small under strong augmentation, and the unique-data premium has been overstated for vision.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Language-model results on data-constrained scaling (repeating data loses value rapidly after a few epochs) are imported into vision planning, but augmentation makes vision epochs non-identical in ways language epochs are not.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under standard crop/color augmentation, the value decay per repetition in vision is governed by augmentation entropy: with strong augmentation, repeated epochs retain most of the marginal value of fresh data for many more repetitions than language-derived intuitions predict, and the decay constant is measurable and augmentation-dependent.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched total samples seen, a corpus repeated 8x with strong augmentation will retain at least 80% of the probe-accuracy gain of an 8x-larger unique corpus, versus under 60% with weak augmentation; the idea is falsified if strong-augmentation retention falls below 65% (vision behaves like language lore) or augmentation fails to modulate retention by at least 10 points.
why_important: Data-constrained domains (medical, industrial, scientific) need to know whether to spend on collection or compute; a measured vision-specific repetition law directly prices that decision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-constrained scaling laws are quantified for language (Muennighoff et al.); the vision analogue with augmentation as the controlling variable appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross unique-data size against repetition factor at matched samples seen, under two augmentation strengths, pretrain small encoders, and fit effective-data retention per repetition.
main_risk: Retention may depend on the pretraining objective family, requiring at least two objectives to claim generality and doubling the run count.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Repeating data more than a few epochs is widely assumed to be nearly worthless relative to fresh data, importing language-model findings wholesale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation may add diversity that is irrelevant to the features that saturate, making vision repetition decay match language decay after all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: About 12 small pretrains on public subsets, one A100: about 4 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: A collection-versus-repetition stopping rule: fitting the repetition-decay law on pilot runs yields a break-even collection cost per image, telling data-constrained teams exactly when to stop collecting real data and start repeating.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Teams in data-scarce domains decide between funding more collection and training longer on what they have using intuition, because no quantitative exchange rate between a marginal collected image and a marginal repetition exists.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The marginal value curves of fresh images and repetitions are both fittable from a small pilot grid, and their ratio yields a break-even collection cost that is stable enough within a domain to serve as a procurement decision rule.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Break-even points predicted from 1/8-scale pilot grids will match those measured on 8x-larger reference grids within a factor of 2 in at least 4 of 5 tested domain datasets; the idea is falsified if pilot-predicted break-evens err by more than 4x in most domains, making the rule useless for procurement.
why_important: This is the everyday economic decision of applied vision in medicine, agriculture, and industry, currently made blind; even a factor-of-2 rule changes real budgets.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-value estimation literatures exist (active learning, data valuation), but a repetition-law-based procurement break-even validated across scales appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 5 public domain datasets, run pilot grids crossing unique-data fractions with repetition factors, fit both marginal-value curves, predict break-evens, and verify against larger reference grids.
main_risk: Marginal value of collection depends on what is collected (tail versus head content), so the rule must be stated for random collection with tail-targeted collection as a separately fitted variant.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More data is always assumed worth collecting if affordable; repetition is a fallback rather than a priced alternative.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Break-even points may drift systematically with scale so pilot fits misprice large-scale decisions in one direction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: About 40 small runs across 5 public domain datasets, one A100: about 6-7 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Memorization onset precedes utility loss under repetition: as epochs accumulate there is a window where accuracy still improves while per-image memorization risk is already climbing steeply, so utility-monitored training silently walks into privacy debt.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Repetition decisions are monitored with validation accuracy alone, while memorization of repeated images is known to grow with exposure count; the relative timing of accuracy saturation and memorization growth is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The exposure-response curve of memorization (measured by membership-signal strength on repeated images) rises significantly before the accuracy-versus-epochs curve flattens, creating a quantifiable window in which continued training buys marginal accuracy at rapidly compounding privacy cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across an epoch sweep, membership-inference AUC on training images will rise by at least 0.10 during the interval in which validation probe accuracy still gains at least 1 point, in 2 of 2 tested objectives; the idea is falsified if membership AUC stays within 0.03 of baseline until after accuracy has saturated (privacy risk arrives only post-utility).
why_important: It defines the correct stopping criterion for privacy-conscious pretraining as a two-curve decision and shows that utility-only monitoring is structurally blind to the cost side.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Exposure-memorization dose-responses and epoch-accuracy curves are studied separately; their relative timing framed as a stopping-rule problem appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain small encoders with checkpointing across a long epoch sweep, at each checkpoint measure probe accuracy and membership-inference AUC on held-in versus held-out splits, and compare curve timings.
main_risk: Membership AUC depends on attack strength, so the timing claim must be shown robust across at least two attack families to avoid measuring attack artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Privacy risk is assumed to track overfitting, and overfitting is assumed visible in validation accuracy, so utility monitoring is believed to catch both.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For strongly augmented vision training, memorization may genuinely arrive only after accuracy saturation, validating current practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 instrumented pretrains plus repeated membership evaluations on public data, one A100: about 4 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Capability onset is set by absolute exemplar count, not scale: injecting a controlled number of capability-relevant real images moves the emergence point of visual capabilities to smaller compute, by a predictable amount.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Capability onsets in vision-language models are reported as functions of model scale or total data, with the implicit story that scale itself produces emergence; the confounded variable is how many capability-relevant examples the model has seen.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For capabilities tied to identifiable data slices, onset is governed by the absolute count of relevant exemplars crossing a threshold, so enriching a fixed-size corpus with relevant real examples shifts onset to smaller models and less compute along a predictable iso-count curve, demoting scale from cause to proxy.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For 3 tested capabilities (e.g., chart-value reading, handwritten-digit-in-scene recognition, clock reading) enrichment that raises relevant-exemplar count 10x at fixed corpus size will shift measured onset to at least 3x smaller compute, matching an iso-count prediction within 2x; the idea is falsified if onset shifts less than 1.5x in compute despite 10x enrichment for most capabilities.
why_important: If onsets are exemplar-count-driven, capability arrival can be engineered cheaply by data enrichment instead of waiting for scale, and emergence forecasting reduces to counting relevant data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency-capability correlations are known observationally; a controlled enrichment intervention that moves measured onset points appears untested in vision.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 3 capabilities with taggable relevant slices, pretrain small model ladders on natural versus enriched corpora at matched size, and locate onset (capability above a fixed criterion) per arm.
main_risk: Capabilities requiring compositional integration of multiple slices may not move with single-slice enrichment, restricting the law to slice-localizable capabilities.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Emergence is discussed as a property of scale, with data composition treated as fixed background.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Capacity thresholds may bind independently of data counts (small models cannot host the capability at any exemplar count), keeping scale causally necessary.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 model ladders (4 sizes) on 2 corpus arms with probe evaluations, one A100: about 6 GPU-days; all data drawn from public corpora.

one_line_idea: Behavioral emergence has representational precursors: linear-probe competence for a capability appears roughly an order of magnitude of compute before behavioral competence, enabling an early-warning forecaster for capability arrival.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Capabilities that look abruptly emergent at the behavior level make scaling forecasts unreliable, and the debate over whether emergence is real or a measurement artifact remains unsettled at the mechanism level.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The information needed for a capability accumulates smoothly in intermediate representations and is detectable by supervised probes well before the model's output behavior expresses it, so probe-competence trajectories across a scale ladder predict the behavioral onset scale ahead of time.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For at least 3 of 4 tested capabilities on a public model ladder, probe competence will reach 80% of its final level at least 5x less compute than behavioral competence does, and onset scale extrapolated from probe trajectories will predict behavioral onset within a factor of 3; the idea is falsified if probes and behavior rise at indistinguishable scales (ratio under 2x) or probe-based forecasts err by over 10x.
why_important: A validated precursor signal converts emergence from a forecasting hazard into a monitorable quantity, directly useful for capability forecasting and for safety-relevant scaling decisions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hidden-competence arguments exist in the emergence debate; a quantified probe-leads-behavior law with forecast validation on vision-language ladders appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public checkpoint ladder, measure behavioral capability curves and layer-wise probe curves for 4 capabilities, quantify the lead ratio, and validate forecasts on a capability held out from protocol design.
main_risk: Probes can exploit features that never causally drive behavior, making the precursor a correlate that fails exactly for the novel capabilities one wants to forecast.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Emergence is argued about via output metrics (abrupt versus smooth), with internal precursors treated as anecdote rather than as a forecasting instrument.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For capabilities requiring output-space coordination (long-horizon composition), representational precursors may genuinely not exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe and behavioral evaluation over about 8 public checkpoints, one A100: about 2-3 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Emergent object grouping in self-supervised attention is a percolation transition: attention-graph connectivity crosses a threshold as data grows, and object-centric data composition moves the transition point.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Self-supervised ViTs develop attention maps that group objects (widely popularized by DINO-style models), and the ability appears qualitatively somewhere along training/data scale, but no mechanism-level account predicts when.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Object grouping arises when within-object token affinity exceeds a graph-percolation threshold: below it, attention components fragment; above it, giant within-object components form abruptly, so the behavioral onset is predicted by graph statistics and is movable by increasing the object-centric share of pretraining data.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a data-scale ladder, the giant-component fraction of thresholded attention graphs will show a sharp transition whose location predicts unsupervised object-discovery onset (CorLoc criterion) within 2x data scale, and object-centric enrichment will shift both together by at least 2x; the idea is falsified if graph statistics evolve smoothly with no transition, or transition location fails to co-move with behavioral onset under enrichment.
why_important: It would be a concrete, testable physics-style mechanism for a celebrated emergent behavior, and the co-movement test distinguishes mechanism from correlation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Emergent attention grouping is well documented; a percolation-theoretic quantitative account with a composition intervention appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train small SSL ViTs across nested data sizes and two composition arms, compute attention-graph percolation statistics at checkpoints, and compare transition locations against object-discovery onset measured by CorLoc (box-level, not mask-level).
main_risk: Choice of attention threshold and layer aggregation could manufacture or hide transitions; robustness across analysis settings is mandatory.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Emergent grouping is treated as a qualitative gift of self-supervision at scale, without a predictive mechanism.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grouping ability may grow continuously and only look abrupt through thresholded metrics, in which case percolation is the wrong formalism.
fastest_falsification_experiment: About 8 small SSL pretrains plus graph analysis, one A100: about 5 GPU-days; CorLoc-based evaluation avoids mask metrics; all data drawn from public corpora.

one_line_idea: Attribute-object binding emerges only when pretraining data decorrelates attributes from objects: binding capability tracks the count of counter-stereotypical pairings, not total data, and can be induced early by decorrelation-targeted resampling.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language models notoriously fail attribute binding (confusing which object carries which color or material), and the failure persists across scale in an irregular way that scale-centric accounts do not explain.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Binding competence is gated by exposure to attribute-object combinations that break natural correlations (yellow bananas teach nothing about binding; blue bananas do), so the capability tracks counter-stereotypical pair counts, and resampling real data to raise decorrelation moves binding scores at fixed total scale.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Raising counter-stereotypical pair share 5x by resampling real data at matched corpus size will improve binding-benchmark accuracy by at least 8 points at a scale where the natural-composition control improves under 2 points from further scale alone; the idea is falsified if decorrelation enrichment moves binding by under 3 points or the control matches it.
why_important: Binding is a canonical unsolved compositionality failure; establishing it as a data-decorrelation dose effect redirects effort from architecture search to targeted real-data sourcing and forecasts which corpora can never teach binding.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Binding failures are heavily documented via benchmarks; a controlled decorrelation-resampling intervention on real pretraining data appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Tag attribute-object pairs in a public captioned corpus, construct matched-size arms differing 5x in counter-stereotypical share, pretrain small contrastive models, and evaluate on public binding benchmarks.
main_risk: Counter-stereotypical real pairs are scarce, capping enrichment factors and possibly requiring capability evaluation at reduced binding difficulty.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Binding failure is treated as an architectural or objective deficiency of contrastive training rather than a statistical property of what the data can disambiguate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive objectives may be structurally unable to represent binding regardless of data statistics, in which case enrichment moves nothing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2-3 small pretrains plus binding benchmark evaluation, one A100: about 4 GPU-days; all data drawn from public corpora.

one_line_idea: Emergence abruptness is predicted by task decomposability: capabilities with probeable independent sub-skills scale smoothly, while non-decomposable capabilities show genuinely discontinuous competence growth even under continuous metrics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The emergence debate has focused on whether discontinuities are metric artifacts, leaving unexplained why some capabilities look abrupt under every reasonable metric while others never do.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When a capability factorizes into sub-skills that accumulate independently, aggregate competence inherits their smooth scaling; when success requires simultaneous adequacy of interlocking components, competence is a product of near-thresholds and rises abruptly, so measured sub-skill structure predicts which capabilities will look emergent under continuous scoring.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Classifying 8 capabilities by sub-skill decomposability (via probe batteries) will predict which show high scaling-curve curvature under continuous partial-credit metrics with at least 7 of 8 correct; the idea is falsified if decomposability fails to predict curvature better than chance (4 of 8) across the battery.
why_important: It resolves the emergence controversy constructively: rather than arguing artifacts, it offers a measurable property that forecasts abruptness, which matters for both capability planning and safety analysis.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The metric-artifact critique and its rebuttals are published; a decomposability-based predictive taxonomy with pre-registered classification accuracy appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 8 visual capabilities on a public ladder, build sub-skill probe batteries, score decomposability, fit continuous-metric scaling curves, and test the predicted association between decomposability and curvature.
main_risk: Decomposability scoring is researcher-dependent; the battery must be pre-registered before curves are seen to avoid circularity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Post-mirage, many researchers default to all emergence is metric artifact, leaving no room for structurally abrupt capabilities.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Apparent non-decomposability may only reflect missing imagination about sub-skills, collapsing the taxonomy once better probes exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe and behavioral evaluation across about 8 public checkpoints, one A100: about 3 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Capabilities emerge in a universal order set by data statistics: onset ordering across capability batteries is nearly identical across architectures trained on the same corpus, and reshuffles when the corpus changes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Capability onsets are catalogued per model family, and it is unknown whether the order in which capabilities arrive reflects architecture-specific learning or corpus-level statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Onset order is determined primarily by data-statistical difficulty (relevant-exemplar frequency times complexity), so different architectures on the same corpus share onset order almost perfectly, while the same architecture on recomposed corpora reorders onsets according to the shifted statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 2 architecture families on one corpus, onset-order rank correlation over a 10-capability battery will exceed 0.8, while recomposing the corpus (targeted enrichment of 3 capabilities' slices) will reorder onsets with rank correlation below 0.5 to the original; the idea is falsified if cross-architecture correlation falls below 0.5 (order is architecture-specific) or recomposition fails to reorder (correlation stays above 0.8).
why_important: Universal, data-determined ordering would let one cheap reference ladder forecast capability schedules for any architecture, and would pinpoint data recomposition as the lever for changing what arrives first.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cross-family behavioral comparisons exist informally; a controlled architecture-versus-composition dissociation of onset order appears unexamined.

one_line_idea: Deja-vu-style memorization in self-supervised encoders follows a scaling law in model size at fixed data: per-image recoverability grows with a fittable exponent, making privacy risk of future releases forecastable.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Self-supervised encoders can memorize individual training images (recovering foreground content from background crops, as shown in deja-vu-style studies), but how this risk scales with model size at fixed data is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image memorization (fraction of training images whose held-out content is recoverable from partial views via the encoder) grows smoothly with model capacity at fixed data, following a power law whose exponent enables extrapolation of privacy risk to larger releases before they are trained.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a 4-point model-size ladder at fixed data, the recoverable-image fraction will fit a power law with held-out-rung prediction error under 30% relative, and the fraction will grow at least 2x from smallest to largest rung; the idea is falsified if memorization is flat in capacity (under 1.2x growth) or so irregular that ladder fits mispredict the held-out rung by over 2x.
why_important: A validated memorization-scaling law converts privacy assessment from post-hoc auditing to pre-release forecasting, exactly the instrument regulators and release teams lack.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Deja-vu memorization is demonstrated at fixed scale; the capacity-scaling law with forecast validation appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 4 SSL encoders of increasing size on a fixed public corpus, run partial-view recovery attacks on a fixed image panel with held-out controls, fit the law on 3 rungs, and validate on the 4th.
main_risk: Recovery-attack strength may itself interact with model size (bigger models are easier to attack for reasons other than memorization), inflating the exponent; attack-normalized controls are needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Memorization risk is discussed as present-or-absent per model family, without a quantitative capacity law for discriminative encoders.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Capacity may be spent on generalizable structure with memorization saturating early, flattening the law precisely where extrapolation matters.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 4 small SSL pretrains plus recovery evaluation on public data, one A100: about 6 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Duplication dose-response for discriminative memorization has a sharp knee: per-image membership signal is near-floor below a duplication threshold and rises steeply above it, giving dedup policy a principled operating point.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Duplication drives memorization in generative models with documented dose-response behavior, but the corresponding curve for discriminative/dense vision models is unmeasured, leaving dedup thresholds for encoder training without a privacy-side justification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Membership-signal strength for an individual image is a threshold-like function of its duplication count in encoder pretraining: negligible below a knee (a few occurrences), then rising steeply and saturating, with the knee location shifting predictably with model size and data size.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Controlled duplicate injection at counts 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 will show membership AUC on injected images within 0.03 of baseline through count 2, then rising by at least 0.15 by count 16; the idea is falsified if AUC grows near-linearly from count 1 (no knee) or stays within 0.05 of baseline through count 32 (no dose effect).
why_important: The knee location is exactly the number dedup pipelines should target: below it, further dedup buys no privacy; above it, every allowed duplicate is quantifiable risk.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Duplication-memorization curves exist for image generators; the discriminative-encoder dose-response with knee localization appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Inject a panel of real images at controlled duplication counts into a fixed pretraining corpus, train matched encoders, and measure per-count membership AUC with strong per-example attacks.
main_risk: Interactions with image atypicality could smear the knee; the panel must stratify typical and atypical images to keep curves interpretable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dedup thresholds for encoder corpora are set by storage and quality considerations, with privacy benefits asserted qualitatively.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation may flatten the dose-response into a slow linear rise, leaving no knee to anchor policy.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2-3 pretraining runs with injected panels plus attack evaluation, one A100: about 4-5 GPU-days on public data.

one_line_idea: Which images a vision model will memorize is predictable before training: a risk score from data-level properties alone (duplication, local density, atypicality) identifies most eventually-memorized images without touching the model.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Memorization audits run after training, when the privacy cost is already incurred; theory (long-tail memorization) suggests which examples get memorized, but a validated pre-training predictor for vision corpora does not exist.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Memorization propensity is dominated by data-level properties measurable on the corpus alone: duplication count, embedding-space local density, and within-cluster atypicality, so a simple score fitted on one training run transfers to new corpora and models, flagging high-risk images before compute is spent.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A data-only risk score will achieve at least 0.80 AUC at retrieving the top-5%-memorized images (ground truth from post-training attacks) on a held-out corpus and architecture, versus near 0.5 for random; the idea is falsified if transfer AUC falls below 0.65, indicating memorization is dominated by training-run idiosyncrasies rather than data properties.
why_important: A pre-training privacy audit enables surgical intervention (exclusion, blurring, count capping) at the only time it is cheap, and converts memorization theory into an operational tool.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Long-tail memorization theory (Feldman) and post-hoc audits exist; a validated cross-corpus, cross-architecture pre-training predictor for vision appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train encoders on 2 public corpora, establish per-image memorization ground truth via attacks, fit the data-only score on one corpus, and evaluate retrieval of memorized images on the other corpus and a different architecture.
main_risk: Ground-truth memorization labels depend on attack sensitivity; weak attacks would understate achievable AUC and unfairly kill the predictor.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Memorization is treated as knowable only by attacking the trained model, making privacy auditing inherently post-hoc.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimization noise may randomize which of the many eligible images actually get memorized, capping predictability regardless of feature quality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 pretrains plus attack-based labeling and score fitting on public data, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Dense models memorize regions, not images: memorization in detectors and depth networks concentrates on rare object instances within scenes, so region-level audits find leakage that image-level audits miss entirely.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Memorization auditing treats the image as the unit of storage, but dense models process scenes containing many objects of very different rarity, and image-level membership tests aggregate away localized effects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For dense prediction models, memorization is spatially localized on rare instances (unusual objects, distinctive signage, specific faces) while the surrounding scene is generically processed, so region-restricted membership statistics dramatically outperform image-level statistics at detecting leakage.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Region-level membership tests focused on rare-instance boxes will achieve at least 0.12 higher AUC than image-level tests on the same trained detectors, and the per-region signal will correlate with instance rarity (correlation at least 0.5); the idea is falsified if region-level AUC exceeds image-level by under 0.03, indicating memorization is spatially diffuse.
why_important: Privacy audits of dense models (surveillance, driving, medical) currently use image-level tools that this hypothesis says are systematically blind; region-level auditing would change what counts as a passed audit.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Membership inference on classifiers and encoders is developed; spatial localization of memorization within scenes for dense models appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a detector and a depth model on public scene data with tracked rare instances, run membership tests at image level and per-region level using localized loss and feature statistics, and compare AUCs against rarity.
main_risk: Region-level statistics have fewer samples per test unit, so the comparison must control the multiple-testing advantage of many regions per image.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Membership and memorization are treated as image-level properties across vision privacy work.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense objectives may spread memorization across scene context (background co-memorized with instance), making image-level tests adequate after all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 downstream trainings plus attack evaluation on public detection/depth data, one A100: about 4 GPU-days; box-level and depth-error signals, no mask metrics.

one_line_idea: Detectors replay memorized rare instances: context similar to a memorized training scene triggers hallucinated detections of the memorized object, a failure mode invisible to aggregate AP and traceable to duplication.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection models produce context-driven false positives, and separately, models memorize rare training instances; whether memorized instances become context-triggered hallucinations is untested.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When a rare instance co-occurs repeatedly with a distinctive context during training, the detector binds them, so presenting the context without the instance at test time elicits a hallucinated detection matching the memorized instance's class and location statistics, at rates that grow with training duplication of the pair.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Injecting rare instance-context pairs at duplication counts 1, 8, and 32, then testing on instance-removed context images, will show hallucinated-detection rates for the memorized class rising by at least 5x from count 1 to count 32, with matched control contexts flat; the idea is falsified if hallucination rates at count 32 are within 1.5x of count 1 or controls rise equally.
why_important: It identifies a concrete, dose-dependent mechanism by which training-data privacy leaks into deployment behavior (the model reveals what it saw), relevant to both reliability and forensic auditing of detectors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context bias and memorization are separately documented; the duplication-dosed replay mechanism with instance-removed testing appears novel territory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite real rare objects into distinctive real scenes at controlled duplication, fine-tune a detector on the augmented corpus, and measure class-specific false positives on instance-removed variants versus controls.
main_risk: Instance removal by editing may leave artifacts that themselves trigger detections; removal must be validated with human inspection and artifact controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detector false positives are attributed to generic context bias, not to replay of specific memorized training instances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection training may regularize instance-context binding away, with hallucinations driven by class-level priors that no duplication dose can modulate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Corpus preparation plus 2-3 detector trainings and evaluation, one A100: about 4 GPU-days; public detection data, box-level metrics.

one_line_idea: Memorization decays under fresh data with a fittable forgetting law: scheduling a clean-data tail at the end of pretraining purges most early-acquired memorization at small utility cost, yielding a data-level privacy mitigation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Memorized examples from early training are partially forgotten as training continues on other data (documented in language models), but the decay law for vision encoders and its exploitability as a scheduling mitigation are unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image membership signal decays approximately as a power law in post-exposure fresh samples seen, so appending a modest clean-data tail (images verified non-sensitive) after the main corpus purges most memorization of earlier sensitive content at a quantifiable utility cost near zero.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A clean tail equal to 10% of training length will reduce membership AUC on early-seen panel images by at least 60% of its excess over baseline while final probe accuracy changes by under 0.5 points; the idea is falsified if AUC excess drops by under 20% or utility cost exceeds 2 points, making the mitigation useless.
why_important: It would be the cheapest known memorization mitigation: no architecture change, no private optimizer, just data ordering, applicable retroactively to any planned run.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Forgetting of memorized data is documented in language settings (Jagielski et al.); the vision-encoder decay-law fit and its deliberate use as a scheduling mitigation appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain with a sensitive panel placed early, vary clean-tail length across arms, and measure panel membership AUC and probe utility per arm.
main_risk: The manipulated variable is data placement, which borders on training-schedule territory; the claim is kept data-level by fixing the optimizer and varying only corpus composition over time.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Memorization mitigation is assumed to require private training methods or data exclusion, not ordering; whatever is seen is assumed retained.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Vision encoders may retain early memorization far longer than language models due to augmentation-anchored representations, flattening the decay.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 3-4 pretrains with panel injection plus attack evaluation, one A100: about 5 GPU-days on public data.

one_line_idea: The marginal capability of the last 10x of encoder scale is disproportionately tail memorization: decomposing scale gains by example typicality shows generalization gains saturating while memorization-like gains keep growing.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Larger encoders both generalize better and memorize more, and headline benchmark gains from the largest scale steps are reported without decomposing which kind of improvement they represent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale gains decompose by test-example typicality: gains on typical examples (generalization-driven) saturate at moderate scale, while gains concentrated on atypical, training-similar examples (memorization-driven) continue, so the largest scale steps mostly buy performance that behaves like lookup rather than abstraction.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across the top decade of a public model ladder, at least 60% of aggregate accuracy improvement will come from the quartile of test examples most similar to training data, with the most-dissimilar quartile contributing under 15%; the idea is falsified if gains are spread within 1.5x across similarity quartiles, indicating scale keeps buying broad generalization.
why_important: If late scale gains are similarity-concentrated, benchmark-driven scale narratives overstate progress in the capability that matters for novel inputs, and evaluation should stratify by training-similarity as standard practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Similarity-stratified evaluation exists for individual models (seen-versus-unseen analyses); applying it to decompose marginal scale gains along ladders appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For an open-data model ladder, index test sets by nearest-neighbor similarity to the training corpus, and decompose per-rung accuracy improvements by similarity quartile.
main_risk: Similarity metrics computed with an embedding model may themselves favor what models find easy, requiring at least two independent similarity measures.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scale improvements are presented and consumed as general capability growth, uniformly meaningful across the input distribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Late-scale gains may genuinely concentrate on hard dissimilar examples (better abstraction), inverting the predicted decomposition.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Similarity indexing plus stratified evaluation of about 6 public open-data checkpoints, one A100: about 2 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Supervised and self-supervised models memorize different things: label-coupled memorization versus content memorization dissociate under attack, and mitigations tuned for one transfer poorly to the other.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Memorization findings from supervised classifiers (label-noise memorization, long-tail effects) and from self-supervised encoders (content recovery) are cited interchangeably, though the objects being memorized differ.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Supervised training memorizes image-label couplings (detectable by label-conditioned attacks, strongest for mislabeled or ambiguous images) while self-supervised training memorizes image content (detectable by content-recovery attacks, strongest for visually atypical images), so the memorized-example sets overlap weakly and defenses transfer asymmetrically.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training matched architectures supervised and self-supervised on the same corpus will yield top-memorized-example sets with Jaccard overlap under 0.3, and a defense effective for one paradigm (e.g., label smoothing versus stronger cropping) will reduce the other paradigm's memorization by under a third of its own-paradigm effect; the idea is falsified if overlap exceeds 0.6 or defenses transfer near-symmetrically.
why_important: Privacy assessments currently borrow evidence across paradigms; showing dissociation would force paradigm-specific auditing standards and defense choices.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both memorization literatures are developed separately; a same-corpus, matched-architecture dissociation study appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train supervised and SSL models on one public labeled corpus, run label-conditioned and content-recovery attacks on both, compare memorized-set overlap, then apply paradigm-typical defenses and measure cross-paradigm mitigation.
main_risk: Attack strength differences between paradigms could masquerade as dissociation; attacks must be power-matched via injected canary panels.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Memorization is treated as a single phenomenon with interchangeable evidence and mitigations across training paradigms.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both paradigms may ultimately memorize the same atypical images for capacity reasons, with attack-visible differences being superficial.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2 trainings plus two attack families and two defense arms on public data, one A100: about 5-6 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Pretraining memorization survives downstream fine-tuning: membership of pretraining images remains detectable from fully fine-tuned dense-task models, so releasing a fine-tuned model leaks the pretraining set.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Organizations assume that fine-tuning on a new task overwrites pretraining specifics, and privacy reviews of released task models rarely consider the pretraining corpus as a leakage surface.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Memorized pretraining content is stored in features that dense-task fine-tuning reuses rather than overwrites, so membership signals for pretraining images persist through full fine-tuning at levels well above chance, and persist more for dense tasks (which preserve spatial features) than for classification fine-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Membership AUC for a pretraining canary panel measured on fully fine-tuned depth and detection models will remain at least 0.60 where the pre-fine-tuning encoder shows at least 0.75, with dense-task persistence exceeding classification persistence by at least 0.05 AUC; the idea is falsified if post-fine-tuning AUC falls below 0.55 everywhere (fine-tuning effectively purges) or the dense-versus-classification ordering reverses.
why_important: If leakage survives fine-tuning, the deployment surface of pretraining privacy violations is every downstream model, not just released encoders, which changes legal exposure and release policy for the entire transfer-learning ecosystem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Membership inference targets encoders or end-task models trained from scratch; persistence of pretraining membership through full fine-tuning for dense tasks appears unmeasured.
