one_line_idea: Memorization dosimetry for vision releases: a standardized panel of real held-out images injected at graded duplication counts turns per-model privacy risk into a measured dose-response curve reportable on model cards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision model releases carry no quantitative memorization metric; audits are ad hoc, non-comparable across models, and usually run by outsiders after release.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Injecting a standardized panel of consented real images at controlled duplication counts during pretraining yields a per-model dose-response curve (membership signal versus count) that is stable across panel choices, enabling standardized cross-model privacy comparison at negligible training cost.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Canary methodology exists for language-model secrets (secret-sharer style); a standardized, duplication-graded real-image panel protocol for vision pretraining releases appears unproposed.

main_risk: Panel images must be statistically typical of sensitive content classes or the curve misprices risk for the content that matters (faces, documents, medical).
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Memorization risk is treated as unquantifiable at training time and is omitted from model documentation entirely.

one_line_idea: Encoders memorize background people: individuals occupying under 5% of image pixels are re-identifiable from embeddings of held-out photos, and selective face/person blurring of the corpus removes the risk at near-zero utility cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web images contain incidental bystanders, and corpus-level face blurring has been shown to cost little accuracy on ImageNet-scale supervised training; whether unblurred incidental people are actually memorized by modern encoders in a re-identifiable way is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Encoders bind identity features of repeatedly appearing individuals even when those individuals are small and incidental, so embedding-space retrieval links held-out photos of such individuals to their training appearances well above chance, and this linkage is eliminated by corpus-side person-region blurring with negligible effect on standard transfer.

why_important: It tests the exact privacy claim regulators care about (are people in the background of web photos extractable from released encoders) and evaluates the practical mitigation in the same experiment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Face-blurring utility costs are measured for supervised ImageNet training; the incidental-person memorization measurement and blurring-as-mitigation test for modern SSL encoders appear missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a corpus with tracked repeated bystanders (public photo collections with identity metadata), pretrain encoders on raw versus person-blurred variants, and run cross-photo identity retrieval plus a utility suite.
main_risk: Public datasets with repeated identifiable bystanders and consent-appropriate licensing are limited; celebrity-in-crowd photo collections may be the only viable substrate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Incidental background people are assumed too small and rare to be memorized, so blurring is framed as an abundance of caution with a feared utility cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sub-5%-area appearances may fall below the resolution at which identity features survive patchification, making incidental memorization physically negligible.

one_line_idea: Structured outputs leak more: membership inference against dense predictors using spatially resolved error patterns beats pooled image-level attacks by a wide margin, because per-location residuals carry per-image fingerprints.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Membership inference methodology was developed for classifiers with scalar outputs, and is applied to dense models by pooling losses over space, discarding exactly the high-dimensional structure dense models expose.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training on an image leaves spatially structured residual patterns (which regions the model fits unusually well) that survive in dense predictions, so attacks that use the spatial residual field as a signature outperform pooled-loss attacks substantially, making dense models strictly leakier than their classification counterparts at matched training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On matched depth-estimation and classification models trained on the same images, a spatial-residual-field attack will exceed pooled-loss attack AUC by at least 0.08 on the dense model, and the dense model's best-attack AUC will exceed the classifier's by at least 0.05; the idea is falsified if spatial structure adds under 0.02 AUC or dense models prove no leakier than classifiers.
why_important: Dense models are deployed in privacy-sensitive settings (driving, medical, mapping) under auditing standards developed on classifiers; if dense outputs are structurally leakier, those standards understate risk categorically.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Membership inference against segmentation exists in scattered work; the spatial-residual-signature formulation with a dense-versus-classifier leakage comparison appears undeveloped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train depth and classification models on the same public image set, implement pooled and spatial-field attacks (residual autocorrelation, per-region ranking features), and compare AUCs under matched threat models.
main_risk: Spatial attacks need ground-truth or proxy targets at test time; attacks must be designed for the realistic setting where the attacker lacks true labels.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense models are implicitly assumed to inherit classifier-level membership risk, with output structure treated as irrelevant to leakage.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense training averages gradients over many spatial locations per image, which may dilute per-image fingerprints below what spatial attacks can recover.

one_line_idea: Average-case membership metrics hide a vulnerable tail whose size is set by the duplication spectrum: TPR at very low FPR is high for a predictable subset even when aggregate AUC looks safe.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-encoder membership studies often report modest average AUC and conclude low risk, while the security-relevant statistic (true-positive rate at very low false-positive rate) is known from classifier work to behave differently from averages.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Membership risk in web-trained encoders is concentrated: a small subset of images (high-duplication, high-atypicality) is confidently identifiable at 0.1% FPR even when population AUC is near 0.6, and the vulnerable-subset size is predictable from the corpus duplication and density spectra alone.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On encoder trainings with realistic duplication spectra, at least 1% of training images will be detectable at TPR 20x the FPR at 0.1% FPR, and the size of this subset will be predicted within 2x by a duplication-density model fitted on a different corpus; the idea is falsified if the low-FPR regime shows TPR under 5x FPR for all subsets (no vulnerable tail) or subset-size predictions err by over 5x.
why_important: Privacy conclusions drawn from average AUC are the norm in vision; demonstrating a predictable vulnerable tail would invalidate safe-on-average claims and supply the corrected reporting statistic.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Low-FPR evaluation is established as the right metric for classifiers (membership inference from first principles); its application to vision encoders with a data-level predictor of tail size appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train encoders on corpora with measured duplication spectra, run per-example strong attacks, compute full TPR-FPR curves, and test tail-size predictions from the data-level model.
main_risk: Estimating TPR at 0.1% FPR needs large member and non-member pools; underpowered evaluation would produce noisy tail estimates.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Modest average membership AUC on encoders is read as encoders are hard to attack, and reporting practice follows averages.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Vision-specific augmentation may genuinely protect even duplicated atypical images, emptying the vulnerable tail that classifier intuitions predict.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 2-3 pretrains with large attack pools on public data, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Bigger is not leakier at web scale: at fixed unique data, membership risk grows with model size, but along the realistic joint-scaling path (data grows with model) per-image risk falls, inverting the intuitive scale-risk narrative.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Public discussion assumes larger foundation models are automatically worse for privacy, but model releases scale data alongside parameters, and the two effects on per-image exposure act in opposite directions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image membership signal increases with capacity at fixed data but decreases with data at fixed capacity (exposure dilution), and along compute-optimal joint scaling the dilution effect dominates, so newer larger releases are less attackable per ordinary image while remaining attackable on the duplicated tail.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a grid crossing model size with data size, membership AUC will rise with capacity at fixed data (at least +0.05 per 4x capacity) and fall along the joint-scaling diagonal (at least -0.04 per diagonal step) for typical images, while high-duplication images stay flat within 0.03; the idea is falsified if AUC rises along the diagonal for typical images, confirming the bigger-is-leakier narrative.
why_important: The result determines whether scale is a privacy problem or (with data discipline) a privacy mitigation, directly informing policy debates that currently assume the former.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Capacity and data effects on membership risk are known separately; the joint-scaling-path analysis with duplication stratification appears unmeasured for vision encoders.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a 3x3 model-size by data-size grid, attack each with a fixed strong attack, stratify results by duplication, and read effects along axes and the diagonal.
main_risk: The diagonal conclusion depends on the assumed joint-scaling policy; results must be reported for at least two plausible scaling paths.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Larger models are assumed monotonically riskier for training-data privacy regardless of accompanying data growth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Bigger models may memorize the tail so much more efficiently that even ordinary-image risk rises along realistic scaling paths.

one_line_idea: Better encoders are more invertible: input-image reconstructability from frozen patch tokens increases with encoder scale, contradicting the intuition that more abstract features are safer to share.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Organizations share dense features (patch tokens, feature maps) across services and vendors on the assumption that features abstract away pixel content, and that stronger models abstract more.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale improves the information efficiency of features: larger encoders preserve more input-specific detail in linearly accessible form, so reconstruction attacks against frozen patch tokens recover inputs with fidelity that increases, not decreases, along scale ladders at fixed token count.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training identical reconstruction decoders against patch tokens from a 4-rung public encoder ladder will show monotone fidelity improvement with scale, with the largest rung beating the smallest by at least 0.1 LPIPS (or 20% relative retrieval-based identification), and the idea is falsified if fidelity is flat within 0.03 LPIPS or decreases with scale.
why_important: Feature-sharing practices and privacy reviews assume an abstraction gradient that this result would invert: the better the model you buy, the more your shared features reveal.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Feature inversion is classical (Mahendran-Vedaldi, Dosovitskiy-Brox era) on individual networks; the scale-trend claim across modern foundation ladders appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a reconstruction decoder architecture and training budget, train one per ladder rung against frozen tokens on public images, and evaluate reconstruction fidelity and identification rate on held-out images.
main_risk: Fidelity differences may be driven by token dimensionality rather than scale per se, requiring dimension-matched controls via random projection.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stronger encoders are assumed to produce more abstract, less pixel-revealing features, making feature sharing safer as models improve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Heavy augmentation in large-model training might genuinely discard instance detail, flattening or reversing the invertibility trend.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 4 decoder trainings against public checkpoints on public images, one A100: about 3 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Global embeddings re-identify: a single CLIP-style image vector suffices to link a person or place across photo collections at rates that make embedding release equivalent to content release for linkage purposes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Image embeddings are stored, shared, and sold at scale (search indices, recommendation systems, analytics) under the assumption that a vector is not personal data in the way the photo is.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Modern foundation embeddings preserve identity- and location-linking information so well that nearest-neighbor search over an attacker's gallery re-identifies the subject or place of an embedded photo at high rates, and linkage success scales with both embedding model quality and gallery size along measurable curves.

minimal_falsification_experiment: Embed held-out photos of subjects with known repeated appearances in a public gallery, run nearest-neighbor linkage across embedding models of increasing scale, and fit linkage-rate curves versus gallery coverage.
main_risk: Linkage rates depend heavily on subject distinctiveness; results must be stratified (landmarks versus persons versus interiors) to avoid one stratum dominating the headline.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Storing embeddings instead of images is widely treated as a meaningful privacy mitigation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For non-famous subjects with sparse galleries, linkage may be so rare that embeddings are effectively safe in realistic threat models.

one_line_idea: Redact-then-encode fails: content masked out of an image before encoding is partially recoverable from the visible-region tokens, because attention mixes neighborhood evidence into every token, and the leak grows with encoder scale.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Privacy pipelines blur or blackout sensitive regions (faces, plates, screens) before running foundation encoders, treating the redaction as final; token-level information flow in ViTs is not part of that threat model.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Visible-region tokens absorb contextual inferences about redacted content (who plausibly stood there, what the screen likely showed at category level), so attribute-recovery attacks on redacted-region content succeed above chance using only visible-region tokens, with success growing with encoder scale and context strength.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Attribute classifiers reading only visible-region tokens of redacted images will recover redacted-region attributes (clothing color, object category, coarse identity group) at least 15 points above chance on average across attributes, and at least 5 points above a pixels-only baseline given the same visible pixels; the idea is falsified if token-based recovery is within 2 points of the pixel baseline, showing encoders add no contextual amplification.
why_important: If encoders amplify contextual leakage beyond what the visible pixels imply, redaction standards for pipelines that share features (not images) are systematically insufficient and need feature-side controls.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attention mixing is well known mechanically; its quantification as a redaction-defeating leakage channel with pixel-baseline controls appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Redact annotated regions on public images, encode with ladder encoders, train attribute probes on visible-region tokens versus visible-pixel baselines, and compare recovery rates across scales.
main_risk: The pixel baseline must be strong (same architecture retrained on redacted pixels) or the encoder amplification claim is confounded by probe capacity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Redaction before encoding is treated as removing the redacted information from all downstream artifacts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Encoders may add little beyond what strong pixel-context models already infer, making the redaction gap a property of context, not of encoding.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe training over public checkpoints on redacted public images, one A100: about 2-3 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: The deep-cut-is-safe heuristic of split inference fails slowly: invertibility declines with cut depth only as a shallow power law, so even late-layer features leak reconstructable content, and the curve quantifies exactly how much safety each layer buys.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Split inference deployments (device computes early layers, server receives intermediate features) choose cut points by compute convenience with a vague belief that deeper cuts protect user images.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reconstruction fidelity from intermediate features declines smoothly and slowly with cut depth fraction rather than dropping at any safe layer, because spatial detail is preserved by residual streams; the fitted depth-leakage curve is stable across encoder scales, making cut-point privacy a quantifiable engineering parameter rather than a hope.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training reconstruction decoders at 6 cut depths across 2 public encoders will show identification-grade reconstruction (top-1 retrieval of the source image from a 100k gallery above 50%) persisting past the 75% depth point, with fidelity following a smooth fit (R-squared at least 0.9) in depth fraction; the idea is falsified if identification collapses below 10% by mid-depth (deep cuts genuinely safe) or the curve is too irregular to fit (R-squared under 0.6).
why_important: Split inference is a mainstream edge-AI pattern; a measured depth-leakage curve replaces folklore in a decision every deployment makes, and the persistence result would force feature-side protections regardless of cut point.

why_important: Every contamination audit today ends with an unquantified shadow over reported results; a transferable inflation law converts audits into corrected leaderboards and settles how-much-does-it-matter disputes with numbers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contamination effects have been measured in isolated language-model studies; a fitted, cross-family-validated inflation law for vision benchmarks appears absent.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Inflation may be dominated by benchmark-specific item structure (some items are far more memorable), defeating any low-dimensional law.

why_it_might_be_wrong: High-duplication contamination may anchor permanently regardless of position, restricting the half-life claim to low-dose leakage.

problem: [KNOWN FACT] Recent language-model work estimates a roughly constant memorization capacity per parameter, but no analogous constant exists for vision encoders, leaving no principled bound on how much specific training content a released vision model can store.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Paired tests are standard in ML broadly, but a pre-registered paired-permutation protocol for COCO-style AP with a measured interval-shrinkage factor and conclusion-flip audit appears unpublished for detection.

main_risk: AP is a set-level statistic that does not decompose exactly into per-image contributions, so the paired proxy may rank models slightly differently than corpus-level AP and the repair could be rejected on faithfulness grounds.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners treat the shared test set as already controlling for difficulty and assume reported AP deltas are comparable without explicit pairing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If between-image variance is small relative to within-image matching noise, pairing buys little and interval widths will barely change.

one_line_idea: A reference-decoder evaluation contract that pins score thresholds, NMS behavior, and max-detections into a single frozen decoding specification makes detector rankings invariant across evaluation harnesses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The same detector checkpoint can receive different AP values and even different rankings under different evaluation harnesses because score thresholds, NMS variants, and per-image detection caps differ across implementations.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-harness rank instability is caused almost entirely by the unpinned decoding stage (thresholding, NMS, caps), not by metric arithmetic, so shipping a frozen reference decoder that consumes raw logits/boxes will eliminate harness-induced rank flips.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across three public evaluation stacks applied to 10 public detectors on COCO val2017, at least two pairwise rank flips will occur under default decoding, and re-evaluating from raw outputs through the frozen reference decoder will reduce flips to zero; kill the idea if flips persist after pinning or if default stacks already agree on all pairs.
why_important: Converts the well-documented harness-variance complaint into an adoptable artifact: a decoding contract that makes leaderboard numbers portable across codebases.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Harness discrepancies have been reported anecdotally, but a decoding-contract artifact with a measured before/after rank-flip count appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Export raw pre-NMS outputs for 10 detectors, evaluate with pycocotools defaults, a second public harness, and a third with altered max-dets/threshold defaults, then re-evaluate all through one pinned decoder and count pairwise rank flips before and after.
main_risk: Some architectures (end-to-end set predictors) have no natural pre-NMS raw output aligned with anchor-based models, making one shared decoding contract partially ill-defined.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Researchers assume pycocotools is a de facto standard and that harness choice is a rounding-error concern.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If most modern models are evaluated through nearly identical default pipelines already, measured flips may be zero and the repair unnecessary.

one_line_idea: Error-decomposition-matched interventions: choosing the training fix whose target matches the dominant TIDE-style error type of a detector yields reliably larger gains than a mismatched fix, making error decomposition an actionable prescription rather than a diagnostic.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Error decompositions in the TIDE style attribute detector AP loss to classification, localization, duplicate, background, and missed-detection components, but papers use them descriptively and pick training interventions by fashion.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Error types are causally separable enough that an intervention targeting the dominant error component (e.g., an IoU-aware localization head when localization error dominates, or a stronger classification loss when classification error dominates) transfers its benefit primarily through that component, so decomposition-matched prescriptions beat mismatched ones under identical budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For two public detectors with different dominant error types on COCO, applying the matched intervention will yield at least +1.0 AP and at least twice the gain of the mismatched intervention applied to the same model; kill the idea if matched and mismatched interventions differ by less than 0.3 AP on both models.
why_important: Turns a widely cited audit instrument into a decision procedure, giving practitioners a falsifiable rule for spending a fixed training budget.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] TIDE is established as a diagnostic; a pre-registered matched-vs-mismatched prescription test appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a localization-error-dominant and a classification-error-dominant public detector, retrain each with both a localization-targeted and a classification-targeted intervention under identical schedules, and compare AP gains in a 2x2 design.
main_risk: Interventions interact (a better localization head can also fix duplicates), blurring the attribution and producing a mixed 2x2 outcome.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Error decomposition is viewed as post-hoc storytelling with no demonstrated prescriptive power.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dominant error types may reflect dataset properties rather than model deficiencies, so any single-model intervention moves all components together.

one_line_idea: A minimum-detectable-difference (MDD) certificate for detection benchmarks, computed from hierarchical resampling over images and seeds, lets leaderboards refuse deltas below the resolvable threshold and changes which published improvements count as real.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] COCO-style leaderboards accept arbitrarily small AP improvements, while the run-to-run and split-to-split variability of AP is rarely quantified or disclosed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection AP variance is dominated by a few quantifiable components (test-image sampling, training seed, nondeterministic kernels), so a benchmark can publish a single MDD number from hierarchical resampling that separates resolvable from unresolvable deltas, and applying it retroactively will reclassify a substantial fraction of small claimed gains.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The hierarchical MDD for COCO val2017 box AP with 3-seed training of a mid-size detector will be at least 0.25 AP, and applying the certificate to 10 sampled published deltas under 0.5 AP will flip the accept decision for at least 3 of them; kill the idea if the estimated MDD is below 0.1 AP or if the certificate flips none of the sampled deltas.
why_important: Replaces recurring noise-in-benchmarks debunks with an operational acceptance rule that any leaderboard can adopt without new annotation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Seed-variance complaints exist for detection, but a packaged MDD certificate with hierarchical decomposition over image sampling and seeds, plus a retroactive reclassification audit, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train one public detector 3 times, evaluate all seeds on 200 bootstrap replicates of val2017, fit a variance-components model, derive the MDD, then apply it to a pre-registered sample of small published COCO deltas reproduced from public checkpoints.
main_risk: MDD depends on the detector family used to estimate it, so a single certificate may under- or over-state resolvability for architectures with different variance profiles.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reviewers believe a shared test set makes any positive delta meaningful, and variance disclosure is treated as optional.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern long training schedules may average away seed variance, making the true MDD small and the certificate toothless.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three 1x-schedule Faster R-CNN trainings on COCO train2017 (MMDetection) plus bootstrap scoring take about 3 single-A100 days; checkpoints for the delta audit come from the public MMDetection and Detectron2 zoos.

one_line_idea: An assignment-cost metric that scores detectors by optimal bipartite matching between predicted and ground-truth sets, replacing threshold-and-NMS-dependent AP, removes the max-detections confound and re-ranks end-to-end versus NMS-based detectors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] AP evaluates a ranked list after NMS and per-image caps, so set-prediction models and NMS-based models are compared through a decoding stage that was designed for one of them.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scoring the predicted set directly with a Hungarian-matched composite cost (localization + classification), as used in DETR-style training losses, yields a decoding-free measure of detection quality, and part of the reported AP gap between end-to-end and NMS-based detectors is an artifact of the decoding stage rather than set quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Among 8 public detectors (4 end-to-end, 4 NMS-based) on COCO val2017, the assignment-cost metric will change at least 2 pairwise ranks relative to AP, concentrated on cross-family pairs; kill the idea if it changes at most 1 rank or if changes are uniform across same-family pairs, indicating the metric adds noise rather than removing decoding bias.
why_important: Provides an evaluation capability that matches how modern detectors are trained and cleanly separates set quality from decoding heuristics, converting a known eval pathology into a usable metric.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hungarian matching is standard as a loss; promoting it to a benchmark metric with a pre-registered cross-family rank-flip prediction appears novel.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute the matched-cost metric and standard AP for 8 zoo checkpoints, compare rank orders, and attribute flips to family membership with a permutation test over family labels.
main_risk: The composite cost has free weightings (class vs box terms) whose choice could be accused of favoring one family; requires a sensitivity sweep to show flips are weighting-stable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] AP after standard decoding is assumed family-neutral because all models pass through the same scorer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: End-to-end models were trained to minimize exactly this cost, so the metric may simply favor them by construction rather than by fairness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference plus matching for 8 MMDetection checkpoints (Deformable DETR, DINO-DETR, Sparse R-CNN, YOLOX, Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet among them) on COCO val2017 takes under 12 hours on one GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Item-response-theory benchmark compression: modeling images as items with difficulty/discrimination and detectors as abilities enables an adaptive 1k-image COCO subset that reproduces full-benchmark rankings at 5x lower evaluation cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Every detector evaluation runs the full test set even though most images barely discriminate between modern models, making large-scale model sweeps needlessly expensive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image detection outcomes follow an item-response structure in which a small subset of high-discrimination images carries almost all ranking information, so an IRT model fitted on an existing detector pool can select a fixed informative subset that preserves rankings for unseen detectors.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A 1,000-image IRT-selected subset of COCO val2017, fitted on 15 public detectors, will rank 10 held-out detectors with Kendall tau at least 0.9 against full-set AP, beating a random 1,000-image subset by at least 0.05 tau; kill the idea if tau falls below 0.75 or if random subsets match IRT selection within 0.02 tau.
why_important: Benchmark compression is an enabling capability for hyperparameter sweeps, continual model audits, and green evaluation, and IRT gives it a principled statistical backbone.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] IRT-based efficient benchmarking has appeared for language-model leaderboards; a detection-specific instantiation with held-out-family generalization tests appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a 2-parameter IRT model on per-image outcomes of 15 zoo detectors, select the top-information subset, then rank 10 held-out detectors (different families/backbones) on subset vs full set and compare tau against random and difficulty-stratified subsets.
main_risk: Item parameters may be family-specific: images that discriminate anchor-based models may not discriminate DETR-style models, hurting generalization to unseen families.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners assume trustworthy detection rankings require the full 5k val set and that subsets are only for quick sanity checks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection scores per image are noisy multi-instance aggregates, which may violate IRT's unidimensional latent-ability assumption badly enough to break subset transfer.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Per-image scoring of 25 public MMDetection checkpoints on COCO val2017 plus IRT fitting runs in about 1 day on one GPU (inference-bound); models and data public.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: ranking correlation between subset and full benchmark

one_line_idea: Automatic consensus completion of missing test-set annotations by heterogeneous-detector agreement reproduces most conclusion changes obtained by expensive human relabeling, turning test-set repair into a zero-annotation capability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Human relabeling efforts of COCO-style ground truth (e.g., the public COCO-ReM re-annotation) changed model scores and some conclusions, but relabeling costs thousands of annotator hours per dataset.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Most consequential ground-truth errors are omissions and coarse masks that a consensus of architecturally diverse public detectors localizes with high precision, so an agreement-gated automatic completion of the ground truth recovers the bulk of the score and ranking corrections that human relabeling produces, at negligible cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scoring 10 public models against consensus-completed COCO val annotations will reproduce at least 70% of the per-model score shifts (sign and at least half the magnitude) observed when scoring against the human-relabeled public reference, and at least 80% of pairwise ranking changes; kill the idea if under 40% of shifts or under 50% of ranking changes are reproduced.
why_important: If automatic completion tracks human relabeling, every benchmark gains a cheap self-repair capability and relabeling budgets can be reserved for genuinely ambiguous cases.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Model-consensus label cleaning exists for classification; validating detection-set completion directly against a public human re-annotation as ground truth for the repair appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build consensus pseudo-annotations from 7 diverse public detectors with high-agreement gating on COCO val2017, score a disjoint set of 10 models against original, consensus-completed, and human-relabeled annotations, and compare shift/ranking reproduction rates.
main_risk: Consensus inherits shared blind spots of current detectors, so exactly the errors humans fixed that models systematically miss will not be recovered, capping the reproduction rate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats human relabeling as the only trustworthy way to fix benchmark ground truth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detector consensus may be confidently wrong on the same categories in correlated ways (shared training data), producing completions that distort rather than repair scores.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference of 17 public checkpoints (MMDetection zoo, e.g., Mask R-CNN, Cascade R-CNN, DINO-DETR, YOLOX) on COCO val2017 plus set operations completes in about 1 day on one GPU; COCO and the public re-annotated reference (COCO-ReM) are both public.

one_line_idea: A human-anchored composite detection metric, fitted on a small set of expert pairwise preferences between model outputs, predicts held-out human judgments substantially better than AP and can be shipped as a frozen scoring function.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] AP weights all error types by a fixed convention (IoU thresholds, confidence ranking) that was never validated against what expert users consider better detection output.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Human preferences between two models' outputs on the same image are systematic and largely explained by a low-dimensional mixture of interpretable error components (missed salient objects, localization slop, hallucinated boxes), so a preference-fitted weighting of these components generalizes to unseen images and models better than AP's fixed convention.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A metric fitted on 400 expert pairwise judgments over COCO images will agree with held-out judgments at least 75% of the time versus at most 62% for AP-difference sign, and will transfer to a disjoint model pair with at least 70% agreement; kill the idea if fitted-metric agreement is within 5 points of AP or if transfer agreement drops below 60%.
why_important: Anchors detection evaluation to task-relevant human judgment with a one-time, reusable tuning-free artifact, repairing the arbitrary-weighting pathology constructively.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Human-anchored metric fitting is established in image synthesis and captioning; a detection-output instantiation with transfer-across-models validation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect ~600 pairwise expert judgments across 3 model pairs on COCO val images (about 20 annotator-hours), fit a logistic mixture over error components, and evaluate held-out and cross-pair agreement against AP-sign baseline.
main_risk: Expert preferences may be task-dependent (surveillance vs captioning users disagree), making a single fitted weighting unstable across rater pools.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] AP is treated as definitionally correct for detection quality, with human judgment considered too noisy to formalize.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pairwise preferences on dense outputs may be dominated by one salient error, yielding a degenerate weighting that just counts big misses.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Model inference on 500 COCO val2017 images with two public MMDetection checkpoints (e.g., Faster R-CNN vs DINO-DETR) takes under 2 GPU-hours; the binding cost is roughly 20 hours of expert annotation (or ~300 USD crowdsourced), so needs_special_resources is set true for the human-judgment component.

one_line_idea: A head-swap attribution harness that retrains every detector head on a fixed frozen backbone (and every backbone under a fixed head) cleanly attributes published AP gains to head versus backbone innovations.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection papers change heads, backbones, schedules, and augmentations together, so the causal source of reported AP gains is usually unidentifiable from the paper's own tables.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Head and backbone contributions to AP are approximately additive for modern detector families, so a two-way swap harness (all heads x fixed backbones) recovers stable marginal effects, and a large fraction of head-attributed gains in recent papers will reattribute to backbones and training recipes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a 4-head x 3-backbone factorial on COCO with shared recipes, the interaction term will account for under 25% of total explained AP variance (supporting additivity), and for at least 5 of 8 recent head innovations the harness will attribute at least 60% of the end-to-end reported gain to non-head factors; kill the idea if interactions dominate (over 40% of variance) making marginal attribution meaningless, or if head attributions match paper claims within 20% throughout (harness unnecessary).
why_important: An attribution harness converts recurring reproducibility complaints into a reusable factorial instrument that any reviewer or lab can run to locate where gains come from.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual controlled comparisons exist; a maintained factorial harness with a pre-registered additivity test and reattribution audit appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the 12-cell factorial (4 public heads: e.g., RetinaNet, FCOS, Faster R-CNN, DINO-DETR; 3 backbones: ResNet-50, Swin-T, ConvNeXt-T) under one shared 1x recipe on COCO and fit a two-way ANOVA on AP.
main_risk: A single shared recipe may be unfair to recipe-sensitive heads, mistaking recipe mismatch for absent head contribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers take papers' ablation tables as sufficient attribution of where gains come from.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Head-backbone interactions (e.g., DETR-style heads needing strong features) may be fundamental, not noise, breaking additivity in an informative but harness-defeating way.

one_line_idea: Verifier-completed federated evaluation: converting LVIS-style federated AP into an estimate of complete AP by running a high-precision presence verifier over unlabeled categories changes rare-class conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Federated benchmarks like LVIS only annotate a subset of categories per image, so AP penalizes or ignores predictions on unverified categories according to bookkeeping conventions rather than actual image content.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A high-precision, low-recall visual verifier (operating in a regime where its own errors are quantifiable on the annotated subset) can adjudicate enough unverified predictions to move federated AP measurably toward the complete-annotation ideal, and this correction differentially affects rare categories, changing method rankings that were artifacts of federated bookkeeping.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On LVIS v1 val, verifier completion will shift rare-category AP by at least 2 points (either direction) for at least 20% of rare classes and change at least 2 of 5 pairwise orderings among public long-tail detection methods on the rare split, while verifier precision measured on held-out annotated categories stays above 95%; kill the idea if class shifts stay under 0.7 points or verifier precision cannot exceed 90%.
why_important: Repairs the federated-evaluation compromise with an auditable correction instead of another critique, directly targeting the debunk-heavy rare-class evaluation literature.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Federated AP's negative-set conventions are documented; an explicit verifier-completion estimator with a precision-controlled correction and ranking audit appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate the verifier operating point on annotated LVIS categories, apply it to unverified predictions of 5 public LVIS models, recompute AP with adjudicated positives/negatives, and compare rare-split rankings before and after.
main_risk: Verifier precision on rare categories may be much worse than on the frequent categories where its operating point is set, silently corrupting the correction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Federated AP conventions are accepted as an unavoidable cost of scaling category counts, not something correctable post hoc.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The verifier is itself a model with long-tail weaknesses, so its adjudications may recapitulate exactly the biases the correction is meant to remove.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Scoring 5 public LVIS checkpoints (MMDetection LVIS configs, plus the public Detic release) and a verifier pass with a public open-vocabulary classifier over ~20k crops takes about 1 day on one GPU; all datasets/models public.

one_line_idea: A seed-versus-data compute-allocation rule for trustworthy detector comparisons: given a fixed GPU budget, splitting compute across 3 short-seed replicates beats one long run for deciding between two training recipes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners comparing detector recipes almost always spend their full budget on one long run per recipe, implicitly assuming seed noise is negligible relative to recipe effects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For typical recipe deltas (under 1 AP), decision accuracy is variance-limited rather than bias-limited, so replicating shorter schedules and testing the seed-averaged difference yields a higher probability of correctly ranking two recipes than a single full-schedule comparison at the same total compute.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a ground-truthed testbed where the true recipe ordering is established by 9-seed full-schedule runs, the 3x(1/3-schedule) protocol will pick the correct recipe in at least 80% of resampled decision trials versus at most 65% for the 1x(full) protocol at equal compute; kill the idea if the replicate protocol's decision accuracy is not at least 8 points higher, or if short schedules invert the true ordering systematically (bias regime).
why_important: Provides an immediately usable budgeting rule that repairs the single-seed comparison pathology without demanding extra compute, aimed at everyday model development rather than leaderboards.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Seed-variance studies exist for classification and RL; a compute-matched decision-accuracy analysis for detection recipe selection with a pre-registered allocation rule appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Choose two recipes differing by a small real effect (e.g., augmentation change on RetinaNet/COCO), run 9 full-schedule seeds each to establish ground truth, then simulate both allocation protocols by subsampling runs and count correct decisions.
main_risk: Short-schedule and full-schedule recipe orderings can genuinely differ (schedule-dependent effects), in which case replicate protocols answer the wrong question no matter their variance advantage.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] One careful long run per configuration is considered the gold standard for recipe decisions in detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If seed variance for modern long schedules is tiny (well under 0.1 AP), single runs already decide correctly and replication wastes compute.
fastest_falsification_experiment: About 18 short and 6 full RetinaNet COCO trainings with MMDetection; using 1/4-scale COCO subsets keeps the whole grid near 10 single-A100 days; all public data and models.

one_line_idea: A frozen-backbone comparison track for detection heads: evaluating head designs on a shared frozen public backbone reproduces full-finetuning rank order at an order of magnitude less compute, enabling cheap pre-screening of architectural claims.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Comparing detection head designs fairly requires expensive full trainings per head, so most published comparisons are underpowered or confounded by unequal tuning.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because modern self-supervised backbones already carry most task-relevant features, the relative ordering of head designs trained on a frozen shared backbone is preserved under full finetuning, making the frozen track a valid low-cost screening instrument (mechanism: head-design effects act mostly on readout and assignment, which are backbone-independent).
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 6 public head designs trained both frozen-on-DINOv2 and fully finetuned on COCO, frozen-track and finetuned rankings will agree with Kendall tau at least 0.8 at roughly 10x less training compute for the frozen track; kill the idea if tau falls below 0.5, which would mean frozen screening is misleading.
why_important: A validated screening track lets the community test many more head ideas with statistical replication, repairing the underpowered-comparison pathology at its economic root.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frozen-backbone probing is standard for representation evaluation; validating it as a rank-preserving screen for detector head design decisions appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train RetinaNet, FCOS, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR, Sparse R-CNN, and DINO-DETR heads on frozen DINOv2 ViT-B and fully finetuned, 2 seeds each, and compare rank orders with bootstrap CIs on tau.
main_risk: Heads that exploit backbone plasticity (e.g., those relying on high-resolution early features) will be systematically undervalued by the frozen track, biasing the screen against a whole design family.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Full finetuning is assumed necessary for any meaningful architectural comparison in detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rank preservation may hold only within head families and break exactly for the novel designs one wants to screen.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Six frozen-backbone trainings (about 0.2 A100-days each with DINOv2 ViT-B) plus six 1x finetunings (~1 A100-day each) on COCO with MMDetection: roughly 8 single-GPU days total; all models and data public.

one_line_idea: Convention-conditioned segmentation: a single model trained with a dataset-convention token on images annotated under two mask conventions matches per-convention specialists and enables continuous convention control at inference.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The same visual concept is masked differently across datasets (e.g., COCO-style coarser polygons vs LVIS-style tighter boundaries on overlapping imagery), and models are normally trained to a single convention.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask conventions are a low-dimensional, learnable output-space transformation rather than noise, so conditioning the decoder on an explicit convention token lets one model represent multiple conventions simultaneously without averaging them into blur, and the token direction supports interpolation between conventions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A convention-token Mask2Former trained on images carrying both COCO and LVIS masks will score within 1.0 mask-AP of single-convention specialist models under each convention and beat a convention-blind mixed-training baseline by at least 2.0 mask-AP; kill the idea if the convention-blind baseline comes within 0.5 mask-AP of the token model, which would mean conventions behave as unlearnable noise.
why_important: Turns the heavily debunked convention-mismatch pathology into a deployable capability: one checkpoint that serves datasets and downstream users with different masking standards.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dataset-token multi-dataset training exists for combining label spaces; explicitly targeting mask-boundary conventions with an interpolation test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble the publicly shared images that carry both COCO and LVIS instance masks, train specialist, blind-mixed, and token-conditioned variants of the same architecture, and evaluate each under both conventions plus intermediate token interpolations scored by boundary tightness.
main_risk: The overlap set of doubly annotated images may be too small to train specialists to convergence, weakening the specialist reference point.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cross-dataset mask differences are treated as annotation noise to be averaged over, not as a controllable output dimension.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Convention differences may be category-specific and inconsistent, defeating a single global token and requiring per-class conventions that no longer fit a compact conditioning scheme.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Finetuning three Mask2Former ResNet-50 variants on the COCO/LVIS shared-image subset takes about 2 days total on one A100; COCO, LVIS, and Mask2Former weights are all public.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: convention-token conditioning vs blind mixing vs specialists

one_line_idea: Rater-conditioned decoding for multi-annotator segmentation: conditioning on an annotator embedding reproduces individual raters' styles and transfers to unseen raters from 5 examples, outperforming consensus-trained models on every rater.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multi-rater datasets (e.g., the QUBIQ challenge data and LIDC-IDRI lesion masks) show systematic per-annotator styles, yet standard training collapses raters into a consensus mask.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Annotator style is a stable, low-dimensional generative factor of the label, so a rater-embedding-conditioned decoder can both reproduce known raters and, because styles occupy a smooth embedding space, adapt to an unseen rater from a handful of examples by embedding regression rather than retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a public multi-rater benchmark, rater-conditioned decoding will beat a consensus-trained baseline by at least 3 Dice points on average when scored against each individual rater, and 5-example adaptation to a held-out rater will recover at least 60% of that gain; kill the idea if the per-rater gain is under 1 Dice point or held-out-rater adaptation recovers under 25% of it.
why_important: Converts annotator variability from a debunk target into a modeling capability that serves label-quality tooling, per-site convention transfer, and ambiguity-aware downstream use.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Probabilistic segmentation models capture label diversity as a distribution; identifiable rater-conditioning with few-shot new-rater transfer appears largely untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train rater-conditioned and consensus U-Net/SegFormer variants on a public multi-rater set with rater identities, evaluate per-rater Dice, then fit only the embedding for a held-out rater from 5 images and re-evaluate.
main_risk: Public multi-rater sets are small and medical-domain-skewed, so style embeddings may overfit dataset idiosyncrasies rather than capture a general mechanism.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Inter-rater variation is treated as noise to average away, and per-rater modeling is seen as overfitting the annotators.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rater differences may be image-conditional (each rater errs on different cases) rather than style-like, in which case no static embedding explains them.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Training small conditioned segmentation models on QUBIQ tasks (public challenge data) with a SegFormer-B0 backbone takes under 1 day on one consumer GPU; data and model weights public.

one_line_idea: Two-pass precision-tiered annotation: labeling most of a dataset coarsely and a small fraction precisely, with a tolerance-weighted loss that knows which pixels are trustworthy, reaches near-full-precision performance at roughly half the annotation cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation annotation cost is dominated by boundary precision, yet training pipelines treat every ground-truth pixel as equally reliable regardless of how carefully it was drawn.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model quality is limited by boundary-region supervision quality, not by interior pixel counts, so an explicit two-tier protocol (coarse pass everywhere, precise pass on a budgeted subset) combined with a per-pixel tolerance-weighted loss recovers nearly all of full-precision performance because the loss stops fitting the unreliable boundary band of coarse masks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training SegFormer on ADE20K with 80% simulated-coarse plus 20% precise masks and tolerance weighting will reach at least 95% of the full-precision mIoU and at least 90% of its boundary-F score, beating the same data without tolerance weighting by at least 1.5 mIoU; kill the idea if the tiered protocol stays under 90% of full-precision mIoU or if tolerance weighting adds under 0.5 mIoU over naive mixing.
why_important: Gives dataset builders a costed, falsifiable protocol for spending precision where it matters, converting the coarse-label pathology into an annotation-economics capability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Coarse-plus-fine annotation exists ad hoc (e.g., coarse extra sets in driving data); an explicit tolerance-map loss tied to a two-pass protocol with a cost-performance frontier appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate coarse passes by boundary-band morphological perturbation of ADE20K masks calibrated to real coarse-annotation statistics, train the three variants (full-precision, tiered+weighted, tiered naive), and compare mIoU/boundary-F against annotation-cost estimates from click models.
main_risk: Simulated coarseness may not match real annotator behavior (which errs structurally, not morphologically), overstating the protocol's real-world recovery rate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Every ground-truth pixel is treated as equally valid supervision, and precision budgeting is left implicit in annotator instructions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may already be robust to boundary-band noise through soft losses and augmentation, leaving tolerance weighting with nothing to fix.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three SegFormer-B2 trainings on ADE20K take about 2 days total on one A100; ADE20K and SegFormer are public and mask perturbation is scripted.

one_line_idea: Divergence-routed relabeling: routing only the instances where architecturally diverse models disagree to human relabeling recovers most of the benefit of relabeling an entire benchmark at a small fraction of the cost, validated against a public full re-annotation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Full benchmark relabeling efforts (such as the public COCO mask re-annotation) are effective but cost thousands of hours, so most datasets never get repaired.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Ground-truth errors concentrate where diverse models jointly diverge from the label rather than where any single model is wrong, so cross-model divergence is an efficient router for a fixed relabeling budget, and the routed 5% of instances captures the majority of score-relevant label errors.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Using the public re-annotated COCO reference as ground truth for which labels needed fixing, divergence routing at a 5% instance budget will cover at least 60% of the instances whose relabeling changes model scores, versus under 20% for random routing; kill the idea if divergence routing covers under 30% at the 5% budget.
why_important: Makes benchmark repair affordable and repeatable — a concrete capability that converts the label-error debunk genre into maintenance tooling any dataset host can run.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Model-disagreement mining for label errors exists in classification (confident-learning lineage); validating routing efficiency against a real, public, full re-annotation of detection masks appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-instance divergence across 6 diverse public detectors on COCO val2017, rank instances, and measure what fraction of the score-relevant fixes (identified by diffing original vs re-annotated references) falls in the top-5% divergence bucket versus random and single-model-error baselines.
main_risk: Divergence flags genuinely ambiguous instances as often as mislabeled ones, so the routed budget may buy adjudication of ambiguity rather than error correction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark repair is assumed to require full-pass human review because errors are believed to be unpredictably distributed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The public re-annotation fixed systematic protocol-level issues (e.g., mask style) that affect all instances equally, which divergence routing cannot prioritize.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference of 6 MMDetection checkpoints (Mask R-CNN, Cascade Mask R-CNN, Mask2Former among them) on COCO val2017 plus set diffing against the public re-annotated masks runs in under 8 hours on one GPU; everything public.

one_line_idea: Format-native mixed-supervision training: consuming polygons, raw pixel masks, and boxes through format-specific losses (instead of converting everything to one format) yields a measurable gain when merging heterogeneous datasets.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Merged training across datasets normally converts all annotations to a lowest-common-denominator format (usually rasterized masks or boxes), discarding format-specific information like polygon vertex placement or box-only uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Each annotation format carries a distinct noise model (polygons: vertex sparsity; rasters: quantization; boxes: extent-only), so format-native losses that model these noise processes extract strictly more information than format conversion, with the gain concentrated in boundary quality and partial-supervision classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training one instance-segmentation model on COCO polygons + Open Images boxes + LVIS masks with format-native losses will beat the convert-everything baseline by at least 1.5 mask-AP on a held-out mixed evaluation, with at least half the gain on boundary-F; kill the idea if the gain is under 0.5 mask-AP, indicating format conversion loses nothing that training can use.
why_important: Dataset merging is the default scaling path for perception, and a validated format-native recipe would raise the value of every existing box-only archive without new annotation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Box-supervised segmentation losses exist (BoxInst lineage); a unified multi-format noise-model formulation with a conversion-vs-native controlled comparison appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a merged training set from COCO, LVIS, and Open Images subsets with per-source format flags, train format-native and converted baselines with matched compute, and evaluate on held-out splits of each source plus a neutral third-party set.
main_risk: Gains may be dataset-mixture-specific: if box-only data dominates, the native losses reduce to existing box-supervision methods and the unified framing adds nothing.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Annotation format is treated as a storage detail to normalize away in dataloaders, not as an information channel.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rasterization at training resolution may already preserve everything the loss can use, making format nativity a no-op outside contrived low-resolution regimes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two Mask2Former-R50 trainings on a 200k-image merged subset take about 3 days total on one A100; COCO, LVIS, Open Images, and BoxInst reference code are public.

one_line_idea: Convention-marginalized training: augmenting ground-truth masks with rule-based convention transforms (dilation, erosion, hole policy, part-inclusion toggles) during training produces models that transfer across datasets with different annotation standards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation models drop sharply when evaluated on a different dataset even for shared classes, and part of that drop tracks annotation-standard differences rather than image-domain shift.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The convention component of cross-dataset degradation is learnable robustness: training against a distribution of rule-based convention transforms of the labels forces the model to place probability mass over the convention family, so its argmax under any single convention degrades gracefully, improving cross-dataset transfer without touching image appearance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A DeepLabv3+ trained on Cityscapes with convention-transform label augmentation will gain at least 2.0 mIoU on BDD100K shared classes relative to standard training, while losing at most 0.5 mIoU on Cityscapes itself; kill the idea if the cross-dataset gain is under 0.5 mIoU, which would attribute the transfer gap almost entirely to image-domain factors.
why_important: Separates and repairs the convention share of the domain-gap story with a zero-annotation training-side fix, complementing image-space domain adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-space augmentation is far less explored than image-space augmentation; using it to marginalize annotation conventions with a cross-dataset kill test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 6 parametric convention transforms, train with and without label augmentation on Cityscapes, evaluate both on Cityscapes val and BDD100K val shared classes, and attribute the delta with a boundary-band error analysis.
main_risk: Aggressive label transforms may blur genuinely learnable boundary detail, trading in-domain precision for a transfer gain that a simple boundary-loss reweighting could match.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cross-dataset drops are attributed to image appearance shift, and label conventions are assumed to be a minor contributor not worth training against.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If convention differences between the chosen datasets are small relative to appearance shift, the intervention has no headroom regardless of the mechanism's truth.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two DeepLabv3+ (MMSegmentation) trainings on Cityscapes plus BDD100K evaluation take about 1.5 days on one A100; both datasets and the model are public.

one_line_idea: Rosetta-subset taxonomy bridging: a small dual-labeled image subset shared between two datasets suffices to learn an empirical label-space mapping that beats name-based taxonomy alignment for training merged-vocabulary models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Merging datasets requires aligning label spaces, which is normally done by name/WordNet matching even though identically named classes have different extensions across datasets (what counts as 'table' or 'bag').
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Class correspondence is an empirical, image-grounded relation (a stochastic mapping with asymmetric inclusions) that can be estimated from a modest dual-annotated 'rosetta' subset, and training with this soft empirical mapping avoids the systematic supervision conflicts that name-matching injects into merged training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Using the COCO/LVIS doubly annotated imagery as a free rosetta set, a merged detector trained with the estimated soft mapping will beat a WordNet/name-matched merge by at least 2.0 AP on the shared-class union evaluation and eliminate at least 70% of cross-dataset supervision conflicts (measured as gradient-conflicting label pairs); kill the idea if the empirical mapping's gain over name matching is under 0.5 AP.
why_important: Every large-scale merged-data effort currently inherits silent taxonomy conflicts; a costed rosetta protocol makes merging a measured, repairable operation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-space unification via learned mappings exists; grounding the mapping in a small dual-annotated subset and quantifying the required rosetta size appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate the class-correspondence matrix from images carrying both COCO and LVIS annotations, train merged detectors under empirical vs name-based mappings at matched compute, and evaluate on held-out portions of both datasets; sweep rosetta size from 100 to 5,000 images to find the sufficiency knee.
main_risk: The free COCO/LVIS rosetta may be unrepresentative of harder merges (e.g., driving + web data), limiting external validity of the sufficiency curve.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Name and hierarchy matching is treated as good enough for label-space merging, with residual conflicts absorbed as noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern robust losses may already absorb name-matching conflicts, leaving little measurable gain for the empirical mapping.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two Faster R-CNN merged trainings on COCO+LVIS subsets with MMDetection take about 2 days on one A100; the dual-annotation overlap ships free with the public datasets.

one_line_idea: Set-valued ground truth evaluation: scoring predictions against the set of plausible annotations (from multi-rater data) with best-match credit changes model rankings relative to consensus-mask scoring.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] When multiple valid annotations exist for the same image, benchmarks score against a single consensus or arbitrary rater, penalizing models that produce a different but equally valid interpretation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For ambiguity-bearing classes, a set-valued protocol (credit for matching any admissible annotation, plus a coverage term for representing the set) measures competence more faithfully, and models differ enough in which raters they resemble that consensus scoring materially misranks them.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scoring 6 public segmentation models on the LVIS doubly annotated subset and a public multi-rater benchmark under best-match set scoring will flip at least 2 of 15 pairwise orderings relative to consensus scoring, with flips concentrated on high-ambiguity classes; kill the idea if no ordering flips and per-model score changes stay under 0.5 points, which would mean consensus scoring is already adequate.
why_important: Provides benchmarks with a drop-in scoring mode that respects annotation ambiguity instead of relitigating it, completing the multi-rater debunk line with an adoptable repair.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Set-valued and distribution-aware evaluation exists in probabilistic segmentation research; a general best-match benchmark protocol with a ranking-flip audit on standard datasets appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble the doubly annotated LVIS imagery and a public multi-rater set, define best-match and coverage scores, evaluate 6 public models under consensus vs set-valued protocols, and locate flips by class-ambiguity quantile.
main_risk: Best-match credit can reward models for confidently producing one rater's style rather than representing ambiguity, so the coverage term's weighting becomes a contested free parameter.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A single consensus mask is treated as the objective target, with rater disagreement filed as noise rather than as admissible answer sets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If model outputs cluster tightly around consensus for all classes, set scoring collapses to consensus scoring and the protocol is redundant.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluating 6 public checkpoints (Mask2Former variants, SegFormer, DeepLabv3+) on the public dual-annotation subsets (the LVIS doubly annotated imagery and QUBIQ) is inference-only and completes in under 6 hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Annotation-time geometric verification: a verifier model that flags boundary-inconsistent masks during labeling catches a majority of the errors that later required a full public re-annotation to fix, at a low false-flag rate.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Label errors are usually discovered years after dataset release (as with the public re-annotation of COCO masks), when fixing them is maximally expensive and disruptive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Most consequential mask errors are geometrically detectable at annotation time (boundary-image misalignment, missing holes, implausible mask-edge curvature relative to image gradients), so a lightweight verifier trained on image-boundary agreement can intercept them in the labeling loop before they enter the dataset.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Treating the diffs between original COCO masks and the public re-annotated reference as the error inventory, a boundary-agreement verifier will flag at least 60% of the fixed instances while flagging under 5% of unchanged instances; kill the idea if recall of fixed instances is under 30% at a 15% false-flag rate.
why_important: Moves benchmark quality control from retrospective debunks to preventive tooling, cutting the cost of quality at the source.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mask quality heads exist for model predictions; validating a verifier against a real re-annotation's fix inventory as annotation-time QC appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a boundary-agreement scorer (image gradients vs mask edges plus learned features) on synthetic perturbations of ADE20K masks, then evaluate its retrieval of the true COCO fix inventory without ever training on the re-annotation.
main_risk: A large share of the re-annotation's fixes may be convention/style changes rather than geometric errors, which no image-grounded verifier should or could flag.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Annotation QC is handled by human review sampling, and automated mask-quality checks are considered too unreliable to gate labeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Verifier flags may concentrate on hard/ambiguous boundaries where annotators disagree legitimately, making the tool an ambiguity detector rather than an error detector.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Training the verifier on perturbed ADE20K and scoring all COCO val2017 instances takes under 1 day on one consumer GPU; COCO, ADE20K, the public re-annotated masks, and a SegFormer backbone are all public.

one_line_idea: Certified-negative annotation: spending a small budget on explicitly verified empty regions (rather than more positives) recovers a large share of the performance lost to federated/missing-label training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Federated and web-scale datasets leave most category-image pairs unverified, forcing training to guess whether unlabeled regions are true negatives, and the standard fix is to buy more positive annotations.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant cost of missing labels is corrupted negative supervision, not scarce positives, so certifying emptiness (a fast human judgment) on a targeted subset of image-category pairs restores clean negative gradients and recovers most of the federated-to-complete gap at a fraction of positive-annotation cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a controlled federated simulation on COCO (hiding labels to mimic LVIS-style sparsity), adding certified negatives on 10% of image-category pairs selected by model confusion will recover at least 50% of the AP gap between federated and complete supervision, versus under 15% for spending the same budget on extra positives; kill the idea if negative certification recovers under 20% of the gap.
why_important: Reorients annotation economics around the cheapest informative judgment (emptiness), a directly actionable protocol for every federated dataset builder.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Negative-set handling appears inside federated-loss designs; treating certified emptiness as a first-class, budgeted annotation product with a measured recovery curve appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate federated sparsity on COCO by label hiding, train Faster R-CNN under (a) federated, (b) federated + certified negatives, (c) federated + equal-budget positives, and (d) complete supervision, and compare AP recovery fractions.
main_risk: Real emptiness judgments carry their own error rate (small objects overlooked), which the clean simulation understates, inflating the apparent recovery.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Annotation budgets should buy positives; negatives are assumed free from the absence of labels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern federated losses that down-weight unverified negatives may already capture most of this benefit without any new annotation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Four Faster R-CNN trainings on COCO subsets (MMDetection) take about 3 single-A100 days; COCO is public and label hiding is scripted.

one_line_idea: Complexity-indexed precision budgeting: allocating polygon vertex budgets by boundary complexity (not uniformly) cuts total annotation clicks by a third at equal downstream segmentation quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Annotation tools and instructions apply one precision standard to all objects, spending as many clicks on a smooth car roof as on a jagged bicycle, without any principled budget allocation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Downstream model quality is sensitive to vertex budget only where boundary complexity (curvature energy / fractal dimension) is high, so a complexity-indexed allocation rule shifts clicks to complex boundaries and achieves the same trained-model quality with substantially fewer total clicks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Simulating annotation via curvature-aware polygon simplification of ADE20K masks, complexity-indexed budgets will match uniform-budget trained mIoU within 0.3 points using at least 30% fewer simulated clicks; kill the idea if the click savings at quality parity is under 10%, which would mean uniform budgeting is already near-optimal.
why_important: Annotation spend is the binding constraint for new dense-prediction datasets; a validated allocation rule is immediately usable by any labeling operation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Polygon simplification and click-budget studies exist for interactive tools; an explicit complexity-indexed budget rule validated by downstream training quality appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate simplified-polygon variants of ADE20K under uniform vs complexity-indexed budgets across a click-budget sweep, train SegFormer on each, and plot trained mIoU against total clicks to compare frontiers.
main_risk: Click-count simulation via polygon simplification may misestimate real annotator time, which includes search and decision costs not proportional to vertices.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Precision standards are set by class or dataset policy, and per-object budget optimization is not considered a modeling question.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training may be dominated by label errors elsewhere (occlusion decisions, class confusion), making boundary vertex budgets a second-order factor at any allocation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Six SegFormer-B0 trainings on ADE20K variants take about 2 days total on one A100; ADE20K and SegFormer are public and simplification is scripted.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: trained mIoU vs simulated click-cost frontier
