one_line_idea: Output-space convention adapters: a small morphological-plus-learned operator fitted on 50 dual-convention examples translates a trained model's masks between annotation standards at evaluation time, recovering most of the convention-induced score gap without retraining.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A model trained under one dataset's masking standard loses points when scored under another standard even when its perception is correct, and the standard remedy is expensive retraining on target-convention labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Convention differences act mostly as a systematic, image-conditional but low-complexity transformation of mask geometry (boundary offset, hole policy, attachment rules), so a compact adapter fitted from very few dual-convention examples can translate outputs post hoc, cleanly separating perception quality from convention compliance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For a Mask2Former trained on COCO-style masks and evaluated under LVIS-style masks on shared imagery, a 50-example-fitted output adapter will recover at least 70% of the convention-induced mask-AP gap (measured against the gap closed by full target-convention finetuning); kill the idea if 50-example adapters recover under 30% or need over 500 examples to reach 50% recovery.
why_important: Provides an eval-time and deployment-time capability that decouples model competence from dataset-specific label politics, with a measured example-efficiency curve.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Post-hoc output adjustment exists for logits; few-shot geometric convention adapters for dense outputs with a recovery-fraction benchmark appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit adapters (parametric morphology + small residual U-Net) on 50/200/500 dual-convention instance pairs from the COCO/LVIS overlap, apply to held-out predictions, and compare recovered mask-AP against the finetuning ceiling.
main_risk: Category-dependent convention rules (e.g., handbag straps in or out) may not be expressible by a compact shared operator, capping recovery well below the finetuning ceiling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Convention mismatch is handled by retraining or ignored, and output-space translation is not treated as a standard tool.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If most of the cross-convention gap reflects genuine perception differences (tighter masks reveal boundary errors), no output transform can recover it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Adapter fitting and evaluation on the public COCO/LVIS dual-annotated overlap with a public Mask2Former checkpoint runs in under 6 hours on one consumer GPU.

one_line_idea: Anchored benchmark refresh: shipping every benchmark version with difficulty-anchor items shared across versions yields a contamination certificate — models whose refreshed-set drop exceeds the anchor-predicted drop are flagged, changing conclusions about claimed progress.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Refreshing a test set (as with the historical ImageNet-to-ImageNetV2 replication) confounds two effects: the new items may be intrinsically harder, and newer models may have been contaminated by or overfitted to the old items.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A shared anchor subset carried unchanged across benchmark versions identifies the difficulty-shift component (all models shift together on anchors), so the residual per-model drop on refreshed items is an interpretable contamination/overfitting signal rather than an unexplained gap.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying anchor correction to 20 public classifiers across ImageNet val and ImageNetV2 will shrink the unexplained spread of per-model drops by at least 50%, and models released after heavy benchmark reuse eras will show systematically positive residuals; kill the idea if anchor correction shrinks spread by under 20%, indicating drops are not decomposable this way.
why_important: Converts the test-set-refresh debunk literature into a versioning protocol any benchmark host can adopt, with a numeric certificate replacing rhetorical contamination accusations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The ImageNetV2 gap and its difficulty analyses are established; packaging anchor-item difficulty correction as a refresh protocol with per-model residual certificates appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a two-component model (shared difficulty shift + per-model residual) on accuracies of 20 public checkpoints over matched anchor and refreshed splits, validate residual stability across anchor choices, and test whether residuals rank models by benchmark-reuse exposure.
main_risk: Anchor items age too: repeated evaluation on carried-over anchors makes them contamination targets themselves, eroding the correction over versions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Version-to-version score drops are read informally as either 'harder set' or 'overfitting' without a supported decomposition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-model drops may be dominated by architecture-specific sensitivity to collection-pipeline differences, which anchors cannot separate from contamination.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluating 20 public timm/OpenCLIP checkpoints (e.g., ResNet-50, ViT-B, CLIP variants) on ImageNet val and ImageNetV2 is inference-only, about 6 hours on one GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Sequential evaluation with early stopping: a sequential probability ratio test over streaming per-image comparisons reaches the same accept/reject decisions as full-test evaluation using a fraction of the images, enabling cheap continuous model monitoring.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Every model comparison evaluates the entire test set even when the outcome is obvious after a few hundred images, wasting compute in sweeps, CI pipelines, and repeated regression checks.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image paired comparisons form an exchangeable stream whose evidence accumulates fast for clearly separated models, so an anytime-valid sequential test can stop early with controlled error rates, and the stopping-time distribution concentrates far below the full test size for most real model pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 45 pairs from 10 public classifiers on ImageNet val and 10 public segmentation models on ADE20K, the sequential protocol at nominal 5% error will agree with full-set decisions on at least 95% of pairs while using at most 30% of images on average; kill the idea if average savings fall below 40% of images or agreement drops under 90%.
why_important: Evaluation cost now rivals training cost in large sweeps; an anytime-valid protocol is an enabling capability for continuous evaluation infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Sequential testing is classical and used in A/B testing; a packaged anytime-valid evaluation protocol for vision benchmarks with measured savings appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement an e-process/SPRT over per-image win/loss/tie streams with random image ordering, run all pairs to their stopping times, and compare decisions and image usage against full evaluation, with sensitivity to ordering seeds.
main_risk: Per-image outcomes are not identically distributed under curated orderings, and clustering effects (e.g., class blocks) could invalidate nominal error control unless randomization is enforced.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Full-test evaluation is treated as the only defensible reporting unit, and early stopping is associated with cherry-picking rather than valid inference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For closely matched models the sequential test will run to the full set anyway, and if most interesting comparisons are close, average savings evaporate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference caches for 10 timm classifiers on ImageNet val and 10 MMSegmentation models on ADE20K plus sequential analysis complete in about 1 day on one GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Battery-level acceptance testing: requiring claimed improvements to survive a hierarchical test across a fixed battery of related benchmarks (instead of one headline dataset) changes which methods count as improvements, and the battery can be assembled entirely from public sets.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Methods are accepted on single-benchmark evidence, and cross-dataset follow-ups regularly fail to reproduce single-benchmark orderings, but there is no standard multi-benchmark acceptance procedure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Treating benchmarks as random draws from a task population and testing the improvement's population-level effect with a hierarchical model distinguishes robust methods from benchmark-specific ones, and enough public segmentation benchmarks exist to make the battery test practical and well-powered.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating 8 public segmentation methods over a 5-set battery (ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO-Stuff, Pascal Context, and a driving alternative), at least 25% of pairwise single-benchmark wins under 1.0 mIoU will fail the battery-level test, while battery conclusions will be stable under leave-one-benchmark-out; kill the idea if under 5% of small wins fail battery testing (single benchmarks were sufficient) or if battery conclusions flip under leave-one-out (population model unusable).
why_important: Replaces post-hoc external-validity complaints with an operational acceptance instrument, changing incentives toward robust methods at submission time.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-dataset reporting is common; a formal hierarchical acceptance test with stability diagnostics as the decision rule appears new for dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect or reproduce 8 methods' scores across the battery with matched backbones, fit a mixed-effects model of method effects across benchmarks, and compare accept/reject sets against single-benchmark rules with leave-one-out stability checks.
main_risk: Public benchmarks are correlated (shared imagery styles and label conventions), shrinking the effective number of independent draws and weakening the population interpretation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] One strong headline benchmark plus qualitative extra tables is treated as sufficient evidence of general improvement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If method-by-benchmark interactions dominate, no population-level effect exists to test and the battery verdicts reduce to noise-averaging.

one_line_idea: Declared-prior evaluation: benchmarks accept a user-declared deployment prior over strata (scene type, object scale, occlusion) and return reweighted scores with variance guarantees, replacing ad-hoc subset evaluations with a supported query interface.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners hand-select benchmark subsets to approximate their deployment (night images, large objects), obtaining numbers with uncontrolled variance and no comparability across papers.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Importance-reweighting benchmark strata to a declared prior, with an effective-sample-size floor that triggers refusal when the prior is unsupportable, provides deployment-relevant scores whose variance is controlled and whose definitions are shared, and such reweighted scores select different models than uniform scores often enough to matter.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Building the strata from public metadata and annotations on COCO and ADE20K, at least 2 of 5 realistic declared priors will change the top-1 model among 10 public models relative to uniform scoring, while every returned score keeps effective sample size above 500 items; kill the idea if no plausible prior changes model selection (uniform scoring suffices) or if most useful priors trip the refusal floor (interface unusable).
why_important: Bridges the benchmark-deployment gap with infrastructure rather than critique, and the refusal mechanism makes honest the cases where the benchmark cannot answer.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Importance weighting is textbook; a benchmark-side declared-prior query interface with variance-floor refusal semantics appears unbuilt.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 6 strata over COCO/ADE20K from public annotations, implement the reweighting service with ESS accounting, evaluate 10 public models under 5 declared priors, and tabulate selection changes and refusal rates.
main_risk: Strata definable from existing annotations may miss the deployment factors users actually care about (weather, sensor), limiting the interface to priors nobody declares.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Uniform benchmark scores plus qualitative judgment are assumed adequate for model selection across deployments.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model rankings may be stratum-stable in practice, in which case the interface returns uniform answers under every prior and adds only bookkeeping.

one_line_idea: Pre-registered tradeoff-cone acceptance: replacing single-scalar improvement tests with a Pareto-dominance test over a declared metric cone (region overlap plus boundary quality) reverses accepted wins that traded one competence for another.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Methods are accepted on scalar headline metrics (mIoU, mask-AP) even when they degrade complementary qualities like boundary sharpness, and multi-metric tables are eyeballed without a decision rule.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A benchmark can pre-register an acceptance cone (the set of metric-change directions counted as improvement, e.g., non-negative in both mIoU and boundary-F with at least one strict gain), and applying cone acceptance to recent method pairs will reverse a measurable fraction of scalar-accepted wins because scalar gains frequently ride on boundary regressions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating 10 public segmentation model pairs on ADE20K with mIoU and boundary-F, at least 2 scalar-accepted wins will fail cone acceptance due to a boundary-F regression exceeding 1.0 points; kill the idea if fewer than 1 in 10 wins fails the cone, meaning scalar and cone acceptance coincide in practice.
why_important: Multi-metric honesty becomes an enforceable rule rather than a table aesthetic, directly repairing the metric-gaming pathology documented by eval audits.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pareto reporting exists in efficiency literatures; pre-registered cone acceptance as a benchmark decision rule for segmentation quality dimensions appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score public checkpoint pairs (successive versions of popular methods) on mIoU and boundary-F, apply scalar and cone rules with bootstrap uncertainty on both metrics, and count acceptance reversals.
main_risk: Cone geometry is a governance choice; adversarial submitters could lobby for cones matching their method's profile, moving the gaming one level up.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A higher headline metric is treated as an improvement by definition, with boundary quality relegated to qualitative figures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary metrics correlate strongly with mIoU on modern architectures, so the cone may almost never bind and the reform would be symbolic.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference-only scoring of 20 public MMSegmentation checkpoints on ADE20K val with mIoU and boundary-F takes under 6 hours on one GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Cryptographic canary items for vision benchmarks: seeding test sets with arbitrary-labeled canary images gives benchmark hosts a statistically powered detector of training-on-test contamination that works as a protocol, not a forensic investigation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark hosts cannot verify whether submitted models trained on test data; current contamination arguments rely on circumstantial evidence assembled long after the fact.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because canary labels are arbitrary (assigned by a keyed rule, not visual content), any above-chance canary accuracy is attributable to test-set exposure, so a small canary set embedded at benchmark creation yields a contamination test with quantifiable power and false-positive control, independent of model internals.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With 200 canaries embedded in a benchmark, a model finetuned on a training set contaminated with the labeled test data will be detected at over 95% power at a 1% false-positive rate, while clean-trained models of any strength stay at chance on canaries; kill the idea if strong clean models exceed chance on canaries (visual-similarity leakage breaks arbitrariness) or if detection power at 200 canaries falls below 60%.
why_important: This is protocol-level infrastructure: it converts contamination disputes into a routine statistical check that benchmark hosts run at submission time, complementing mechanism-focused memorization research without overlapping it.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Canary strings are established for language-model privacy auditing; a benchmark-side canary protocol for vision test-set contamination with power analysis appears undeveloped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a benchmark from ImageNet-subset classes plus 200 keyed-label canaries, finetune ViT-B and ResNet-50 (timm) under clean and deliberately contaminated regimes at several contamination fractions, and trace detection power versus canary count.
main_risk: Sophisticated contamination (training on test images without labels, or on near-duplicates) would evade label-keyed canaries, limiting the protocol to the crudest contamination mode.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Contamination policing is assumed to require either data-pipeline transparency or post-hoc similarity forensics, both impractical at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Public leaderboards may face mostly unlabeled-image contamination, for which this protocol is blind by design, making its deterrence value marginal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: A dozen short finetunes of timm ViT-B/ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100-scale subsets with injected canaries run in about 2 days total on one A100; all components public or scripted.

one_line_idea: Noise-ceiling-normalized leaderboards: estimating each benchmark's inter-annotator ceiling and reporting scores as fractions of remaining headroom changes which improvements look meaningful, especially near saturation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Leaderboards report raw scores with no reference to the benchmark's annotation-noise ceiling, so a 0.5-point gain reads the same at 60% and at 95% of the achievable maximum.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Inter-annotator agreement data (double-annotated subsets that several public datasets already ship) supports estimating a per-benchmark, per-class noise ceiling, and headroom-normalized reporting reorders both class-level priorities and model-level conclusions in the saturation regime.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Using public double-annotation subsets to estimate ceilings on Cityscapes and LVIS, at least 20% of classes will show current best models within measurement noise of the ceiling (making further class gains unmeasurable), and headroom-normalized ranking will flip at least 1 of the top-3 model orderings on one benchmark; kill the idea if estimated ceilings exceed raw best scores by more than 10 points everywhere, meaning saturation is nowhere near and normalization changes nothing.
why_important: Prevents the community from spending compute on classes and benchmarks that are already measurement-limited and redirects it to real headroom, as a reporting capability rather than a critique.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Noise ceilings are standard in neuroscience model evaluation; systematic ceiling-normalized reporting for vision benchmarks appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate per-class ceilings from annotator-pair agreement on the double-annotated subsets, propagate uncertainty, and re-render public leaderboard slices (top-10 checkpoints) in headroom units with flip analysis.
main_risk: Double-annotated subsets are small and possibly unrepresentative, giving ceiling estimates with error bars wide enough to swallow the conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Raw metric points are treated as having constant meaning across the score range, and saturation talk stays qualitative.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model errors and annotator disagreements may be qualitatively different, so agreement-based estimates may not bound achievable model scores in either direction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ceiling estimation from public agreement subsets plus re-scoring 10 public checkpoints (MMSegmentation for Cityscapes, MMDetection for LVIS) is inference-plus-analysis, about 1 day on one GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Difficulty-matched test refresh: replacing stale test images with fresh ones matched on anchor-model difficulty profiles preserves model rankings while breaking URL-level and hash-level contamination, enabling routine benchmark rotation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks cannot rotate their test sets without breaking comparability, because fresh images shift difficulty and invalidate historical numbers, so test sets stay static and contaminable for a decade.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] An image's difficulty profile (per-anchor-model scores across a frozen anchor ensemble) is a sufficient statistic for its effect on rankings, so sampling fresh images to match the joint difficulty-profile distribution of retired images yields a replacement set on which rankings and score levels are preserved for non-anchor models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Swapping 50% of a COCO-classes evaluation set with difficulty-matched fresh images drawn from Open Images will preserve the ranking of 10 held-out public detectors with Kendall tau at least 0.9 and mean absolute score shift under 0.5 AP, versus tau under 0.8 for unmatched refresh; kill the idea if matched refresh does no better than unmatched or tau falls below 0.7.
why_important: Routine rotation is the strongest structural defense against test-set contamination and overfitting, and difficulty matching is the missing piece that keeps longitudinal comparability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Difficulty estimation per item exists; using anchor-profile matching to certify ranking-preserving test refresh appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score anchor and held-out detector pools on COCO val2017 and a relabeled Open Images candidate pool, run matched and random 50% swaps, and compare ranking preservation and score-level drift across 20 refresh replicates.
main_risk: Cross-dataset label-convention differences between the source and refresh pools could dominate the swap effect, confounding the difficulty-matching evaluation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Test sets are treated as irreplaceable artifacts whose rotation necessarily resets all historical comparisons.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Difficulty profiles from anchors may not span the factors that differentiate future models, so preservation for today's held-out pool may not extend to tomorrow's architectures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference of ~16 public MMDetection checkpoints on COCO val2017 and an Open Images subset with shared classes takes about 1 day on one GPU; both datasets and all models public.

one_line_idea: Partial-pooling estimators for rare-class metrics: hierarchical shrinkage of per-class AP/IoU stabilizes long-tail leaderboards, halving bootstrap rank volatility and changing which long-tail methods win.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Rare-class metrics on long-tail benchmarks rest on a handful of instances per class, so per-class scores and the rare-split averages built from them are wildly unstable, yet leaderboards report them as point values.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-class scores share structure (class prototypes, frequency bands), so an empirical-Bayes partial-pooling estimator borrows strength across classes to produce rare-split estimates that are both lower-variance and better predictors of scores on a second sample, changing method comparisons that currently hinge on noise.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On LVIS v1 val, partial-pooled rare-class AP will reduce bootstrap rank volatility among 6 public long-tail methods by at least a factor of 2 and will flip at least 1 published pairwise ordering; cross-validated prediction of held-out-split class scores will improve (lower MSE) for at least 80% of rare classes; kill the idea if volatility reduction is under 1.2x or held-out prediction does not improve.
why_important: Long-tail research currently optimizes against noise on the rare split; a stabilized estimator redirects the subfield toward real effects and is adoptable by the benchmark host directly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Empirical-Bayes shrinkage is classical; its application to long-tail vision leaderboards with a rank-stability and flip audit appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit hierarchical models over per-class AP of 6 public LVIS checkpoints, compare raw vs pooled estimates under bootstrap resampling and split-half validation, and audit ordering flips on the rare split.
main_risk: Shrinkage pulls genuinely exceptional per-class performances toward the mean, and methods specializing on a few rare classes would be systematically under-credited.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-class point estimates are treated as the honest raw data, with shrinkage viewed as statistical tampering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If method effects on rare classes are strongly class-idiosyncratic, no pooling structure fits and the estimator's cross-validation advantage disappears.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Scoring 6 public LVIS checkpoints (MMDetection configs and the public Detic release) plus hierarchical fitting runs in about 8 hours on one GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Boundary-affinity point supervision: growing instance masks from a 10-click-per-image budget through an affinity field trained only on click pairs reaches most of full-mask panoptic quality, because clicks constrain topology while affinities carry geometry.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Full mask annotation costs about two orders of magnitude more than point clicks, yet point-supervised panoptic pipelines still trail full supervision by a wide margin.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The residual gap is not information-theoretic but architectural: clicks uniquely identify instances (topology) while modern self-supervised features already encode boundary geometry, so a pairwise affinity head trained on click co-membership, decoded with a graph partitioner, converts 10 clicks into masks that capture most of what polygons supply.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO panoptic with 10 simulated clicks per image, affinity-grown supervision will reach at least 88% of the full-mask-trained PQ of the same architecture, and at least +4 PQ over strongest point-loss-only baselines; kill the idea if it stays under 80% of full-mask PQ or within 1 PQ of point-loss baselines.
why_important: A validated 10-click protocol changes the economics of building new panoptic datasets and gives weak supervision a mechanism-level explanation of when clicks suffice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Point-supervised segmentation exists (point-based training losses); the explicit topology-vs-geometry decomposition with click-pair affinity training and a percentage-of-full-PQ kill line appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate click budgets on COCO panoptic, train a Mask2Former variant with click-pair affinity supervision on DINOv2 features vs point-loss baselines and full masks, and compare PQ at matched compute.
main_risk: Click simulation (uniform interior sampling) flatters the method relative to real annotator click distributions, which cluster near object centers and miss thin parts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Weak supervision is expected to trade large accuracy losses for cost, and points are seen as too impoverished for panoptic-quality masks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Affinity fields may fail exactly on the classes where masks matter most (articulated, thin, overlapping objects), leaving the gap concentrated and unacceptable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three trainings (affinity, point-loss, full) of Mask2Former-R50 on COCO panoptic subsets take about 3 days total on one A100; COCO and DINOv2 are public.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: click-pair affinity supervision vs point-loss and full masks

one_line_idea: Box-plus-one-interior-point supervision: adding a single interior click to each box annotation closes more than half of the box-only-to-full-mask instance segmentation gap by resolving the figure-ground ambiguity that box supervision cannot.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Box-supervised instance segmentation (BoxInst lineage) works surprisingly well but plateaus below full-mask training, and the annotation-cost ladder between boxes and masks has no validated intermediate rung.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant failure of box-only training is figure-ground inversion inside the box (mask latches onto background or a co-occurring object), a single guaranteed-foreground point removes exactly this ambiguity, so its marginal value is far higher than its marginal cost of about one click.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO, box-plus-one-point training will close at least 55% of the mask-AP gap between box-only and full-mask training at under 5% additional annotation time; kill the idea if the gap closure is below 30%, which would mean box-only failures are not point-addressable.
why_important: Defines a new, costed rung on the supervision ladder that dataset builders can adopt immediately, with a mechanism (figure-ground disambiguation) that predicts where it helps.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Points and boxes have each been used as weak supervision; the marginal-value analysis of exactly one interior point on top of boxes, with a gap-closure kill line, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train BoxInst-style models under box-only, box+1-point (simulated from GT interiors), and full-mask regimes on COCO, then stratify gains by figure-ground-confusion cases identified in the box-only error analysis.
main_risk: The single point may be redundant with pairwise color-affinity terms already used in box-supervised losses, yielding gains well under the predicted closure.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The supervision ladder is assumed to jump from boxes to masks, with intermediate signals dismissed as engineering noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Box-only failures may be dominated by boundary imprecision rather than figure-ground inversion, which a single point does nothing to fix.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three CondInst/BoxInst trainings on COCO with MMDetection (about 1 A100-day each) plus error stratification complete in about 3 single-GPU days; all public.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: fraction of box-to-mask AP gap closed per annotation cost

one_line_idea: Scribble supervision with a topology-preserving connectivity loss recovers thin-structure segmentation (poles, fences, sign posts) that standard scribble training loses, at unchanged cost on thick classes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Scribble-supervised segmentation approaches full supervision on bulky classes but collapses on thin, elongated structures, whose continuity is exactly what pixel-wise losses fail to enforce from sparse scribbles.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Thin-class failure under scribbles is a connectivity problem, not a data-quantity problem: adding a differentiable connectivity/topology penalty that requires predicted thin-class components to connect scribble endpoints restores continuity, so most of the thin-class gap closes without any extra annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes with simulated scribbles, adding the connectivity loss will recover at least 60% of the thin-class (pole, traffic sign pole, fence) IoU gap between scribble and full supervision while changing thick-class IoU by under 0.5; kill the idea if thin-class gap recovery is under 25% or thick classes degrade by over 1.0 IoU.
why_important: Thin structures carry outsized downstream importance (infrastructure inspection, driving) and are the acknowledged weak point of every cheap-supervision protocol; a targeted repair makes scribbles viable end-to-end.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Topology-aware losses exist for full supervision in specialized pipelines; coupling them to scribble endpoints as a weak-supervision repair with a gap-recovery kill line appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate skeleton-based scribbles for Cityscapes, train DeepLabv3+ with and without the connectivity penalty, and report per-class IoU deltas stratified by structure thinness.
main_risk: Differentiable topology penalties are computationally heavy and unstable at high resolution, and a proxy (e.g., skeleton-overlap loss) may weaken the mechanism claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Thin-class failure is filed under insufficient supervision, with the assumed fix being more or denser annotation rather than a structural loss.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Thin-class failure may be dominated by feature-resolution limits of the backbone, in which case no loss on top of the same features can restore continuity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two DeepLabv3+ trainings on Cityscapes (MMSegmentation) plus scribble generation run in about 1.5 days on one A100; data and models public.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: connectivity/topology penalty tied to scribble endpoints

one_line_idea: SSL-native weak supervision: replacing CAM-style seeds with clustering of frozen self-supervised features as the seed generator lifts image-label-only segmentation by a measurable margin under an otherwise identical pipeline.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Image-label-only semantic segmentation pipelines still bootstrap from class activation maps, a mechanism designed for supervised classifiers a decade ago, while frozen self-supervised features now carry strong object geometry.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] CAM seeds are the binding constraint of weakly supervised pipelines (their errors propagate through refinement), and attention/feature clustering of a frozen SSL backbone produces seeds with strictly better boundary recall at matched precision, so swapping only the seed generator improves the whole pipeline without new hyperparameter tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Pascal VOC 2012 with an identical refinement and training stack, SSL-cluster seeds will improve final mIoU by at least 3.0 points over CAM seeds, and seed-quality metrics (boundary recall at matched precision) will improve by at least 10 points; kill the idea if final mIoU gains are at or under 1.0 point, meaning refinement already saturates seed quality.
why_important: Isolates and upgrades the weakest module of a widely used cheap-supervision recipe, and the seed-quality-to-final-quality transfer curve is itself a reusable diagnostic capability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] SSL features have been used for unsupervised segmentation; a controlled seed-swap study inside a standard weakly supervised pipeline with a propagation analysis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Hold refinement (CRF/affinity) and final training fixed on VOC; compare CAM, improved-CAM variants, and DINOv2-cluster seeds; regress final mIoU on seed quality across the variants.
main_risk: SSL clusters lack class labels, and the assignment of clusters to image-level labels may introduce a new error mode that cancels seed-quality gains.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Progress in weakly supervised segmentation is expected from better refinement and losses, with CAM seeding treated as a settled component.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern refinement stages may already correct most seed errors, making the pipeline insensitive to seed quality above a low floor.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Seed generation with public DINOv2, plus two full VOC weakly supervised trainings (DeepLabv2/v3+ stack), completes in about 1.5 days on one consumer GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Complement-masked training for disjointly labeled dataset unions: masking the loss over classes a source did not label, plus cross-image class banks, trains one model from three partially labeled datasets to near fully-labeled-union quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real datasets label different class subsets (driving sets lack indoor classes and vice versa), and naive union training punishes correct predictions of classes the current source treats as background.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The union-training failure is a supervision-semantics bug, not a data limitation: treating unlabeled classes as ignore (complement masking) removes the false-negative gradients, and a class-bank memory that replays confident cross-dataset features restores the missing positive signal, together recovering nearly all of the fully-labeled-union performance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Splitting ADE20K classes into three disjoint label groups across three sub-datasets, complement masking plus class banks will train a model within 2.0 mIoU of the fully-labeled-union reference, versus a naive-union baseline at least 8 mIoU below it; kill the idea if the method stays more than 5 mIoU below the reference, meaning partial labeling loses irrecoverable information.
why_important: A validated recipe for disjoint-label unions unlocks training on the union of existing public datasets without any re-annotation, one of the cheapest data-scaling moves available.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Partial-label semantics and cross-dataset training have been studied piecemeal; a controlled disjoint-split benchmark with a recovery-gap kill line appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create the controlled three-way split of ADE20K, train naive-union, complement-masked, masked-plus-bank, and full-union references with SegFormer, and compare mIoU and per-group breakdowns.
main_risk: Class banks rely on confident pseudo-features whose errors could compound for visually similar cross-group classes, capping recovery below the target.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners assume datasets with different label spaces cannot be merged without relabeling or per-dataset heads.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Context co-occurrence across groups may be irreplaceable: without seeing labeled sofa and labeled wall in the same image, boundary discrimination between them may never form.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Four SegFormer-B0 trainings on ADE20K splits take about 2 days total on one A100; ADE20K and SegFormer are public.

one_line_idea: A clicks-to-quality scaling law: interactive annotation quality follows a power law in click budget whose exponent is shared across datasets and interfaces, enabling annotation-budget planning from a 50-image pilot.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Annotation campaigns set click and time budgets by folklore, with no quantitative law connecting per-instance interaction budget to achieved label quality across datasets.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Achieved mask quality as a function of interaction budget follows a saturating power law whose exponent reflects boundary complexity statistics that are broadly shared across natural-image datasets, so a small pilot suffices to fit the curve and predict the budget needed for any target quality on a new dataset.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Fitting the law on 50-image pilots from COCO and ADE20K (simulated interaction via public interactive-segmentation models) will predict the full clicks-to-IoU curve on Cityscapes and Pascal VOC within 5% quality error across budgets of 1-20 clicks; kill the idea if cross-dataset prediction error exceeds 15% or if fitted exponents differ across datasets by more than a factor of 2, breaking the shared-exponent claim.
why_important: Turns annotation budgeting into measurement: a lab can decide clicks-per-instance and campaign cost from a one-afternoon pilot instead of guesswork.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Interactive segmentation papers report clicks-to-IoU curves per method; treating the curve as a transferable dataset law with pilot-based extrapolation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a public interactive segmentation model (SimpleClick or RITM) with simulated user policies across click budgets on four datasets, fit the power law per dataset, and test pilot-to-full and cross-dataset extrapolation.
main_risk: Simulated clicking underestimates human variability, so the law may hold for robot users but fail for real annotator populations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Clicks-to-quality behavior is assumed method-specific and dataset-specific, not law-like or transferable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary-complexity distributions may differ enough across domains (driving vs indoor) that no shared exponent exists even approximately.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Simulated interactive annotation with the public SimpleClick checkpoint over subsets of COCO, ADE20K, Cityscapes, and VOC runs in under 8 hours on one consumer GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Train-time depth as free boundary supervision: distilling depth-discontinuity and normal-discontinuity maps from RGB-D training data into a 2D segmentation model improves boundary quality with zero test-time depth requirement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Public RGB-D datasets carry precise geometric discontinuities that align with object boundaries, yet 2D segmentation training typically ignores the depth channel even when it is available at training time.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Boundary supervision is the scarcest part of the segmentation signal, and depth/normal discontinuities provide a dense, annotation-free boundary teacher; an auxiliary boundary-distillation loss from train-time depth therefore improves boundary-F on RGB-only inference more than equivalent-compute image-only auxiliary losses.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On NYUv2 (RGB-only at test), depth-discontinuity distillation will improve boundary-F by at least 3.0 points and mIoU by at least 1.0 over the no-auxiliary baseline, and by at least 1.5 boundary-F over an edge-detector-distillation control at matched compute; kill the idea if it fails to beat the edge-distillation control by 0.5 boundary-F, meaning geometry adds nothing beyond photometric edges.
why_important: Recasts existing RGB-D archives as free supervision for ordinary 2D models, a capability claim about supervision sources rather than architectures, with a control that isolates the geometric contribution.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Depth-aware segmentation typically consumes depth at test time; train-only geometric-boundary distillation with a photometric-edge control appears under-examined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train SegFormer on NYUv2 RGB with (a) no auxiliary, (b) edge-distillation from a public edge detector, (c) depth-discontinuity distillation from the dataset's depth channel, and compare boundary-F/mIoU; replicate on SUN RGB-D.
main_risk: Sensor depth is noisy at exactly the thin structures where boundary supervision matters, potentially teaching the model sensor artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Depth is treated as a test-time modality choice, not as a train-time supervision source for RGB-only models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Photometric edges may already contain the usable boundary signal, with geometric edges adding only redundancy that matched-compute controls will expose.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three SegFormer-B0 trainings on NYUv2 take under 1 day total on one consumer GPU; NYUv2, SUN RGB-D, and public edge detectors are all public.

one_line_idea: One-exemplar dataset bootstrapping: a single annotated exemplar per class, propagated through frozen-feature retrieval and geometric verification, generates pseudo-labels sufficient to train a segmentation model to a large fraction of full supervision.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Bootstrapping a new segmentation dataset currently starts from hundreds of labeled images per class, because pseudo-labeling pipelines need a trained teacher to begin with.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Frozen self-supervised features make one careful exemplar per class a viable teacher: dense retrieval finds visually corresponding regions across the unlabeled corpus, geometric verification (cycle-consistent matching) filters false positives, and the surviving pseudo-labels carry enough signal that standard training recovers most of full-supervision quality for medium-frequency classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Pascal VOC with 1 exemplar mask per class and 10k unlabeled images, the bootstrap will train a model to at least 60% of full-supervision mIoU, with cycle-consistency filtering contributing at least 10 mIoU over unfiltered retrieval; kill the idea if final quality is under 40% of full supervision or filtering contributes under 3 mIoU.
why_important: Reduces the cold-start cost of new dense-prediction domains to one annotation per class plus compute, and quantifies which mechanism (retrieval vs verification) carries the capability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Few-shot segmentation and retrieval-based propagation exist; an end-to-end one-exemplar dataset-bootstrap protocol with a filtering-ablation kill line appears new.

main_risk: Single exemplars encode one pose/context, so classes with high intra-class variation (chairs, plants) may bootstrap poorly, concentrating failure where data is most needed.

one_line_idea: Verified negatives are the high-value half of weak supervision: human-verified negative image-level labels (already shipped in Open Images) improve weakly supervised detection more per label than an equal number of extra positives.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open Images ships millions of human-verified negative image-level labels alongside positives, but weakly supervised detection research consumes positives and treats negatives as incidental.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant error source in weak detection training is corrupted negative evidence (classes assumed absent that are actually present), so explicitly verified negatives repair the loss where it is most wrong, delivering more AP per label than additional positives, which mostly duplicate existing evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In matched-label-count experiments on Open Images subsets, adding N verified negatives will improve weakly supervised detection AP by at least 2x the gain from adding N extra verified positives, with at least +3.0 AP absolute at N equal to one negative per training image; kill the idea if the per-label value ratio falls below 1.2x, meaning negatives are not preferentially valuable.
why_important: Reprices an already-existing, underused public resource and gives annotation campaigns a measured reason to buy cheap emptiness judgments alongside positives.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Verified negatives are used internally by some pipelines; a controlled per-label marginal-value comparison of negatives vs positives for weak detection appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a weakly supervised detector on Open Images image-level labels with (a) positives only, (b) positives + N verified negatives, (c) positives + N extra positives, at matched label budgets, and compare AP on the Open Images detection validation split.
main_risk: Verified negatives in Open Images are non-uniformly sampled (verification followed model uncertainty), so their measured value may not transfer to fresh annotation campaigns.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Weak-supervision value is assumed to live in positive labels, negatives being effectively free from absence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern weak-detection losses with noise modeling may already discount unverified negatives well enough that explicit verification adds little.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three weakly supervised detection trainings on a 100k-image Open Images subset (WSDDN-style or a modern reimplementation) run in about 2.5 days total on one A100; dataset and baseline code public.

one_line_idea: Budget-optimal supervision mixing: a cost-model-driven allocator that chooses per-image supervision grade (clicks, boxes, or masks) from image statistics beats any single-grade budget spend on final model quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Annotation campaigns choose one supervision grade for a whole dataset, even though per-image difficulty and per-grade information value vary enormously across images.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The information value of upgrading an image from boxes to masks is predictable from cheap image statistics (instance count, boundary complexity, class rarity), so a greedy allocator that spends a fixed budget where upgrade value is highest dominates uniform single-grade allocations on the trained model's quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO with simulated costs (masks 8x boxes, boxes 5x clicks), the allocator's mixed portfolio will beat the best single-grade allocation at equal budget by at least 2.0 mask-AP, and a value-model ablation (random mixing at the same grade proportions) will capture under half the gain; kill the idea if the allocator beats the best single grade by under 0.5 mask-AP, meaning mixing has no exploitable structure.
why_important: Converts supervision-grade choice from a policy decision into an optimization, directly reducing the cost of every future dense-prediction dataset.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mixed-supervision training methods exist; a budgeted allocation policy with a validated per-image value model and matched-budget dominance test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate grade costs on COCO, train models under single-grade and allocator-chosen mixed portfolios at three budgets using existing mixed-supervision losses, and compare mask-AP frontiers with the random-mixing control.
main_risk: The value model is fitted on proxy runs whose transfer across architectures is unproven; a value model that overfits one architecture family would undermine the general claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Supervision-grade uniformity is assumed operationally necessary and near-optimal, with mixing seen as tooling complexity for marginal benefit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Under matched budget the extra images affordable at lower grades may always dominate the precision of fewer high-grade labels, collapsing the optimum to a single grade after all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: About eight Mask R-CNN trainings on COCO subsets (MMDetection) across budgets and portfolios take roughly 5 single-A100 days; COCO and mixed-supervision baseline code are public.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: value-model-driven grade allocation vs single-grade budgets

one_line_idea: Occlusion-order supervision is sufficient for amodal completion: training with only pairwise over/under relations (free from existing overlap annotations) yields amodal masks competitive with fully amodal-supervised training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Amodal segmentation datasets are rare and expensive because annotators must imagine hidden object extents, while ordinary datasets contain abundant implicit occlusion evidence (overlapping instances with depth order).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The hard part of amodal completion is knowing which regions are occluded rather than hallucinating shape: pairwise occlusion-order labels identify the occluded support, and generic class shape priors fill it, so order supervision plus modal masks recovers most of what explicit amodal masks teach.

why_important: If order labels suffice, amodal capability can be added to any instance dataset for a fraction of amodal-annotation cost, unlocking occlusion-robust downstream use broadly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Amodal methods typically train on amodal masks; a controlled sufficiency test of order-plus-modal supervision with a percentage-of-supervised kill line appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train three variants (modal-only, modal+order, fully amodal) of the same amodal head on KINS and COCOA, evaluating amodal AP and stratifying by occlusion severity.
main_risk: Shape priors may carry most of the signal for rigid vehicle classes in KINS, flattering the method in one domain and hiding failures on deformable categories.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Amodal completion is assumed to require amodal ground truth; order relations are treated as auxiliary metadata.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Occluded-extent prediction may depend on instance-specific evidence (pose, articulation) that order labels do not constrain, capping recovery below usefulness.

one_line_idea: Amodal-extent anchor assignment: assigning training targets by estimated full-object extent instead of visible-box overlap recovers detections of heavily occluded objects that visible-IoU assignment systematically starves of positive anchors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detector training assigns positives by IoU with the visible box, so heavily occluded objects receive few or no positive anchors and are undertrained precisely where detection is hardest.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The occlusion performance gap is partly a label-assignment artifact: using amodal extents (from annotation or a completion model) for assignment gives occluded objects a fair share of positive anchors, improving occluded-slice recall without harming visible-object precision, because the assignment change only adds positives where evidence exists.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On KINS, amodal-extent assignment will improve AP on the over-50%-occluded slice by at least 2.0 points with under 0.3 overall AP change, and the gain will correlate with the increase in positive-anchor counts per occluded instance; kill the idea if the occluded-slice gain is under 0.5 AP, meaning assignment starvation is not a binding constraint.
why_important: Locates a concrete, fixable training mechanism behind the well-documented occlusion weakness of detectors, and the fix is a few lines in the assigner rather than a new architecture.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Occlusion-robust detection work focuses on losses and NMS; amodal-extent-based label assignment with an anchor-count mediation analysis appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Modify the assigner of Faster R-CNN and FCOS to use amodal boxes on KINS, train matched pairs, and report occluded-slice AP plus the mediation analysis on anchor counts.
main_risk: Amodal boxes overlap neighboring objects heavily, so added positives may inject label confusion between occluder and occludee, trading one error for another.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Occlusion failures are attributed to representation limits, with label assignment assumed neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Occluded instances may lack the visible evidence to exploit extra positives, so anchors were never the bottleneck.

one_line_idea: Context-driven proposal of fully hidden objects: a detector head trained on synthetic full-occlusion composites learns to propose completely invisible objects from scene context at usable precision, a capability absent from every current detector.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Contextual object priors (co-occurrence, support surfaces, partial arrangements) carry enough information that a model trained on real images with instances deliberately occluded by pasted occluders learns above-chance hidden-object proposal, and this capability transfers to naturally occluded scenes rather than exploiting compositing artifacts.

why_important: Establishes a new, measurable perception capability (object permanence from context in stills) with direct value for robotics and search applications, framed constructively rather than as a failure audit.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context modeling for detection is old, but a trained-and-benchmarked hidden-object proposal capability with an artifact-control kill clause appears new.

problem: [KNOWN FACT] Amodal training data covers few categories (vehicles and people dominate KINS; COCOA is broader but small), and it is unknown whether amodal completion must be learned per category.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Amodal completion decomposes into category-generic components (occlusion-boundary detection, symmetry and continuation priors, support from visible fragments) plus a small category-specific residual, so a category-agnostic head trained with category-held-out protocols retains most of its completion quality on novel classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training on KINS vehicle classes and evaluating on COCOA non-vehicle classes, the category-agnostic head will retain at least 70% of the amodal-IoU improvement (over a modal-copy baseline) that it achieves on held-in classes; kill the idea if retention is under 40%, meaning amodal completion is essentially category-memorization.
why_important: A transfer-positive result licenses a universal amodal module usable on any dataset without amodal labels, multiplying the value of the few existing amodal annotations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Amodal papers report within-dataset results; a category-held-out transfer quantification with a retention kill line appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the amodal head on KINS with category-agnostic targets, evaluate amodal IoU over modal-copy baseline on held-in and held-out (COCOA) categories, and decompose errors into boundary vs extent components.
main_risk: KINS's rigid, road-scene shapes may teach continuation priors that actively mislead on articulated or deformable held-out categories.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Amodal completion is assumed to lean on category shape knowledge, implying poor novel-category transfer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The measured retention may be dominated by trivially easy small occlusions, overstating generic skill; occlusion-severity stratification is needed to expose this.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One amodal-head training on KINS and inference-only evaluation on COCOA takes under 1 day on one consumer GPU; both datasets and Detectron2 baselines are public.

one_line_idea: Layered panoptic decoding: representing the scene as depth-ordered mask layers instead of a flat label map fixes boundary-ownership errors between overlapping instances, improving contested-boundary accuracy at equal overall quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Panoptic decoders emit one flat label per pixel, forcing overlapping instances to compete for boundary pixels, and boundary-ownership errors between adjacent overlapping objects are a persistent error mode.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Boundary ownership is a layering question: decoding into ordered layers (each instance keeps a complete mask in its layer, flattened by learned order) lets the model represent the occlusion relation explicitly, converting ownership conflicts into order decisions it can learn, so contested-boundary errors drop without any backbone change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO panoptic, layered decoding will reduce boundary-ownership error (misassigned boundary-band pixels between overlapping instance pairs) by at least 25% relative and improve boundary-F on contested bands by at least 2.0 points, at overall PQ within 0.3 of the flat decoder; kill the idea if contested-band improvement is under 8% relative or PQ drops by more than 1.0.
why_important: Boundary ownership drives downstream failures in editing and robotics grasping; a decoding-level repair that needs no new labels is immediately deployable on existing panoptic stacks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Layered scene representations are classical and appear in image editing; wiring them into panoptic decoding with a contested-band error metric and kill line appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Add a layer-ordered decoding path to Mask2Former panoptic, train matched pairs on COCO panoptic, and evaluate the contested-band metrics computed from overlapping ground-truth pairs.
main_risk: Layer count and order supervision (from mask overlap heuristics) introduce new hyperparameters whose tuning could account for any observed gains.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Flat per-pixel labeling is treated as the natural output space for panoptic tasks, with ownership errors accepted as annotation-level ambiguity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The ownership errors may originate in feature resolution rather than output-space expressiveness, in which case layering changes nothing measurable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two Mask2Former-R50 panoptic trainings on COCO take about 2.5 days total on one A100; COCO panoptic and Mask2Former are public.

one_line_idea: Backbone-portable feature upsamplers: a high-resolution feature upsampler trained once on one frozen backbone transfers to other backbones with most of its dense-task benefit intact, so upsampling can ship as a universal plug-in rather than a per-model accessory.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Frozen vision backbones emit coarse feature grids (stride 14-16), and learned upsamplers that restore spatial detail (FeatUp lineage) are trained per backbone, multiplying cost across the model zoo.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The information an upsampler exploits is dominated by image-side statistics (edge-guided detail reconstruction) rather than backbone-specific feature idiosyncrasies, so an upsampler trained on backbone A composes with backbone B after only a cheap linear input adapter, retaining most of the dense-task gain.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An upsampler trained on frozen DINOv2 and transferred to OpenCLIP ViT-B with a linear adapter fitted on 1k unlabeled images will retain at least 75% of the linear-probe segmentation mIoU gain it delivers on its home backbone (measured on ADE20K over bilinear upsampling); kill the idea if retention is under 40%, meaning upsamplers are backbone-specific artifacts.
why_important: A portable upsampler makes high-resolution dense readout a commodity component, cutting the per-backbone retraining tax and clarifying what upsamplers actually learn.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Learned feature upsampling is established (FeatUp lineage); its cross-backbone portability with an adapter-only transfer protocol appears untested. Scope note: this concerns feature-space readout for dense prediction, not image super-resolution or restoration.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the upsampler on DINOv2, freeze it, fit linear adapters to OpenCLIP and a supervised ViT, and compare ADE20K/VOC linear-probe mIoU with home-trained upsamplers, bilinear, and adapter-only controls.
main_risk: Feature-space geometry may differ enough across pretraining objectives that a linear adapter cannot align what the upsampler needs, forcing nonlinear adapters that blur the portability claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Upsamplers are assumed to be backbone-married components retrained per model as a matter of course.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gain retention may be dominated by trivial edge alignment achievable by guided filtering, making the portability finding true but practically empty against cheap baselines.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Upsampler training plus adapter fits and linear-probe evaluations on ADE20K with public DINOv2/OpenCLIP checkpoints run in about 1.5 days on one consumer GPU; all public.

one_line_idea: Implicit coordinate-based dense readout beats deconvolutional heads at matched compute on boundary accuracy, because continuous decoding removes the grid-aliasing that upsampling stacks bake into predictions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense heads reconstruct full-resolution predictions through fixed upsampling stacks whose outputs show grid-aligned artifacts, and boundary quality lags region quality across architectures.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A coordinate-conditioned implicit head (query any continuous location against local feature neighborhoods) eliminates resampling alias by construction, so at matched compute it converts the same features into sharper boundaries, with the advantage growing at evaluation resolutions above training resolution.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On ADE20K with a frozen DINOv2 backbone, the implicit head will beat a parameter-matched deconv head by at least 2.0 boundary-F at equal mIoU (within 0.3), and the boundary-F advantage will at least double when evaluating at 2x training resolution; kill the idea if the boundary-F advantage is under 0.5 at native resolution and does not grow with resolution.
why_important: Locates a persistent boundary-quality pathology in the readout stage rather than the representation, and offers a drop-in head that any frozen-backbone user can adopt.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Implicit decoding heads exist in scattered forms (point-based refinement, implicit fields); the matched-compute aliasing-attribution comparison with a resolution-scaling kill clause appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train implicit and deconv heads of matched FLOPs on frozen features, evaluate mIoU/boundary-F at 1x and 2x resolution on ADE20K and Cityscapes, and verify the alias mechanism via frequency-domain analysis of error maps.
main_risk: Point-sampled training may converge slower, and compute matching by FLOPs may not match wall-clock or memory, muddying the fairness of the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boundary softness is attributed to coarse features, with the readout stack assumed to be a neutral resampler.
why_it_might_be_wrong: PointRend-style refinement may already capture most of this benefit, leaving the implicit head a marginal variant rather than a distinct capability.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Head-only trainings on frozen DINOv2 features for ADE20K take under 1 day total on one consumer GPU; datasets and backbones public.

one_line_idea: A standardized dense-probe suite (multi-task, nonlinear-local, resolution-swept) for frozen backbones produces backbone rankings that differ from linear-probe rankings and better reflect finetuned downstream ordering.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Frozen backbones are compared by linear-probe scores on one or two dense tasks at one resolution, and the community treats these as the canonical measure of dense feature quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Linear probing at fixed resolution confounds feature quality with linear separability and stride artifacts, so a standardized suite that adds local-window nonlinear probes, multiple dense tasks, and a resolution sweep produces rankings that reorder backbones and agree better with full-finetuning outcomes, becoming the missing standard instrument for dense representation evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 8 public backbones, suite-based rankings will differ from linear-probe rankings for at least 2 of 8 positions and will agree with full-finetune segmentation rankings at Kendall tau at least 0.15 higher than linear probes do; kill the idea if suite and linear rankings coincide or the suite's tau advantage is under 0.05, meaning linear probing was already sufficient.
why_important: Backbone choices for dense tasks are billion-FLOP decisions currently made on a shaky instrument; a validated richer suite upgrades the community's measurement standard.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual probing conventions abound; a validated multi-axis suite with an explicit agreement-with-finetuning criterion appears missing for dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble the suite (segmentation, boundary, depth-free ordinal tasks; linear and 3x3-window MLP probes; 3 resolutions), evaluate 8 backbones (DINOv2, OpenCLIP, MAE, supervised ViT/ConvNeXt among them), and compare rankings against 1x-schedule finetuning references on ADE20K.
main_risk: The finetuning reference itself is noisy at 1x schedules, so the agreement comparison may lack the power to separate the instruments.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Linear probes at standard resolution are assumed to measure dense feature quality adequately.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nonlinear probes may mostly measure probe capacity rather than the backbone, adding variance without validity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe suite over 8 public backbones (DINOv2, OpenCLIP, MAE among them) on ADE20K subsets plus eight 1x finetunes takes about 5 days on one A100; all checkpoints and data public.

one_line_idea: Frequency-matched layer selection: choosing which backbone layers to fuse for a dense task by matching layer frequency response to the task's spatial-frequency demand replaces exhaustive layer search at a tenth of the cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense pipelines fuse hypercolumns from backbone layers chosen by exhaustive search or convention, and the optimal subset changes per task and backbone, making re-search a recurring cost.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A layer's usefulness for a dense task is largely determined by the match between its effective spatial-frequency transfer (measurable once per backbone with probe stimuli) and the task's output frequency spectrum (measurable from labels), so a frequency-matching rule selects near-optimal layer subsets without task-specific search.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On 4 dense tasks (semantic segmentation, boundary detection, part segmentation, ordinal layout) across 3 public backbones, frequency-matched subsets will come within 0.5 points of exhaustive-search subsets on each task metric while using under 10% of the search compute; kill the idea if the gap to exhaustive search exceeds 2.0 points on 2 or more task-backbone pairs.
why_important: Replaces a ubiquitous engineering search with a measurement-based rule, and validates a mechanism-level account of what layers contribute to dense readout.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Layer-choice studies and frequency analyses of CNNs/ViTs exist separately; an operational frequency-matching selection rule validated against exhaustive search appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-layer frequency responses with band-limited probe stimuli on DINOv2, MAE, and ConvNeXt; compute task spectra from ADE20K/PACO labels; compare matched vs exhaustive vs conventional subsets with frozen-feature probes.
main_risk: Semantic (what) and spatial (where) contributions of layers may be inseparable in a frequency account, making the rule accurate for boundary-like tasks but wrong for semantics-heavy tasks.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Layer selection is treated as an empirical per-pipeline hyperparameter without a governing principle.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern multi-scale fusion heads may be insensitive to input layer choice, making all subsets near-equal and the rule unnecessary.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Frozen-feature probe trainings across subsets and tasks on public backbones (DINOv2, MAE, ConvNeXt) take about 2 days on one consumer GPU; ADE20K, PACO, and all backbones public.

one_line_idea: Anti-aliased patch embedding: replacing the ViT patchify stem with an anti-aliased convolutional downsampler measurably improves thin-structure segmentation at equal compute, because patchify aliases exactly the high-frequency content thin classes live in.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] ViT stems downsample by non-overlapping patch projection, a maximally aliasing operation, and dense predictors built on ViTs are notoriously weak on thin structures like poles and sign posts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Thin-structure failure is partly stem-level information loss: sub-patch-width structures alias into unrecoverable feature noise at patchify, so an anti-aliased stem (low-pass filtered strided convolutions) preserves their evidence and improves thin-class IoU specifically, with negligible effect on thick classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training matched ViT-S segmentation models on Cityscapes from identical initialization recipes, the anti-aliased stem will improve thin-class IoU (pole, traffic light, traffic sign) by at least 2.0 points with under 0.5 change on thick classes and under 3% compute overhead; kill the idea if thin-class gains are under 0.7 points, meaning the bottleneck lies deeper than the stem.
why_important: Identifies and repairs a concrete architectural aliasing mechanism behind a well-known failure mode, with a class-stratified prediction that cleanly separates the mechanism from generic capacity effects.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anti-aliased CNN downsampling is established; targeting the ViT patchify stem with a thin-class-stratified kill test appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train ViT-S + UPerNet variants (patchify vs anti-aliased stem) on Cityscapes and ADE20K from scratch-equivalent schedules, report class-stratified IoU, and verify the mechanism by measuring stem-output energy for band-limited thin-structure probes.
main_risk: Stem changes alter optimization dynamics beyond aliasing (effective receptive fields, early-layer statistics), confounding the mechanism attribution despite matched budgets.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Thin-structure weakness is attributed to token resolution and decoder design, with the stem treated as a neutral tokenizer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pretraining dominates dense quality; a stem fix evaluated without large-scale pretraining may show effects that vanish once models are pretrained at scale.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two ViT-S trainings on Cityscapes (ImageNet-initialized, MMSegmentation) take about 2 days total on one A100; all data and code public.

one_line_idea: Retrofit register tokens for dense readout: adding register tokens during a short continued-pretraining phase cleans the high-norm artifact tokens of existing ViT checkpoints and improves frozen-feature dense probes without full re-pretraining.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large ViTs develop high-norm artifact tokens that corrupt feature maps for dense use, and the register-token remedy is applied at pretraining time, leaving deployed checkpoints unrepaired.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The artifact mechanism (the network storing global statistics in spatial tokens for lack of scratch space) can be retrofitted: continuing pretraining briefly with added registers re-routes the global computation into the new tokens, cleaning spatial features at under 1% of original pretraining cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Retrofitting registers into a public artifact-bearing ViT with a 20-epoch continued-pretraining phase on ImageNet-scale public data will remove at least 80% of high-norm outlier tokens and improve frozen-feature linear-probe mIoU on ADE20K by at least 1.5 points; kill the idea if outlier reduction is under 30% or dense-probe gains are under 0.5, meaning artifacts require from-scratch pretraining to fix.
why_important: Converts a pretraining-time insight into a retrofit capability applicable to the deployed checkpoint zoo, multiplying the reach of the register mechanism.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Register tokens are established as a pretraining fix (ViT-registers lineage); the cheap-retrofit protocol with quantified artifact and probe outcomes appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a public artifact-bearing checkpoint, add 4 registers, continue pretraining briefly on ImageNet-1k with the original objective, and measure outlier-token statistics plus dense-probe deltas against the untouched checkpoint and a no-register continued-pretraining control.
main_risk: Continued pretraining itself (regardless of registers) may alter dense-probe scores, which the no-register control must cleanly separate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Artifact tokens are assumed baked in by pretraining and fixable only by re-pretraining with registers from scratch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The global-statistics routing may be structurally entrenched in attention patterns that short continued training cannot re-route.
fastest_falsification_experiment: A 20-epoch continued pretraining of ViT-B on ImageNet-1k takes about 2-3 days on one A100 with modern recipes; ImageNet, ADE20K, and public checkpoints (timm/DINOv2 lineage) suffice.
