one_line_idea: Underwater detectors implicitly regress object range from wavelength-dependent color loss, so swapping the water's optical type at test time moves detections in a direction predictable from attenuation physics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Water absorbs red light far faster than blue-green, so an object's color balance shifts systematically with camera-to-object distance; underwater detection models are trained and evaluated without controlling for this coupling.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection confidence in underwater models is partly a function of the red-to-blue channel ratio acting as a learned range prior, so physically re-rendering the same scene under a different Jerlov-style water type will shift confidences in the direction predicted by the attenuation coefficients, not randomly.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-attenuating test images from coastal-type to oceanic-type water (physically parameterized channel-wise exponential re-rendering with known per-channel coefficients) will change per-object confidence with a sign agreement of at least 70% with the physics-predicted direction; kill the idea if sign agreement is below 55% (chance-like) or if confidence shifts are uncorrelated with the applied per-channel attenuation delta (|r| < 0.2).
why_important: If color-as-range is load-bearing, cross-site underwater deployment failures are predictable and correctable from water optical properties measured with a $100 transmissometer reading rather than requiring new labels.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Underwater enhancement work manipulates color for human viewing, but a signed, physics-predicted confidence-shift test on detectors appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a public underwater detection set, estimate per-image channel attenuation, re-render each image under two other water types via channel-wise exponential scaling with plausible ranges, run a trained detector, and test sign agreement between confidence deltas and physics-predicted deltas.
main_risk: Per-image attenuation estimation without known range maps is noisy, which could dilute the signed prediction even if the mechanism is real.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners treat underwater color shift as generic domain gap to be erased by enhancement or augmentation, not as a structured range cue the model has internalized.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may rely mostly on shape and local contrast, with color contributing too little for a measurable signed shift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: DUO or RUOD underwater detection images with a YOLOv8 checkpoint fine-tuned on the same training split; channel-wise re-rendering plus inference over 2k images is under 6 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$10).

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Supplying a per-pixel range estimate from a monocular depth model and inverting the channel-wise exponential attenuation along that range removes most of the spatially varying cast, and the residual color error will be roughly range-independent, unlike global white balance whose error grows with range.

why_important: Color-faithful underwater imagery matters for species identification, coral health scoring, and any downstream model consuming color features; a physics-grounded per-pixel correction is deployable without paired training data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Physics-based underwater correction exists, but using modern monocular depth predictions as the range field and pre-registering a range-dependence kill criterion on physical color charts appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public underwater dataset containing color charts at annotated distances, compare CIEDE2000 of (a) gray-world, (b) global diagonal transform, (c) per-pixel inversion using a monocular depth model's range map scaled by the chart distances.
main_risk: Monocular depth models trained on air imagery may produce range fields too distorted underwater for the inversion to help (interacts with the refraction bias of O-005).
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Enhancement is treated as an image-to-image learning problem; explicit range conditioning is seen as unnecessary given enough training pairs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Backscattered ambient light adds a range-dependent additive term that pure attenuation inversion ignores, possibly dominating the residual.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: the SQUID underwater dataset (color charts at multiple distances) with Depth Anything as the range estimator; full comparison runs in under 4 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$8).

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors trained on ROV imagery learn illumination-conditional detection: recall is a strong function of local irradiance rather than object size or contrast alone, and synthetically flattening the illumination field (dividing out a fitted radial falloff model) shifts detections toward the periphery without any change in scene content.

why_important: Ecological surveys quantify abundance from ROV video; an irradiance-conditional recall function biases abundance estimates toward the light cone and is correctable in software once characterized.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Deep-sea ML papers report overall mAP; an irradiance-stratified recall law with a flattening intervention appears unmeasured.

one_line_idea: Flat-port refraction breaks the pinhole model underwater, so air-trained monocular depth models should exhibit a specific radially increasing depth bias underwater that a Snell-law correction largely removes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Cameras behind flat housings image through an air-glass-water interface; refraction makes the system non-single-viewpoint with field-angle-dependent effective focal length, violating the pinhole assumption baked into monocular depth training.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Monocular depth models applied to flat-port underwater imagery show a structured error field: relative depth increasingly overestimated toward the image periphery following the Snell-law magnification curve, and pre-warping images with a physically derived refractive correction removes most of the radial component.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The radial component of relative depth error will grow monotonically with field angle with amplitude at least 10% of median depth at the corners, matching the refractive prediction within a factor of two, and physical pre-warping will cut that radial component by at least 50%; kill the idea if no monotonic radial structure exists (amplitude < 3%) or if pre-warping fails to reduce it by at least 20%.
why_important: Monocular depth is increasingly used for underwater robotics and photogrammetry scaling; a known, correctable systematic bias is far more useful than an unexplained accuracy drop.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Refractive geometry is standard in underwater photogrammetry, but nobody appears to have tested whether foundation depth models inherit the predicted radial bias or whether physical pre-warping fixes them zero-shot.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a monocular depth model on a public underwater dataset with metric depth ground truth, fit the radial error profile, compare against the Snell-law prediction for a flat port, and re-evaluate after refractive pre-warping.
main_risk: Some datasets use dome ports (which approximately restore single-viewpoint geometry), which would dilute the effect if port metadata is missing.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Underwater depth failure is attributed to appearance shift (color, particles), not to a deterministic geometric model violation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Depth models may rely on object-scale priors more than perspective geometry, making them insensitive to the refractive distortion.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: the FLSea underwater visual-inertial dataset (metric depth) with Depth Anything; error-field fitting and pre-warp re-evaluation is under 6 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$12).

one_line_idea: Pathology foundation models trained on single-magnification tiles have weak cross-magnification feature consistency, and enforcing pyramid-consistency at pretraining measurably improves slide-level diagnosis that depends on multi-scale context.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pathologists integrate 4x architecture, 10x patterns, and 40x cytology; pathology foundation encoders are pretrained on tiles from one or mixed magnifications without any constraint that the same tissue region yields coherent representations across pyramid levels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Current encoders map the same region at different magnifications to poorly aligned features (low cross-scale retrieval), and adding a cheap pyramid-consistency term (same-region different-level tiles as correspondence pairs, freely available from WSI pyramids) improves multiple-instance-learning diagnosis on tasks requiring architecture-plus-cytology integration.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Baseline same-region cross-magnification retrieval will sit below 40% top-1 (versus above 90% within-magnification), and pyramid-consistent pretraining will lift slide-level AUC by at least 2 points on grading tasks while leaving single-scale tasks unchanged; kill the idea if baseline cross-scale retrieval already exceeds 75% or grading gains are under 0.5 points.
why_important: WSI pyramids give correspondence supervision at zero annotation cost; if it fixes a measurable representation defect, every pathology foundation model should adopt it.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-scale MIL architectures exist; a diagnosis-linked audit of cross-magnification feature coherence in current foundation encoders, plus the free-pyramid fix, appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure cross-magnification retrieval of public pathology encoders on registered pyramid tiles, then continue pretraining with a consistency loss and re-evaluate retrieval plus downstream MIL grading.
main_risk: Grading gains may be dominated by MIL aggregation design, drowning the encoder-level improvement.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scale handling is considered the MIL aggregator's job; encoder cross-scale coherence is assumed adequate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Different magnifications genuinely carry different content (cytology vs architecture), so forcing consistency could destroy scale-specific information and hurt.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: PANDA prostate grading slides with UNI or CTransPath encoders; retrieval audit plus a short consistency fine-tune runs in about 30 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$60).

one_line_idea: Archival stain fading makes slide age a decodable covariate in retrospective pathology cohorts, and age-confounded splits inflate reported prognostic performance because outcome follow-up length correlates with slide age.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Eosin and hematoxylin fade over years in storage; retrospective cohorts digitize slides spanning decades, and long-follow-up outcome labels (the most informative ones) come disproportionately from the oldest, most faded slides.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on retrospective cohorts partially decode slide age from fading signatures and exploit the age-outcome correlation as a shortcut, so (a) slide age is regressable from color statistics, and (b) matching color distributions across age strata (fading normalization) will reduce apparent prognostic performance by a measurable amount, exposing the inflated component.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Slide age will be predictable within 5 years MAE from color features on cohorts spanning 15+ years, and fading normalization will drop prognostic AUC by at least 0.02 where age-outcome correlation exists; kill the idea if age MAE exceeds 10 years (no fading signal) or normalized AUC drops under 0.005.
why_important: Retrospective validation is the pathway to clinical claims for pathology AI; an age shortcut would mean some published prognostic signals partly measure storage chemistry.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Stain variation is studied cross-lab; the temporal fading axis within cohorts and its coupling to follow-up length appears unaudited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public cohort with digitization/collection dates, regress slide age from color statistics, quantify age-outcome correlation, and re-evaluate a prognostic model after distribution-matching colors across age strata.
main_risk: Scan date and slide age are often confounded with scanner model; the analysis must condition on scanner metadata.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cohort heterogeneity is handled by staining normalization for lab differences; within-cohort temporal fading is assumed negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern rescan programs may re-stain old blocks rather than scan faded slides, removing the fading signal from public cohorts.

one_line_idea: DAB chromogen deposition in immunohistochemistry is optically nonlinear and non-stoichiometric, so end-to-end learned IHC scorers inherit a saturation bias that a physics-corrected optical-density front end measurably reduces.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] DAB (the brown IHC chromogen) scatters as well as absorbs light and saturates at high antigen density, so pixel intensity is not proportional to protein amount; learned scorers regress clinical scores directly from RGB anyway.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Learned IHC quantifiers systematically compress differences between high-expression cases (saturation regime) and over-weight staining area versus intensity, and inserting a physically motivated DAB transfer-function correction before the network reduces high-end compression, improving agreement with quantitative reference assays on strongly stained cases.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On strongly stained cases, the physics-corrected front end will improve correlation with reference quantification by at least 0.1 (Spearman) over raw-RGB models, with no loss on weakly stained cases; kill the idea if the high-end improvement is under 0.03, implying networks already learn the inverse transfer function.
why_important: IHC scoring gates therapy decisions (e.g., HER2); saturation-regime compression maps directly onto the clinically critical boundary between score categories.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] DAB optics are documented in quantitative pathology, but coupling a transfer-function correction to modern learned scorers with a regime-stratified kill criterion appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using a public IHC dataset with quantitative references or serial-dilution controls, train scorers with and without the physical front end and compare agreement stratified by staining intensity regime.
main_risk: Public IHC datasets with trustworthy quantitative references are scarce; serial-dilution calibration slides may need to be sourced.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] End-to-end learning is assumed to absorb chromogen nonlinearity given enough labels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Clinical scores are ordinal and coarse, so saturation compression may not move cases across score boundaries often enough to matter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: the DeepLIIF public IHC dataset with a ResNet-18 regressor; the comparison runs in about 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$20); quantitative-reference confirmation may need lab collaboration.

one_line_idea: Scanner-to-scanner color shift in pathology is a low-dimensional physical transform (illuminant plus sensor response), estimable from unlabeled tiles without correspondence, and applying the estimated transform recovers most cross-scanner accuracy without retraining.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The same glass slide scanned on two devices yields different colors due to illuminant spectra, filters, and sensor response; deployed models degrade on unseen scanners and current fixes retrain or heavily augment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because the physical chain is approximately a per-channel linear map in optical-density space, the scanner shift is captured by a low-parameter transform (under 12 parameters) that can be estimated by matching stain-vector statistics between unlabeled tile populations, and applying it at inference recovers the majority of the cross-scanner drop for a frozen model.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The estimated low-parameter transform will recover at least 60% of the cross-scanner accuracy drop on average across scanner pairs; kill the idea if recovery is under 25%, which would mean scanner shift is dominated by non-color factors (sharpness, compression) for modern backbones.
why_important: A correspondence-free 12-parameter calibration is deployable in clinical IT within existing validation frameworks, unlike retraining; it also cleanly measures how much of 'scanner shift' is color at all.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Stain normalization is a crowded field; framing scanner shift as an identifiable low-parameter physical transform with a recovery-fraction kill test against non-color residuals appears sharper than existing comparisons.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-scanner benchmark with same-tissue rescans, estimate the transform from unlabeled tiles only, apply at inference to a frozen model, and decompose the remaining gap using sharpness/compression matching.
main_risk: Population differences between the unlabeled tile sets (tissue composition) can bias statistic matching, requiring composition-robust estimators.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scanner robustness is pursued via heavy augmentation or per-site fine-tuning; explicit physical calibration is considered legacy preprocessing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation-scale pathology encoders may already be color-robust, making the recovered fraction small because the drop itself is small.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: MIDOG multi-scanner data with a frozen Phikon or CTransPath encoder; estimation and evaluation run in about 8 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$15).

one_line_idea: Predictions from WSI models are inconsistent across pyramid levels of the same slide, and enforcing cross-level agreement at inference (a free ensemble over the pyramid) improves robustness to scanner sharpness differences.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] WSI formats store precomputed multi-resolution pyramids of identical content; models are typically run at one chosen level, and the choice interacts with scanner sharpness and downsampling filters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-slide predictions vary across adjacent pyramid levels far more than sampling noise would explain, this variance predicts cross-scanner fragility, and averaging or consistency-selecting across levels reduces the cross-scanner drop at zero training cost because pyramid disagreement captures resolution-sensitive feature reliance.

why_important: Every WSI ships with its pyramid; if a free inference-time ensemble buys measurable scanner robustness, it is immediately adoptable in deployed systems awaiting regulatory-friendly, training-free mitigations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Test-time augmentation is common, but exploiting the native pyramid as a physically grounded resolution ensemble with a fragility-prediction link appears unexamined.

main_risk: Some models are strongly level-specialized, so naive averaging could hurt; consistency-weighted combination may be needed.

one_line_idea: OCR and handwriting models increasingly read from language priors instead of pixels as degradation grows, measurable by a matched pseudoword substitution test whose accuracy gap quantifies hallucination risk.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Modern text recognizers embed strong implicit language models; under degradation they output plausible words, and errors are increasingly 'fluent' substitutions rather than character garbles, which is dangerous for names, numbers, and codes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The visual-evidence share of recognition can be isolated by comparing accuracy on real words versus orthographically matched pseudowords rendered/written identically: the word-pseudoword gap grows monotonically with degradation strength and differs sharply across architectures, providing a scalar 'prior dominance index' that predicts hallucinated-content rates on named entities.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The word-vs-pseudoword accuracy gap will at least triple from clean to heavily degraded conditions, and models ranked by this index will rank identically (Spearman rho >= 0.7) on named-entity hallucination rates in a held-out corpus; kill the idea if the gap stays flat with degradation or the index fails to predict entity hallucination (rho < 0.3).
why_important: Archives, banking, and legal pipelines need to know when an OCR output is evidence versus guesswork; a portable index of prior dominance directly supports deployment policy (e.g., route high-index conditions to human review).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Psycholinguistics uses pseudowords routinely; using matched pseudoword rendering as an instrument to decompose OCR into visual versus prior components appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate matched word/pseudoword pairs, render or collect them in identical visual conditions, sweep degradation strength, and measure the accuracy gap per model; validate the index against entity-level hallucination on real degraded documents.
main_risk: Pseudoword handwriting samples are scarce; synthetic rendering covers print OCR well but handwriting requires style-transfer generation with its own artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Language priors in OCR are viewed as purely beneficial; hallucination is treated anecdotally rather than as a measurable, growing function of degradation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Character-level decoders may show negligible word/pseudoword gaps even degraded, making the index trivial for half the model zoo.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: IAM handwriting and rendered corpora with TrOCR and Tesseract; the full sweep runs in about 8 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$15).

one_line_idea: Bleed-through in double-sided historical documents is a mirrored, blurred copy of the verso page, so jointly modeling recto and verso scans inverts it physically and beats single-side restoration for downstream recognition.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Ink from the reverse side shows through aged paper as a mirrored, attenuated, slightly diffused image; archives usually scan both sides, yet restoration methods treat each side independently as generic noise removal.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because the interference source is available (the verso scan predicts the bleed-through pattern up to a mirror transform, per-region attenuation, and a diffusion kernel), a two-input model that explicitly registers and subtracts the transformed verso will remove bleed-through more accurately than any single-image method, with the largest gains where recto and verso strokes overlap.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Joint recto-verso restoration will cut downstream character error rate on bleed-through-affected regions by at least 30% relative to the best single-side baseline, with gains concentrated (at least 2x) in stroke-overlap regions; kill the idea if the relative CER gain is under 10%.
why_important: Millions of archival pages suffer bleed-through; the verso scan is an unused, freely available side channel that turns an ill-posed inpainting problem into a well-posed source-separation problem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Classical recto-verso separation was studied pre-deep-learning on small examples; integrating it with learned registration and evaluating by downstream recognition on public benchmarks appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pair recto/verso scans from public archival collections, train the two-input restoration model against single-side baselines, and evaluate OCR/HTR error on affected regions.
main_risk: Non-rigid paper distortion between the two scans complicates registration; failure of registration silently degrades to the single-side baseline.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Bleed-through is bundled into generic document enhancement, and the verso side is ignored as a modeling input.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Heavy diffusion through thick paper may destroy the geometric correspondence needed for subtraction to beat learned single-side priors.

one_line_idea: Binarization, still the first step of many document pipelines, destroys stroke-interior and grayscale evidence that end-to-end recognizers exploit, and the information loss can be quantified as a degradation-dependent CER penalty law.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Historical document pipelines inherited a binarize-then-recognize structure from the fax era; competitions still optimize binarization quality metrics as if they were proxies for recognition quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The recognition penalty from binarization grows with degradation (faint ink, stains) because grayscale carries the discriminative evidence there, so the penalty curve (CER with binarization minus CER without, as a function of degradation level) rises steeply, and binarization quality metrics fail to predict the penalty across binarization algorithms.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The binarization CER penalty will at least quadruple from clean to degraded strata, and rank correlation between binarization quality metrics and actual downstream CER across algorithms will be under 0.4; kill the idea if the penalty stays under 5% relative everywhere or if quality metrics predict CER at rho >= 0.7, which would validate the legacy pipeline.
why_important: The result would redirect a whole competition ecosystem: if binarization metrics do not predict recognition outcomes, the field is optimizing a proxy detached from its purpose.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] End-to-end superiority is folklore; a pre-registered penalty law across degradation strata plus the metric-decoupling test appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched recognizers on grayscale versus binarized versions of public benchmarks stratified by degradation, sweeping several binarization algorithms, and correlate binarization metrics with downstream CER.
main_risk: Recognizers trained mostly on clean data may underuse grayscale evidence, understating the true information loss.

one_line_idea: Repeated photocopying acts as an iterated contraction on glyph shapes with predictable attractors, so augmenting OCR training with physically iterated copy-degradation beats single-pass noise models for multi-generation documents.

why_important: Multi-generation copies are a large, ignored slice of real-world OCR failure (legal, governmental, archival); the iterated-operator insight is cheap to implement and tests a general principle about compositional degradations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Document degradation models exist, but treating copy iteration as a dynamical system with attractors and testing composition-structure against strength-matched noise appears new.

one_line_idea: Urbanization is nearly irreversible at monitoring timescales, and decoding land-cover time series under a monotonicity constraint removes temporal flicker while leaving accuracy unchanged, exploiting process physics that frame-independent models ignore.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Per-date land-cover maps from independent inference flicker (pixels oscillate urban/non-urban across dates), forcing ad-hoc post-hoc smoothing; urban conversion, however, is a directional process that essentially never reverts within monitoring horizons.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Enforcing class-transition monotonicity (urban absorbing state) as a decoding constraint over the time series will eliminate most flicker and slightly improve per-date accuracy near transition dates, because the constraint is true of the underlying process; the transition-date estimates will also sharpen, measured against high-confidence construction records.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Monotone decoding will cut urban-class temporal flicker (reversal rate) by at least 80% while changing per-date accuracy by no worse than -0.5 points and improving transition-date MAE by at least 20%; kill the idea if accuracy drops more than 1.5 points or transition dating does not improve, meaning flicker was carrying real signal.
why_important: Urban growth statistics drive planning and climate models; flicker forces arbitrary smoothing choices that bias growth-rate estimates, while a process-true constraint is principled and parameter-free.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal smoothing is ubiquitous; framing irreversibility as a decodable absorbing-state constraint with transition-dating validation appears rare in the deep-learning era.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run per-date inference on a public dense-time-series benchmark, apply monotone dynamic-programming decoding on urban classes, and evaluate flicker, per-date accuracy, and transition-date error against labels.
main_risk: Demolition-to-greenfield does occur (rare); the constraint needs an escape probability or it will propagate rare errors forward indefinitely.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Temporal consistency is pursued with generic smoothing or recurrent models, not with process-specific transition structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern temporal architectures may already produce near-monotone outputs, leaving little flicker to remove.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] False-positive void detections cluster at physics-predictable artifact loci, and providing the detector with a simulated artifact-susceptibility map (computed by polychromatic forward projection through the part's CAD or reconstructed geometry) lets it discount artifact-consistent darkness, reducing false calls while preserving true porosity sensitivity.

why_important: False calls drive re-inspection cost in foundries and erode trust in automated CT inspection; a physics side-channel fix requires no new annotation and is auditable by quality engineers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Beam-hardening correction is standard reconstruction practice; feeding residual artifact susceptibility to learned defect detectors appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate polychromatic scans of parts with known void placements, train detectors with and without the susceptibility channel, and evaluate false-call rates at matched sensitivity on held-out geometries.
main_risk: Public industrial CT defect data is scarce; simulation-heavy validation invites the objection that real scanner artifacts differ, requiring at least one physical validation scan.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Artifact handling is assumed to belong entirely to the reconstruction stage, with detection models expected to cope with residuals via data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern iterative reconstruction may suppress artifacts sufficiently that residual false calls stem from other causes (scatter, noise).

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The diagnostic signal lives in the decay dynamics (when and how a region deviates from the intact cooling curve), so sequence models will detect deep defects that are invisible in every individual frame, with the frame-vs-sequence gap growing with defect depth exactly as diffusion physics predicts.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Thermographic signal processing has classical transforms; a controlled frame-vs-sequence learning comparison with depth-resolved physics validation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate heat diffusion over parts with buried defects at controlled depths (finite-difference solver), train frame and sequence detectors, validate the depth law, and confirm on any available real thermography sequences.
main_risk: Simulation-to-real transfer of thermal dynamics depends on material property accuracy; real-sample confirmation needs a flash-thermography rig.

one_line_idea: Monocular depth underwater is not scale-ambiguous the way it is in air: wavelength-dependent attenuation provides an absolute range cue, so a lightweight attenuation-reading head can convert relative depth maps into metric depth without stereo or sonar.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Monocular depth estimation in air recovers only relative depth up to an unknown global scale because pinhole projection is scale-invariant; underwater, per-channel light attenuation ties an object's color shift to its absolute optical path length, and public underwater RGB-D data exists.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A small head on a frozen relative-depth backbone that estimates global metric scale from red-to-green attenuation statistics recovers metric depth without geometric cues, because water itself acts as an absolute rangefinder that air lacks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On held-out FLSea dives, an attenuation-conditioned scale head will cut median absolute metric-depth error to below 60% of the best constant-per-dive scale baseline, with per-scene scale estimates correlating with true scale at Spearman rho >= 0.6; kill the idea if error reduction is under 15%, if rho < 0.3, or if more than 80% of the gain disappears when fit and test dives have different water types.
why_important: Metric monocular depth would let low-cost AUVs and diver cameras do collision avoidance and photogrammetric measurement without stereo rigs or active sonar, exploiting a physical cue that only exists underwater.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Underwater depth work treats attenuation as a nuisance to correct or relies on geometry alone; using attenuation explicitly as the absolute-scale oracle for monocular depth appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a scale head on FLSea training dives using per-image channel-ratio statistics against metric ground truth; evaluate scale-factor recovery and metric error on held-out dives against constant-scale and least-squares oracle-scale baselines.
main_risk: Artificial lighting and albedo variation may confound channel ratios enough that the scale signal is only usable in sunlit shallow water.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners assume metric monocular depth requires known camera height, stereo, or learned scene-size priors, and treat underwater color shift purely as degradation to remove.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scene albedo diversity may make channel-ratio statistics too noisy for per-scene scale estimation, leaving only a weak dataset-average prior that the constant baseline already captures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: FLSea underwater RGB-D sequences with a frozen Depth Anything relative-depth backbone plus a small MLP scale head; fitting and held-out evaluation is under 8 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$12).

why_important: Robust long-term relocalization without per-survey retraining is the bottleneck for repeat-site AUV monitoring missions (vents, reefs, pipelines), and a closed-form photometric fix is deployable on embedded hardware.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Underwater place-recognition studies treat cross-survey degradation as generic appearance change handled by data-hungry domain adaptation; attributing it to a low-parameter physical transform and correcting descriptor inputs in closed form appears untested.

one_line_idea: Species discrimination from fisheries echosounder data improves with added acoustic frequencies according to a saturating law whose per-species-pair knee is predicted by swim-bladder resonance physics, not by generic more-channels-help arguments.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Learned echogram classifiers gain accuracy from an added frequency in proportion to how much that band changes the physics-predicted relative frequency response between the species pair, so gains are pair-specific and predictable from scattering models rather than uniform across bands.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across species pairs, the per-pair accuracy gain from adding a frequency channel will correlate with the scattering-model-predicted response divergence of that pair at that band at Spearman rho >= 0.5; kill the idea if rho < 0.2 or if measured gains are statistically indistinguishable across bands (uniform-gain null holds).
why_important: Surveys could then choose minimal frequency sets per target stock with known discrimination limits, cutting instrument cost and making single-frequency archive reanalysis quantitatively honest about what it cannot distinguish.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multifrequency discrimination is established in fisheries acoustics via hand-built relative-frequency-response rules, but a predictive law connecting scattering physics to learned-classifier marginal gains per band appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a fixed CNN on labeled echogram patches (e.g., sandeel versus mackerel versus 0-group schools) using nested frequency subsets; compare measured per-pair gains against resonance-model-predicted response divergences.
main_risk: School-level labels in public archives are imperfect and species mixtures within schools could blur pair-specific effects.

one_line_idea: Under a shrinking photon budget, microscopy classes fail in an order predicted by the spatial scale and contrast of their diagnostic features (a Rose-criterion ordering), making low-dose robustness a per-class physical quantity rather than a model property.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fluorescence imaging noise is photon-limited (Poisson), dose reduction to limit phototoxicity is routine, and the Rose criterion ties feature detectability to contrast, feature size, and photon count.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] As synthetic dose reduction deepens, per-class accuracy of a fixed classifier collapses in an order determined by each class's diagnostic spatial-frequency content: fine-textured phenotypes collapse first and coarse-morphology phenotypes last, with the ordering stable across architectures because it is set by optics, not by learning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The rank correlation between per-class collapse dose and a physics-derived detectability score (feature scale times contrast, computed from held-out high-dose images) will be >= 0.6, and class orderings will agree across two architectures at Kendall tau >= 0.5; kill the idea if the correlation is < 0.3 or if orderings disagree across architectures (tau < 0.2).
why_important: Imaging scientists could budget light dose per assay from physics alone, predicting which phenotypes remain readable at low phototoxicity without retraining or recollecting data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Low-dose robustness is usually reported as a single dataset-level curve; a per-class collapse-ordering law grounded in the Rose criterion, with architecture-independence as an explicit test, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply calibrated Poisson dose scaling to a public high-SNR phenotype-classification set, train two classifier families, measure per-class collapse doses, and correlate them with detectability scores computed from an independent split.
main_risk: Diagnostic-feature scale must be estimated from data, risking circularity unless the detectability score is computed from splits and channels disjoint from evaluation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats low-dose degradation as a uniform noise-robustness property of the model, to be fixed by denoisers or augmentation, not as a class-structured optical limit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deep classifiers may rely on distributed features whose effective scale differs from the visually diagnostic structures, breaking the physics-derived ordering.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: BBBC021 mechanism-of-action fluorescence images with ResNet-50 and a small ViT; Poisson dose sweeps, two trainings, and evaluation are under 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$15).

one_line_idea: TCGA's paired frozen and FFPE slides of the same tumors are an untapped natural experiment: the frozen-section gap is a task-structured quantity — largest for nuclear-texture-dependent predictions — and predictable per case from an ice-artifact severity score.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Frozen sections suffer ice-crystal formation, compression, and inferior staining compared to FFPE; TCGA publicly provides both frozen and FFPE slides for many of the same cases, and intraoperative AI must run on frozen sections.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For a fixed pathology foundation encoder, within-case cross-preparation disagreement is systematic and task-structured: nuclear-texture-dependent predictions degrade far more than tissue-architecture-dependent predictions on the same paired slides, and per-case degradation scales with a measurable ice-artifact severity score.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Cross-preparation within-case prediction agreement will be at least 15 points lower for a nuclear-texture probe than for a tissue-architecture probe on the same paired cohort, and per-case degradation will correlate with an ice-artifact severity proxy at Spearman rho >= 0.4; kill the idea if the task-structure difference is < 5 points or if rho < 0.15.
why_important: Intraoperative deployment is the highest-stakes pathology AI setting; knowing which task families survive freezing artifacts, and predicting per-slide reliability from artifact severity, determines what is safe to deploy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frozen-vs-FFPE degradation is reported anecdotally as a domain gap; exploiting TCGA's within-case pairing to measure a task-structured gap law with an artifact-severity predictor appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select TCGA cases having both DX (FFPE) and TS/BS (frozen) slides; run a public pathology foundation encoder with linear probes for one texture task and one architecture task; compare within-case agreement and correlate with a lacunae-statistics ice-severity proxy.
main_risk: Frozen and FFPE slides of a case sample different tissue blocks, so genuine spatial heterogeneity contributes to disagreement and must be bounded with within-preparation controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats the frozen-section gap as one scalar domain shift to be closed with style transfer, rather than as a structured, per-task, per-severity quantity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If foundation encoders already abstract away nuclear texture into robust features, both probe families may degrade similarly and the structure disappears.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: TCGA paired FFPE/frozen slides with public CTransPath or UNI encoders and linear probes; probing a few hundred paired slides is under 12 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$18).

one_line_idea: Newsprint halftone screens are periodic and FFT-detectable, so per-page physics-based descreening — notching the measured screen frequency before recognition — beats generic learned denoising for OCR on scanned newspapers at near-zero compute.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Printed photographs and shaded regions in newspapers are halftone screens: periodic dot lattices with a measurable ruling and angle; rescanning aliases these lattices into moire and dot noise that overlaps thin text strokes, and public newspaper scan corpora are enormous.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] OCR errors on scanned newsprint concentrate where halftone spectral energy overlaps stroke frequencies, and a per-page descreen filter built by detecting lattice peaks in the Fourier spectrum and notching them removes this error mass more effectively than blind learned denoisers at matched runtime, because the artifact is exactly periodic.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On halftone-adjacent text lines, FFT-notch descreening will cut character error rate by >= 20% relative to no preprocessing and beat a public blind denoiser at matched runtime by >= 5% relative; kill the idea if the improvement is < 5% relative or if the blind denoiser matches the notch filter within 2% relative.
why_important: Mass digitization projects (national libraries, archives) OCR billions of newspaper pages with fixed pipelines; a closed-form preprocessing gain at CPU cost translates into corpus-scale text-quality improvement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Descreening exists in prepress tooling, but quantifying halftone-caused OCR error concentration and testing physics-notch filtering against learned denoisers for recognition (not visual quality) appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate halftone printing and rescanning on born-digital pages for exact ground truth, plus a spot check on real newspaper scans; classify text lines by halftone proximity; measure CER under no preprocessing, FFT-notch descreening, and a public blind denoiser at matched runtime.
main_risk: Real scans mix multiple degradations (ink spread, yellowing), so the halftone-specific share of errors may be smaller in the wild than in simulation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community default is that generic learned enhancement subsumes any hand-built preprocessing, making physics-specific filters obsolete.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern recognizers may already be robust to periodic dot noise through training-data diversity, leaving little error mass for descreening to recover.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: Library of Congress Chronicling America page scans and halftone-simulated DocBank pages with public Tesseract and TrOCR checkpoints; filtering plus OCR over a few thousand lines is under 4 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$6).

one_line_idea: OCR breakdown under low resolution is governed by x-height in pixels, not DPI, font, or model: character-error curves from different documents and recognizers collapse onto one sampling-limited master curve with a knee near the stroke Nyquist limit.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Text legibility is limited by sampling: strokes narrower than about two pixels cannot be represented without aliasing; document benchmarks confound scan DPI, font size, and content, so reported low-quality robustness mixes these factors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For modern recognizers, character error rate is chiefly a function of physical glyph sampling (x-height in pixels), so curves measured across fonts, documents, and recognizers collapse onto a single master curve whose knee location is set by stroke-width sampling, and benchmark difficulty is largely explained by where items sit on this curve.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across at least five fonts and two recognizers, CER-versus-x-height-in-pixels curves will collapse with inter-condition spread under 30% of the total dynamic range and a knee in the 6-10 pixel x-height band; kill the idea if the spread is >= 60% (no collapse) or if the knee location shifts by more than a factor of two across fonts or models.
why_important: A validated master curve turns 'this scan is too low quality' into a measurable per-item quantity, enabling principled triage of digitization backlogs and honest cross-benchmark difficulty comparison.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Robustness papers sweep noise and blur but conflate resolution with content; an explicit sampling-theory master-curve claim with a collapse test across fonts and recognizers appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render text lines from public-domain books at controlled x-heights with several public fonts; evaluate TrOCR and Tesseract; overlay normalized curves; validate on DocBank pages re-rasterized at controlled scales.
main_risk: Recognizer language priors partially compensate for illegible glyphs, which could flatten the knee differently per model and per text predictability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community reports robustness against DPI or generic 'low quality' labels, implicitly assuming resolution difficulty is model-specific rather than a shared physical curve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Super-resolution-like internal features in large recognizers might break pure sampling determinism, especially for predictable text where priors dominate pixels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: DocBank pages and Project Gutenberg text rendered with public fonts, evaluated with public TrOCR and Tesseract; the full sweep is under 5 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$8).

one_line_idea: Document VQA models often answer forms from layout-template priors instead of reading: swapping a field's printed value in place (font-matched, pixel-consistent) leaves a measurable fraction of answers stuck at the old value, concentrated on frequent templates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Document VQA benchmarks contain recurring form and invoice templates in which answer fields sit at predictable positions with predictable value formats, so a model can score well by mapping question type to field position and emitting a prior-typical token.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A calibrated in-place value-substitution test (rendering a different but format-valid value into the same field with matched font and background) will show that current models frequently return the original or a prior-typical value instead of the printed one, with the failure rate substantially higher on high-frequency templates than on rare layouts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On edited fields where the model was previously correct, at least 20% of answers will fail to flip to the newly printed value for a strong public model, and the flip-failure rate will be at least 2x higher on high-frequency templates; kill the idea if flip-failure is < 8% overall or shows no template-frequency dependence (ratio < 1.2x).
why_important: Production document AI reads values that change across document versions; a model answering from template priors silently returns stale values — an unmonitored, high-cost failure class that benchmark accuracy cannot see.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Perturbation audits exist for natural-image VQA, but a pixel-consistent in-place value-substitution protocol measuring reading fidelity versus template priors on document VQA appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Auto-render font-matched substitutions on a few hundred DocVQA/FUNSD fields (estimate font and background locally), rerun public Donut and LayoutLMv3 pipelines, and measure answer-flip rates stratified by template frequency.
main_risk: Imperfect font matching introduces edit artifacts that models might detect, confounding 'did not read' with 'read the artifact'; an artifact-only control edit is required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats DocVQA accuracy as evidence of reading ability, assuming positional priors are a minor contributor for state-of-the-art models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: End-to-end models with strong OCR backbones may genuinely read edited values, yielding flip-failure rates below the kill threshold — which would itself be a useful negative result.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: DocVQA and FUNSD with public Donut and LayoutLMv3 checkpoints; editing and re-inference over about 1k fields is under 4 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$6).

one_line_idea: Professionally typeset pages sit on a hidden baseline grid; estimating the grid from projection-profile autocorrelation and snapping line hypotheses to it removes the merge/split errors that dominate dense-layout parsing, with no learning required.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Typesetting systems place text on regular baseline grids (near-constant leading within blocks); line-detection errors on dense multi-column pages are dominated by merged adjacent lines and split tall glyphs, and the grid period is recoverable from autocorrelation of horizontal projection profiles.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A post-processing layer that estimates per-block baseline period and phase, then vetoes line hypotheses inconsistent with the grid (merges spanning two periods, splits at off-grid positions), removes a large share of line-level errors of any underlying detector, with gains concentrated on dense layouts and vanishing on sparse ones — a mechanism-specificity signature.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Grid snapping will remove >= 40% of merge/split line errors on dense pages (newspapers, two-column academic) while altering < 2% of correct detections, and gains will shrink toward zero on sparse layouts; kill the idea if merge/split removal is < 15% or if correct-detection damage exceeds 5%.
why_important: Line-level structure errors propagate into reading order, table extraction, and LLM document ingestion; a deterministic typographic constraint that fixes them costs nothing at inference and stacks with any detector.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Layout post-processing is usually learned or heuristic per system; an explicit baseline-grid estimator with a snap-and-veto rule evaluated by error-class accounting appears untested on modern benchmarks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a public layout model's line outputs on DocLayNet and PubLayNet dense categories; implement autocorrelation grid estimation and snapping; count per-error-class changes (merges, splits, correct-detection damage) by layout density.
main_risk: Pages mixing multiple leading values within a block (footnotes, display math) can defeat a single-period grid model and require piecewise estimation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community default is that better detectors and more training data are the path to fixing line errors, treating typography as latent structure the network should learn implicitly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern detectors may already internalize grid regularity, leaving too few grid-inconsistent errors for the post-processor to matter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: DocLayNet and PubLayNet with a public DiT or Faster R-CNN layout checkpoint; post-processing and error accounting are under 3 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$5).

one_line_idea: Cross-dataset transfer in layout analysis is predicted by a computable layout-grammar distance (region-type transition and geometry statistics), not by visual similarity: transfer drops fall on one curve against grammar distance across dataset pairs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Layout models transfer poorly across document collections; public datasets (scientific articles, corporate/legal documents, magazines, forms) differ in structural conventions, and region-type sequences plus geometry statistics are computable from annotations alone without images.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pairwise transfer degradation between layout datasets is largely explained by divergence in layout-grammar statistics (region-type transition matrices, column-count distributions, region position/aspect statistics), and visual-domain distance adds little predictive power once grammar distance is controlled.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across at least 12 ordered train-test dataset pairs, transfer F1 drop will correlate with grammar divergence at Spearman rho >= 0.6 and will outpredict an image-level visual distance (e.g., FID between page renders) by a rho margin >= 0.2; kill the idea if rho < 0.3 or if visual distance predicts transfer equally well.
why_important: A validated grammar-distance law lets teams predict where a deployed layout model will fail and choose source datasets by structural coverage instead of visual similarity folklore.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Transfer studies in document AI report pairwise numbers; an explicit predictive law from annotation-only grammar statistics, with a visual-distance control, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train one architecture on each of four public layout datasets; evaluate all ordered pairs; compute grammar divergences from annotations and FID from page images; compare rank correlations against transfer drops.
main_risk: Label-taxonomy mismatches across datasets require careful class mapping, and residual mapping error could masquerade as grammar distance.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners attribute cross-collection failure to visual domain shift (scan quality, fonts, color) and expect image-space adaptation to fix it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grammar and visual distances are correlated across real collections, so disentangling them may need matched-visual synthetic controls that weaken external validity.

one_line_idea: Born-digital PDFs carry exact vector primitives (rules, paths, glyph boxes) that pixel-based table models throw away by re-rasterizing; a primitive-aware input stream recovers borderless and hairline-ruled structure that no practical raster resolution restores.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Most production documents are born-digital PDFs whose drawing commands specify rules, cell borders, and glyph placements exactly; standard document AI rasterizes pages and re-detects that structure from pixels, where hairline rules alias or vanish at common working resolutions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Feeding parsed vector primitives (line segments, glyph bounding boxes) as an auxiliary input stream to a table-structure model improves structure accuracy specifically on thin-ruled and borderless tables, and the gain cannot be matched by raising raster resolution at equal or greater compute — because the information is lost to sampling, not to model capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On rule-weight-stratified PubTables-1M subsets, a primitive-augmented model will improve structure TEDS by >= 4 points on hairline and borderless strata while a 2x-resolution pixel-only model gains <= 2 points at higher compute; kill the idea if primitive gains are < 1.5 points or if the resolution increase matches them at comparable cost.
why_important: Enterprise document extraction overwhelmingly processes born-digital PDFs; exploiting the native vector substrate is a free accuracy and compute win that current raster-first pipelines structurally forgo.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hybrid text+layout models use OCR tokens, but injecting the drawing-command geometry itself (rules and paths) as a first-class model input with a sampling-theory framing appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract vector primitives from PubTables-1M source PDFs; add a primitive-token stream to Table Transformer; train on a subset and compare against pixel-only models at 1x and 2x raster resolution with matched compute accounting.
main_risk: PDF generators vary wildly in how they encode rules (strokes, filled rects, images), so the primitive parser needs normalization that could leak engineering effort into the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community default is that scaling image resolution and model capacity subsumes structured inputs, so raster-only pipelines are considered asymptotically sufficient.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For most real tables, whitespace and text alignment may carry enough structure that primitives add little beyond the hairline edge cases.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: PubTables-1M (built from PDFs with word and structure annotations) with the public Table Transformer (TATR); primitive extraction plus one subset training is under 16 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$24).

one_line_idea: Homogeneous industrial surfaces are stationary random textures, so spectral whitening — flattening the normal class's estimated power spectrum — is the physically matched preprocessing for texture anomaly detection, lifting patch-based detectors selectively on texture categories.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many inspected surfaces (fabric, carpet, wood, leather, foam) are approximately stationary random fields; anomalies are local violations of stationarity, and patch-embedding anomaly detectors compare features whose statistics are dominated by the texture's autocorrelation structure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Whitening images with a filter derived from the normal class's average power spectrum amplifies statistical deviations relative to background and improves anomaly scoring on stationary-texture categories while leaving object categories unchanged or slightly degraded — a category-selective gain predicted by the stationarity assumption itself.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Spectral whitening will raise image-level AUROC on MVTec AD texture categories by >= 1.5 points mean for PatchCore and PaDiM while changing object categories by within +-0.5 points, and per-category gains will correlate with a measured stationarity index at Spearman rho >= 0.5; kill the idea if the mean texture gain is < 0.5 points or if gains show no stationarity correlation (rho < 0.2).
why_important: A closed-form preprocessing step that provably targets texture categories closes part of the texture-object performance split on industrial benchmarks and costs microseconds per image in deployment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Whitening is classical signal processing, but deriving it from the nominal class spectrum as an anomaly-detection preprocessing with a stationarity-selectivity prediction appears untested on modern benchmarks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate per-category normal power spectra, build whitening filters, rerun PatchCore and PaDiM through anomalib, compute per-category stationarity indices, and test the gain-selectivity correlation.
main_risk: ImageNet-pretrained backbones may internally decorrelate textures already, absorbing the whitening effect into a null result.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats preprocessing as obsolete for deep anomaly detection, expecting backbones and memory banks to handle texture statistics implicitly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Whitening also amplifies sensor noise, which could raise false-positive scores on high-ISO captures and cancel the theoretical gain.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: MVTec AD and VisA with public PatchCore and PaDiM implementations from anomalib; the full sweep is under 6 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$9).

one_line_idea: Speckle is temporally uncorrelated while the scene persists, so temporal multilooking of Sentinel-1 stacks is the physically matched denoiser for SAR crop classification — beating stronger spatial despeckling at equal compute and following the predicted inverse-square-root variance law.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SAR speckle is multiplicative interference, uncorrelated between repeat passes over stable surfaces, while spatial despeckling trades resolution for variance; Sentinel-1 provides free regular revisits and public parcel-labeled crop datasets with radar time series exist.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For parcel-level crop classification, averaging k co-registered acquisitions (temporal multilook) yields more accuracy per unit compute than spatial filtering or learned per-date despecklers, with marginal gains tracking the 1/sqrt(k) speckle-variance law until scene change breaks temporal stationarity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Accuracy versus k for temporal multilooking will exceed spatial-filter and learned-despeckler baselines at matched effective looks by >= 2 points parcel accuracy for k in [2, 8], and marginal gains will fit a power law with exponent in [-0.7, -0.3]; kill the idea if temporal multilook fails to beat the spatial baselines anywhere in that range or if the fitted exponent falls outside [-1.2, -0.1].
why_important: Operational crop monitoring runs on free SAR exactly where clouds block optical sensing; knowing that cheap temporal averaging dominates expensive learned despecklers changes preprocessing standards at continental scale.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal multilooking is known in SAR engineering, but a compute-matched head-to-head against learned despecklers for downstream classification, with the variance-law fit as a mechanism check, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On PASTIS-R Sentinel-1 stacks, build inputs with varying temporal-look counts versus spatially despeckled and SAR2SAR-denoised per-date inputs; train a fixed classifier per condition and compare accuracy at matched compute.
main_risk: Rapid crop growth between acquisitions violates stationarity, so the optimal look count may be short and phenology-dependent, complicating the clean law.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community default is that learned despecklers are the modern replacement for multilooking, and that preprocessing choices wash out after deep training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporal averaging may destroy short-lived phenological signals that the classifier needs, so accuracy could peak below the noise-optimal look count.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: PASTIS-R with the public U-TAE implementation and public SAR2SAR as the learned-despeckler baseline; the sweep is under 12 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$18).

one_line_idea: Tide height at acquisition time is exactly computable from harmonic models, yet coastal change detection treats intertidal exposure as scene change; tide-stage-aware pairing or conditioning removes a dominant class of false coastal 'changes' at zero labeling cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Intertidal zones flood and expose on tidal cycles; satellites sample quasi-random tidal stages; tide height at any coastal location and time is predictable from public harmonic tide models, and public optical archives densely cover coastlines.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large share of detected coastline and coastal-change events between image pairs is explained by tidal-stage difference alone, so matching pairs by tidal stage or feeding predicted tide height as a conditioning input removes most of these false events while preserving sensitivity to genuine change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On stable coastal strips, flagged-change area will increase monotonically with absolute tide-height difference (Spearman rho >= 0.6), and tide-stage matching or conditioning will cut the false change-event rate by >= 50% at unchanged recall on injected genuine changes; kill the idea if flagged change is tide-insensitive (rho < 0.2) or if false-event reduction is < 15%.
why_important: Coastal monitoring (erosion, construction, aquaculture) is a major operational use of free satellite imagery, and a deterministic astronomical covariate that halves false alarms costs nothing to compute.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Tide correction is standard in shoreline-mapping products, but quantifying the tide-attributable share of learned change-detector false events and fixing it by conditioning appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble same-location image pairs over stable coasts spanning a range of predicted tide differences; run a public Siamese change detector; regress flagged-change area on tide delta; then fine-tune with tide-difference conditioning or tide-matched pairing and re-measure false events against injected true changes.
main_risk: Wave setup, wind-driven surge, and seasonal beach profiles deviate from harmonic predictions, capping the share of variance that predicted tide explains.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats coastal false changes as generic noise to be handled by more training data, not as a deterministic, exactly predictable astronomical covariate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In micro-tidal seas the tide-attributable share may be too small to matter, restricting the fix to macro-tidal coasts.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: Sentinel-2 coastal imagery with NOAA/FES-style public harmonic tide predictions and a public Siamese change-detection model (e.g., BIT pretrained on LEVIR-CD); evaluation plus light fine-tuning is under 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$15).

one_line_idea: UAV crop-monitoring orthomosaics carry a BRDF hotspot artifact: view-sun geometry varies across flight lines, imprinting periodic stripes into model predictions that follow solar geometry rather than the field — a quantifiable, correctable bias in precision-agriculture maps.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vegetation reflectance is strongly directional (BRDF), peaking near the hotspot where view and sun directions coincide; UAV orthomosaics stitch images taken at systematically varying view angles along parallel flight lines, so apparent canopy brightness varies within a single mosaic in a geometry-determined pattern.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models applied to UAV orthomosaics inherit flight-line-periodic prediction artifacts: predicted stress/weed/anomaly fractions oscillate at the flight-line spatial frequency in excess of any periodicity present in the labels, and the stripe phase aligns with the mosaic's view-sun geometry rather than with agronomic ground truth.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Spectral analysis of predicted class-fraction maps along the across-track direction will show a peak at the flight-line frequency with amplitude >= 2x the same statistic computed on ground-truth labels for a majority of evaluated fields, and stripe phase will align with the view-geometry pattern above chance; kill the idea if predicted stripe amplitude is <= 1.2x label amplitude or if phase alignment is at chance.
why_important: Variable-rate application decisions are made directly from these maps, so geometry-induced stripes translate into misapplied fertilizer and herbicide; once measured, the artifact is deterministically correctable from flight and solar geometry.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] BRDF effects are established in satellite radiometry, but quantifying hotspot-induced striping in learned UAV prediction maps — and separating it from label periodicity — appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run public segmentation baselines on public UAV/aerial agriculture datasets; compute across-track spatial spectra of predictions and labels; estimate flight-line direction from mosaic seams or metadata; test amplitude excess and phase alignment.
main_risk: Agronomic practices (drill rows, tramlines, sprayer tracks) are also periodic and must be separated from flight-line frequency by orientation and period, or the audit conflates management patterns with optics.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners treat orthomosaics as radiometrically uniform maps and attribute within-field prediction patterns to real agronomic variation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mosaic blending and vignetting correction in modern photogrammetry pipelines may already suppress hotspot contrast below detectability.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: WeedMap multispectral UAV orthomosaics and Agriculture-Vision aerial field imagery with a public U-Net/DeepLabv3+ baseline; inference plus spectral analysis is under 4 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$6).

one_line_idea: Cross-site failure in wheat-head detection is substantially a physical sampling mismatch: deterministic ground-sample-distance standardization closes a large share of the domain gap that heavy scale augmentation fails to close, and the residual correlates with non-scale factors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The Global Wheat Head Detection benchmark spans dozens of acquisition sites with different sensors and flight heights, hence different ground-sample distances; cross-site performance drop is the benchmark's central difficulty, and physical scale is a controllable variable given metadata or object-size statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of the cross-site AP drop is attributable to GSD mismatch rather than to agronomic or illumination differences, so deterministic standardization (resampling every site to a fixed centimeters-per-pixel, with per-site scale from metadata or median head size) recovers much of the gap, and per-site recovery scales with that site's GSD deviation from the training distribution.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] GSD standardization will close >= 35% of the mean cross-site AP drop for a fixed detector while random-scale augmentation at equal budget closes <= 20%, and per-site recovery will correlate with per-site GSD deviation at Spearman rho >= 0.5; kill the idea if standardization closes < 10% of the gap or fails to beat scale augmentation.
why_important: It would show that cheap deterministic physics beats expensive learned invariance on a flagship agricultural benchmark, and the recipe generalizes to any aerial task where metric scale is recoverable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale augmentation is the default remedy for size variation; an explicit attribution of the GWHD domain gap to GSD, with deterministic standardization as the intervention and a residual-factor analysis, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a detector on GWHD source domains; evaluate held-out sites raw versus GSD-standardized; compare against a scale-jitter-augmented model at equal budget; correlate per-site recovery with GSD deviation.
main_risk: Per-site GSD metadata is incomplete, so scale must partly be estimated from head-size statistics, which assumes head sizes are comparable across genotypes and stages.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community default is that domain gaps in agricultural imagery are dominated by biology and illumination, requiring learned domain adaptation rather than deterministic resampling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Wheat-head physical size genuinely varies across genotypes and growth stages, so size normalization could remove real signal along with the sampling artifact.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: Global Wheat Head Detection 2021 with a YOLOv8 detector; two trainings plus cross-site evaluations are under 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$15).
